 29. As long as the FRICTION parameter is not FIXED or LOCK, the contact may slip accord-
     ing to the load and frictional coefficients. Usually this also means that the solution heavily
     depends on the history of all loads, e.g. whether a press-fit condition is applied before a
     torque or after - doing this simultaneously in one load step is not(!) appropriate.
     Therefore a load history has to be defined using $NLLOAD as soon as friction with fric-
     tional coefficients 0.0 < µ < ∞ (≡ FIXED or LOCK) are taken into account.

 30. Since the contact analysis used is a pure static procedure, sliding friction cannot be han-
     dled exactly but only in an approximative manner. To that end, coefficients for sliding
     (Coulomb) friction may be input, which must be less or equal to the corresponding coef-
     ficients for static friction. Definition of sliding friction without definition of static friction is
     not possible.

 31. If only static friction coefficients µ0 (and optionally µ0z ) are specified, the same value is
     used for the sliding friction coefficient, i.e. µ1 = µ0 (and optionally µ1z = µ0z ).

 32. Anisotropic friction coefficients can be defined if both tangential directions are treated
     with friction and FRICTION = COULOMB,COULOMB or FRICTION = USER,USER is
     specified (mixing COULOMB and USER option is not supported). If in this cases µ0z is
     not given then µ0 is used for both directions, i.e. isotropic static coefficients are applied
     (note that still µ1z defaults to µ0z , not µ1 ).

 33. For anisotropic treatment of frictional directions (remark 5) or anisotropic frictional co-
     efficients (remark 32) both tangential DOFs must be present and must have a unique


V 19.00.287                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                               3-577
   corresponding function value, i.e.

                                           µ1 ′ = µ1 ∗ fun(x)

   The referred function may depend on the position in space, prescribed slip velocity (given
   by $VELOSTATE) or topological information, i.e. the following arguments are available:

                  f argµ   f argµ -Alias   Description
           xn        X          R          1st coordinate of point with respect to f rsysµ
           yn        Y         PHI*        2nd coordinate of point with respect to f rsysµ
           zn        Z       THETA*        3rd coordinate of point with respect to f rsysµ
          nid      NID        NODE         Node identifier (as floating point number)
           µ0      MU0        MUE0         Static frictional coefficient from data line
           µ1      MU1        MUE1         Basic sliding frictional coefficient from data line
         ṽstat    DVS      DVSTATE        Prescribed gap velocity state ($VELOSTATE)

   If no argument is selected (i.e. if no f argµ is given), then the 3 coordinates (xn , yn , zn )
   are passed to the function.

5. If one special argument is selected via f argµ then only that variable is passed as inde-
   pendent variable to the load function. This is usefull to pass other arguments than just
   xn to load functions with one independent variable only, e.g. f argµ = z for sin(zn ). If
   f argµ is a text string with a comma separated list of arguments then only these argu-
   ments are passed to the load function (in given sequence), e.g. f argµ = ’z,dvs,nid’ or
   f argµ = ’(z,dvs,nid)’.
   For non-cartesian reference systems the alternative f argµ symbols R, PHI and THETA
   may be used for the 1st, 2nd and 3rd coordinate, respectively.

6. For FRICTION = USER slipping forces are calculated by calling the user supplied sub-
   routine USER_FSLIP, see section 4.1.7 of PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU) for details.

7. If FRICTION = FIXED is specified, then for a closed contact the tangential DOF of the
   contact nodes is connected, corresponding to an infinite value for the static friction coef-
   ficient. Nevertheless, in case of an initially open gap, a free tangential movement may
   occur before the contact is active and tangentially fixed. Therefore FRICTION = FIXED is
   not identical to FRICTION = LOCK (see remark 39).

8. FRICTION = LOCK_IF_ACTIVE or LOCK_IF_STICK freezes the tangential offset of a
   preceding load step at all contact pairs which were closed respectively closed and stick
   at the preceding load step. For the frictional directions which are not locked, the frictional
   behavior is determined by the remaining contact loads given at the current load step. That



ote that PHI and THETA are swapped for spherical f rsysµ with $RSYS SPHERE.




78                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                             V 19.00.287
     For a static analysis with independent load patterns and without load history this is use-
     less and thus not allowed.

 39. FRICTION = LOCK freezes the tangential offset of a preceding load step for active and
     passive contact pairs, just like the corresponding NORMAL = LOCK does for the normal
     direction (see remark 24). This is often used in combination with NORMAL = FORCE
     to inhibit tangential movement during a pretension phase, or with NORMAL = LOCK in
     order to completely freeze all relative movements between two contact partners (e.g. for
     welding of a pre-deformed structure).

    1002 -0.01

  $CONTACT LOAD LPAT = 102 GAPWIDTH = ABS FRICTION = COULOMB,COULOMB

    RIGHT_END 0.5 : 0.25, 0.23

  $CONTACT LOAD LPAT = 104 GAPWIDTH = ADD FRICTION = LOCK,COULOMB
    1002      0.0 : 0.03 : 0.02
    LEFT_END 0.5 : 0.15
!

  $CONTACT LOAD LPAT = 106 GAPWIDTH = ADD FRICTION = FREE,LOCK_IF_ACTIVE
    1002 0.0

  $CONTACT LOAD GAPWIDTH = ADD LPAT = 2
    SHAFT_HUB 1.0,17,phi,100

    SHAFT_HUB LEFT : -0.1,19,z,101 ! function 19 in left pointing cyl. rsys
    SHAFT_HUB MID    : -0.1           ! constant overlap in the middle
    SHAFT_HUB RIGHT : -0.1,19,z,102 ! function 19 in right pointing cyl.rsys
!

marks:

1. Distributed loads given within data block $DISLOAD are specified at element nodes for
   elements or element sets. Which element nodes can be loaded depends on element type
   and load type, see element description.
2. For one element, one load pattern and one load type loadtype only one distributed load
   definition by $DISLOAD, $DISLOADF, $DISLOADN, $DISLOADR or $DISLOADS is pos-
   sible.
3. If NODES = LIST is specified, for all loaded nodal points one load value (e.g. pressure)
   or the components of the load vector (e.g. three components for 3D volume loads) have
   to be given. For NODES = ALL only one load value or one load vector, respectively, must
   to be given.
4. Depending on element type, identification of the loaded edge for line loads or the loaded
   face for surface loads may be necessary. This can be done by a list of node identifiers
   (element node identifiers or corresponding external node identifiers) or by a face or edge
   identifier.
5. If a list of node identifiers is given on the data line, the sequence of load data (scalars
   or vectors) is determined explicitly by this node sequence. However, if NODES = ALL (or
   NODES = AUTO with 1 load value or load vector only) is given and the list of nodes are
   used to identify a face or edge (according to element and load type) then all nodes of that
   face / edge will get the same load value (not only the possibly fewer nodes used to identify
   the face / edge).
6. If the sequence of load data is not defined explicitly (i.e. no node list on data line,
   face / edge identification not required or done by face / edge identifier) then the following
   rules for the load data sequence are valid:


82                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           V 19.00.287
     The sequence of corner nodes or element nodes, respectively, is defined in the element
     description. If NODES = ALL is specified (or NODES = AUTO with 1 load value only) all
     corresponding nodes get the same load data.

  7. If no function identifier is specified, load value is given by l = l0 .

  8. Each load value may depend on the position in space, its factor l0 and topological infor-
     mation. If for a load value a tuple l0 , fun is input, the actual load value is calculated as a
     product of basic value l0 and the value of the function fun (Label (integer, name or text
     string)) according to




                                                                                                       Loading
                                               l = l0 ∗ fun(x)




                                                                                                         DAT
     where x is a vector of up to seven independent variables defined in the following table:


                             x(1)    xn         x-coordinate of loaded point
                             x(2)    yn         y-coordinate of loaded point
                             x(3)    zn         z-coordinate of loaded point
                             x(4)    l0         basic load value
                             x(5)    eid        element identifier
                             x(6)    nid        node identifier
                             x(7)    idcomp     load component identifier

     xn , yn , zn are the cartesian coordinates of node nid referring to component system. If
     the load values are not defined at element nodes but for the whole element (e.g. beam
     initial strains), then nid is equal zero and xn , yn , zn contains the mean value of the node
     coordinates of the element.

  9. The load value function can be defined as general function with up to seven independent
     variables, see $FUNCTION. $FUNCTION SUM or $FUNCTION CHAIN may be used to
     assemble functions with an arbitrary number of variables.
     For the meaning of the independent variables see remark 8 above. Node identifier nid,
     element identifier eid and load component identifier idcomp are transferred as real values.

 10. If the load value function is defined with k < 7 independent variables, only the variables
     up to x(k) are available in the function.

 11. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all load values l0 of current data block
     are multiplied by the given value f actor.

                               For functional dependency of load values see remark 6.


Remarks:

   1. Line heat sources for shells are available for shell and shell surface convection elements.
      One data line defines the line loads at upper and lower surface for one element edge.
      Load values are specified at the end nodes of the loaded edge.

   2. Edge identification by edge identifier or node list is always mandatory. For details see
      element description.


V 19.00.287                           PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                3-605
   element normal of the underlying shell element, not by the orientation of the shell surface
   convection element.

5. Line heat sources refer to the actual length of element or element edge, not to projected
   length.

6. Each load value qLu etc. may be replaced by a tuple qL,0 , fun where qL,0 is the basic load
   value and fun the label of a space-dependent function, see remark 8 ff. on page 3-583.
   The actual load value is then given by

                                       qL = qL,0 ∗ fun(x)

7. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all heat source values of current data
   block are multiplied by the given value f actor.

  CONS_SET 2 : 0.0 24.5,101      0.0 25.5,101

Data lines:

             (          )          (               )
                 eid           h          f cid            i       h        i∗
                                                       :       p       pi
                 eset                  list(nid)



Item(s)         Type        Explanation

eid           I>0           Element identifier.
eset        name/text       Element set name.
f cid         I>0           Face identifier.
list(nid)     I>0           List of nodal point identifiers.
p              R            Pressure value (force / area), one value per node.
                            For functional dependency of load values see remark 7.


Remarks:

   1. Pressure loads are available for surfaces of membrane, solid, shell, load carrying mem-
      brane, gasket, axisymmetric membrane and axisymmetric solid elements. One data line
      defines the pressure load for one element surface. Load values are specified at the cor-
      ner nodes of the loaded surface. For details see element description.
      Furthermore, internal pressure is available for fluid filled pipe elements FSCPIPE2, where
      one data line defines the pressure load for one element, and load values are specified at
      element end nodes.

   2. Surface identification by face identifier or node list is always mandatory for solid elements.



V 19.00.287                        PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      3-611
   element normal.

5. For solid elements positive pressure acts in the direction of negative face normal. If the
   node sequence in the element definition coincide with the regular sequence in the element
   description then positive pressure acts always towards the interior of solid elements.

6. For fluid filled pipes positive pressure values mean internal pressure higher than external
   (reference) pressure.

7. Each load value p may be replaced by a tuple p0 , fun where p0 is the basic load value and
   fun the label of a space-dependent function, see remark 8 ff. on page 3-583. The actual
   load value is then given by
                                       p = p0 ∗ fun(x)

8. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all pressure values of current data
   block are multiplied by the given value f actor.

ample:

$DISLOAD PRESS     LPAT = 45    NODES = ALL                      ! constant pressure
  PLATE 10.0

$DISLOAD PRESS LPAT = 1        IDS = ELNODES                     ! variable pressure
  2001 1 2 3 4 : 1.1           1.2 1.2 1.1

$DISLOAD PRESS LPAT = 6 IDS = NODES NODES = ALL                  ! external node ids
  2005 110 111 121 120 : 1.5E06,2001                             ! functional dependency

$DISLOAD PRESS LPAT = 4        IDS = ELGEO    FACTOR = 2.5       ! variable pressure
  286436 2 : -1.5 -1.6         -1.4                              ! on face 2 of TET4

ase refer to examples CA2, MNL3, DEV5 and FS3 of [um550].

                                                                                                   DAT
Data lines:

             (           )
                  eid           h                   i           h        i∗
                                    list(nid)   :           T       Ti
                  eset




Item(s)          Type        Explanation

eid           I>0            Element identifier.
eset        name/text        Element set name.
list(nid)     I>0            List of nodal point identifiers.
T              R             Node temperature.
                             For functional dependency of load values see remark 6.


Remarks:

   1. Node temperatures leading to initial strains due to thermal expansion are available for
      flange, membrane, solid, beam, shell, load carrying membrane, gasket and all axisym-
      metric elements and are specified at all element nodes. For details see element descrip-
      tion.

   2. See remarks on page 3-582 for the rules of specification for list(nid) and NODES = ALL.

   3. Initial strains due to temperature are calculated according to following:
      For constant thermal expansion coefficients:

                                                        εϑ = α (T − T0 )



V 19.00.287                         PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)               3-659
   with


          εϑ       Vector of thermal strains.
          α        Constant thermal expansion coefficient.
          α (T )   Total temperature-dependent thermal expansion coefficient from
                   reference temperature Tref to actual temperature T .
          T        Actual temperature.
          T0       Corresponding element reference temperature.
          Tref     Expansion coefficient reference temperature.

4. The corresponding element reference temperature T0 is the temperature at which ther-
   mal expansion of the element is zero, and may be defined for each element and each
   load pattern by data blocks $REFVAL TEMP, see page 3-872. If not defined, the com-
   ponent reference temperature for thermal expansion is used as default, see parameter
   REFTEMP within data block $PARAMETER, page 3-852.

5. Since initial strains are calculated from the temperature difference T − T0 , input of zero
   temperatures will lead to initial strains if the corresponding element reference temperature
   T0 is not equal zero as well.

6. Each load value T may be replaced by a tuple T0 , fun where T0 is the basic load value
   and fun the label of a space-dependent function, see remark 8 ff. on page 3-583. The
   actual load value is then given by

                                        T = T0 ∗ fun(x)

7. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all temperature values of current data
   block are multiplied by the given value f actor.

ample:

! constant and variable load on two element sets
$DISLOAD TEMP LPAT = 101 NODES = ALL
  HEXE_SET 45.9                                 ! constant
  PENT_SET 45.9,822                             ! variable (function 822)

! variable load on PENTA6, external node ids
$DISLOAD TEMP LPAT = 201 IDS = NODES
  20645 301    302   303   403   402   501 :
 &       25.0 26.1 27.3 26.8 26.7 30.9

ase refer to examples LS1 and MNL2 of [um550].

Data lines:

                   (           )
                        eid         h                   i                           h                              i∗
                                        list(nid)   :           T   Tx′ ′   Ty′ ′       Ti   Tx′ ′ ,i   Ty′ ′ ,i
                        eset




 Item(s)                Type       Explanation

eid                  I>0           Element identifier.
eset               name/text       Element set name.
list(nid)            I>0           List of nodal point identifiers.
T, Tx′ ′ , Ty′ ′      R            Temperature and temperature gradients with respect to local x′ - and y ′ -
                                   axis, three values per node.
                                   For functional dependency of load values see remark 6.


Remarks:

    1. Node temperatures and temperature gradients leading to initial strains due to thermal
       expansion are available only for beam elements and are specified at all element nodes.
       For details see element description.

    2. See remarks on page 3-582 for the rules of specification for list(nid) and NODES = ALL.

    3. Initial strains due to temperature are calculated according to following:
       For constant thermal expansion coefficients:

                                                            εϑ = α (T − T0 )



V 19.00.287                             PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                            3-667
   with


          εϑ       Vector of thermal strains.
          α        Constant thermal expansion coefficient.
          α (T )   Total temperature-dependent thermal expansion coefficient from
                   reference temperature Tref to actual temperature T .
          T        Actual temperature.
          T0       Corresponding element reference temperature.
          Tref     Expansion coefficient reference temperature.

   From initial strains εϑ the initial deformations of beam elements are derived.

4. The corresponding element reference temperature T0 is the temperature at which ther-
   mal expansion of the element is zero, and may be defined for each element and each
   load pattern by data blocks $REFVAL TEMP, see page 3-872. If not defined, the com-
   ponent reference temperature for thermal expansion is used as default, see parameter
   REFTEMP within data block $PARAMETER, page 3-852.

5. Since initial strains are calculated from the temperature difference T − T0 , input of zero
   temperatures will lead to initial strains if the corresponding element reference temperature
   T0 is not equal zero as well.

6. Each load value T etc. may be replaced by a tuple T0 , fun where T0 is the basic load
   value and fun the label of a space-dependent function, see remark 8 ff. on page 3-583.
   The actual load value is then given by

                                        T = T0 ∗ fun(x)

7. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all temperature values of current data
   block are multiplied by the given value f actor.

ample:

! constant load
$DISLOAD TEMPGRAD      LPAT = 101    NODES = ALL
  BSET 20.0 0.2        0.5

! variable load,
! nodes specified with external ids
$DISLOAD TEMPGRAD LPAT = 101 IDS = NODES
  4011 101 201 : 20.0 0.2 0.0       25.0 0.25             0.0

nid          I>0           Nodal point identifier.
nset       name/text       Node set name.
fun          I>0           Label (integer, name or text string) of function.
            name/text
rsys ′       I≥0           Reference system for coordinates the function refers to.
            name/text



V 19.00.287                       PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        3-689
                      Default: MODE = INTPOL.
max      R ≥ 0.0      Maximum distance from boundary for value assignment, see remark 6.


marks:

1. Distributed loads defined within data block $DISLOADF are calculated by evaluation of a
   general function, see $FUNCTION. Each element connected to a loaded node and able
   to carry that loadtype is loaded. Which elements can be loaded depends on element type
   and load type, see element description. The load distribution is available for postprocess-
   ing by UCI command DEFAULT SET VERIFICATION = MODEL (refer to chapter 6.1.2 for
   further information).

2. The load values are calculated by reference to a general function which defines values
   in space or on a local x′ y ′ -plane referring to coordinates in a local x′ -space. The local
   reference system x′ must be a cartesian one, and must always be specified by parameter
   CSYS on data line.
   Hence a function f (x′ ) will create loads on the local x′ -axis only, a function g(x′ , y ′ ) only
   in the local x′ y ′ -plane.
   So, for discretization in 3D, the general function must have three (or two, if MODE = EXP3D
   is selected) independent variables, for axisymmetric structures two (or one, respectively)
   independent variables.

3. The load values at nodes are calculated with respect to the original node coordinates.
   Coordinate modifications due to nonlinear analysis, optimization etc. do not change the
   load values at nodes, but may of course change the loads of the connected elements
   since the element geometry may be changed.

4. For one element, one load pattern and one load type loadtype only one distributed load
   definition by $DISLOAD, $DISLOADF, $DISLOADN, $DISLOADR or $DISLOADS is pos-
   sible.

5. The function evaluation is controlled by some mode keys defined by parameter MODE on
   the data line:

         Mode key     Explanation
         INTPOL       Calculation of nodal point values by function evaluation (interpola-
                      tion for tabular function).
         ASSIGN       Nodal point values are taken from grid point with smallest distance
                      (only applicable for tabular functions defined at grid points).
         EXP3D        Function values defined on a x′ , y ′ -plane are valid for all z ′ -values
                      (expansion of plane function in space).




 90                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                              V 19.00.287
     smaller than dstmax from the boundary of the definition range are loaded. dstmax may
     be specified explicitly by parameter MAXDIST, else one half of the corresponding grid
     width is used as default value.
  7. Reference to a function is available only for the following types of distributed loads:

                                                 Values per point
                loadtype      RSYS Number Items Meaning
                For degree of freedom type DISP:
                PRESS            NO           1        p         pressure




                                                                                                      Loading
                TEMP            NO       1     T                 temperature




                                                                                                        DAT
                For degree of freedom type TEMP:
                TEMPFILM        NO       1     TF                surrounding temperature
                LINEHS          NO       1     ql                heat flow per line
                SURFHS          NO       1     qs                heat flow per surface
                VOLHS           NO       1     qV                heat flow per volume
                For degree of freedom type PRES:
                VOLFL           NO       1     fV                fluid load per volume
                For degree of freedom type POTE:
                VOLEC           NO       1     ρ                 volume electric charge

     For applicability to element types, see element description. In general, since load values
     are defined at structural nodes, the same restrictions are valid as for direct input at struc-
     tural nodes by $DISLOADN.
     For scalar values like temperatures etc. the function must look like
                                 T = f (x′ , y ′ , z ′ ) or T = f (x′ , y ′ )

  8. If load values refer to a coordinate system (e.g. vectors, see table in remark 7), then
     parameter RSYS must be specified in any case. For RSYS = 0 the function values refer
     to component system, else they refer to the reference system given by parameter RSYS.
     Reference to local node coordinate systems is not applicable.
     If the reference system rsys is a cylindrical or spherical one, then input data refer to a
     local cartesian system which is generated according to the generation rules defined on
     page 1-11.
  9. Initial strains due to temperature are calculated according to following:
     For constant thermal expansion coefficients:
                                            εϑ = α (T − T0 )
     For temperature-dependent thermal expansion coefficients:
                             εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )


V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           3-691
          α        Constant thermal expansion coefficient.
          α (T )   Total temperature-dependent thermal expansion coefficient from
                   reference temperature Tref to actual temperature T .
          T        Actual temperature.
          T0       Corresponding element reference temperature.
          Tref     Expansion coefficient reference temperature.

0. The corresponding element reference temperature T0 is the temperature at which thermal
   expansion of the element is zero, and may be defined for each element and each load
   pattern by data blocks $REFVAL TEMP. If not defined, the component reference tem-
   perature for thermal expansion is used as default, see parameter REFTEMP within data
   block $PARAMETER, page 3-852.

1. Since initial strains are calculated from the temperature difference T − T0 , input of zero
   temperatures will lead to initial strains if the corresponding element reference temperature
   T0 is not equal to zero as well.

constant extrapolation in z-direction

                nid

            name/text




V 19.00.287                         PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      3-693
   loaded. Which elements can be loaded depends on element type and load type, see
   element description.

2. For one element, one load pattern and one load type loadtype only one distributed load
   definition by $DISLOAD, $DISLOADF, $DISLOADN, $DISLOADR or $DISLOADS is pos-
   sible.

3. If no function identifier is specified, load value is given by l = l0 .

4. Each load value may depend on the position in space, its factor l0 and topological infor-
   mation. If for a load value a tuple l0 , fun is input, the actual load value is calculated as a
   product of basic value l0 and the value of the function fun (Label (integer, name or text
   string)) according to
                                             l = l0 ∗ fun(x)
   where x is a vector of up to seven independent variables defined in the following table:


                           x(1)    xn         x-coordinate of loaded point
                           x(2)    yn         y-coordinate of loaded point
                           x(3)    zn         z-coordinate of loaded point
                           x(4)    l0         basic load value
                           x(5)    eid        element identifier
                           x(6)    nid        node identifier
                           x(7)    idcomp     load component identifier

   xn , yn , zn are the cartesian coordinates of node nid referring to component system. If
   the load values are not defined at element nodes but for the whole element (e.g. beam
   initial strains), then nid is equal zero and xn , yn , zn contains the mean value of the node
   coordinates of the element.

5. The load value function can be defined as general function with up to seven independent
   variables, see $FUNCTION. $FUNCTION SUM or $FUNCTION CHAIN may be used to
   assemble functions with an arbitrary number of variables.
   For the meaning of the independent variables see remark 4. Node identifier nid, element
   identifier eid and load component identifier idcomp are transferred as real values.

6. If the load value function is defined with k < 7 independent variables, only the variables
   up to x(k) are available in the function.

7. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all load values of current data block
   are multiplied by the given value f actor.

ta lines:

            (          )
                nid
                              T
                nset




m(s)         Type          Explanation

             I>0           Nodal point identifier.
t          name/text       Node set name.
              R            Node temperature.
                           For functional dependency of load values see remark 5 and 6.


marks:

1. Node temperatures leading to initial strains due to thermal expansion, defined at structural
   nodes, are available for flange, membrane, solid, beam, shell, load carrying membrane,
   gasket and all axisymmetric elements. For details see element description.

2. Initial strains due to temperature are calculated according to following:
   For constant thermal expansion coefficients:

                                               εϑ = α (T − T0 )

    For temperature-dependent thermal expansion coefficients:

                                  εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )

    with




36                         PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                     V 19.00.287
              T      Actual temperature.
              T0     Corresponding element reference temperature.
              Tref   Expansion coefficient reference temperature.

  3. The corresponding element reference temperature T0 is the temperature at which ther-
     mal expansion of the element is zero, and may be defined for each element and each
     load pattern by data blocks $REFVAL TEMP, see page 3-872. If not defined, the com-
     ponent reference temperature for thermal expansion is used as default, see parameter
     REFTEMP within data block $PARAMETER, page 3-852.

  4. Since initial strains are calculated from the temperature difference T − T0 , input of zero




                                                                                                    Loading
     temperatures will lead to initial strains if the corresponding element reference temperature




                                                                                                      DAT
     T0 is not equal zero as well.

  5. Each load value T may be replaced by a tuple T0 , fun where T0 is the basic load value
     and fun the label of a space-dependent function, see remark 4 ff. on page 3-694. The
     actual load value is then given by

                                           T = T0 ∗ fun(x)

  6. The input values T and T0 , respectively, are available for postprocessing by UCI command
     DEFAULT SET MODEL = VERIFICATION.

  7. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all temperature values of current data
     block are multiplied by the given value f actor.

  8. Trailing zeroes in data list may be omitted.

Example:

Please refer to examples BA2, CA2, LS1 and MNL2 of [um550].

  $DISLOADN TEMP LPAT = 101
    NODE_SET 45.9

  ! variable load; temperature depends on function 50001
  $DISLOADN TEMP LPAT = 141
    NODE_SET 45.9,50001

Remarks:




                                                                                                 Loading
  1. Distributed loads defined within data block $DISLOADR are calculated using the specified




                                                                                                   DAT
     results of another situation.
  2. If RANGE = COMP is specified, the load definition is valid for current component only,
     and each element which is able to carry that load type loadtype is loaded. Which elements
     can be loaded depends on element type and load type, see element description.
     If parameter RANGE is omitted or RANGE = CONFIG (default) is specified, the load
     definition is valid for whole configuration.
     Attention: RANGE = CONFIG is not yet available for substructure analysis.
  3. TIME = CURRENT ia applicable only in nonlinear static analysis (UCI command NLMATERIAL)
     and means that from a transient heat transfer analysis (DIRECT TEMPerature) always the
     actual temperature is extracted as load. The time range of the heat transfer analysis must
     match the range of the quasi-steady nonlinear static analysis.
  4. Only one result specification is possible for one loading case and one loadtype.
  5. Since by $DISLOADR all suitable elements of the component are loaded, for speci-
     fied load pattern and loadtype no further load definitions of corresponding loadtypes by
     $DISLOAD, $DISLOADF, $DISLOADN or $DISLOADS are possible:
        • For loadtype = TEMP further load definitions by TEMP, TEMPDIFF or TEMPGRAD
          are not allowed.
  6. Initial strains due to temperature are calculated according to following:
     For constant thermal expansion coefficients:
                                          εϑ = α (T − T0 )
     For temperature-dependent thermal expansion coefficients:
                             εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )
     with




V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       3-763
          T       Actual temperature.
          T0      Corresponding element reference temperature.
          Tref    Expansion coefficient reference temperature.

7. The corresponding element reference temperature T0 is the temperature at which thermal
   expansion of the element is zero, and may be defined for each element and each load
   pattern by data blocks $REFVAL TEMP. If not defined, the component reference tem-
   perature for thermal expansion is used as default, see parameter REFTEMP within data
   block $PARAMETER, page 3-852.

8. Since initial strains are calculated from the temperature difference T − T0 , input of zero
   temperatures will lead to initial strains if the corresponding element reference temperature
   T0 is not equal zero as well.

9. Loads due to steady electric current for magnetostatic problems are calculated through
   R = CAφ φ̇, where C is the elemental conductivity matrix and φ̇ the electric scalar poten-
   tial.

0. RElement loads due to power dissipation for temperature problems are calculated via R =
     V E C, where E is the element electric field strength and C the element electric current.
        t


1. Element surface loads due to magnetic
                                       H    (electric) Maxwell stress tensor for mechanical
   problems are calculated via R = S T n, where T is the magnetic (electric) Maxwell
                                          t

   stress tensor and n is the element normal.

2. If no further selection is specified, COLUMN = LAST, i.e. the last column of result book
   is assumed.

ample:

$DISLOADR TEMP LPAT = 101 DOFTYPE = DISP              ! load for mechanical analysis
  SITUATION = HEAT_SYM LPAT = 10

$DISLOADR STELCUR LPAT = 100 DOFTYPE = POTE
  SITUATION = STEADY_CURR LPAT = 3

ase refer to the following examples of [um550] for various load types.

LS1: $DISLOADR MAFORCE.
HT1: $DISLOADR POWERDIS.
S4: $DISLOADR STELCUR.
LS1 to HTLS3 and HTDEV1: $DISLOADR TEMP.

Data lines:

            (           )                      
                surf
                                list(l0 , fun       )
                sfset




Item(s)       Type          Explanation

surf         I>0            Label (integer, name or text string) of surface.
            name/text
sfset      name/text        Surface set name.
l0            R             Basic load value.
fun          I>0            Label (integer, name or text string) of load value function, see remark 4.
            name/text




V 19.00.287                          PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      3-765
   type, see element description.

2. For one element, one load pattern and one load type loadtype only one distributed load
   definition by $DISLOAD, $DISLOADF, $DISLOADN, $DISLOADR or $DISLOADS is pos-
   sible.

3. If no function identifier is specified, the load value is given by l = l0 .

4. Each load value may depend on the position in space, its factor l0 and topological infor-
   mation. If for a load value a tuple l0 , fun is input, the actual load value is calculated as a
   product of basic value l0 and the value of the function fun (Label (integer, name or text
   string)) according to
                                             l = l0 ∗ fun(x)
   where x is a vector of up to seven independent variables defined in the following table:


                           x(1)    xn         x-coordinate of loaded point
                           x(2)    yn         y-coordinate of loaded point
                           x(3)    zn         z-coordinate of loaded point
                           x(4)    l0         basic load value
                           x(5)    eid        element identifier
                           x(6)    nid        node identifier
                           x(7)    idcomp     load component identifier

   xn , yn , zn are the cartesian coordinates of node nid referring to component system.

5. The load value function can be defined as general function with up to seven independent
   variables, see $FUNCTION. $FUNCTION SUM or $FUNCTION CHAIN may be used to
   assemble functions with an arbitrary number of variables.
   For the meaning of the independent variables see remark 4. Node identifier nid, element
   identifier eid and load component identifier idcomp are transfered as real values.

6. If the load value function is defined with k < 7 independent variables, only the variables
   up to x(k) are available in the function.

7. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all load values l0 of current data block
   are multiplied by the given value f actor.

marks:

1. Node temperatures leading to initial strains due to thermal expansion, defined at surfaces,
   are available for membrane, shell and load carrying membrane elements. For details see
   element description.

2. Initial strains due to temperature are calculated according to following:
   For constant thermal expansion coefficients:

                                                εϑ = α (T − T0 )

    For temperature-dependent thermal expansion coefficients:

                                   εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )

    with




92                          PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                    V 19.00.287
              T      Actual temperature.
              T0     Corresponding element reference temperature.
              Tref   Expansion coefficient reference temperature.

  3. The corresponding element reference temperature T0 is the temperature at which ther-
     mal expansion of the element is zero, and may be defined for each element and each
     load pattern by data blocks $REFVAL TEMP, see page 3-872. If not defined, the com-
     ponent reference temperature for thermal expansion is used as default, see parameter
     REFTEMP within data block $PARAMETER, page 3-852.

  4. Since initial strains are calculated from the temperature difference T − T0 , input of zero




                                                                                                    Loading
     temperatures will lead to initial strains if the corresponding element reference temperature




                                                                                                      DAT
     T0 is not equal zero as well.

  5. Each load value T may be replaced by a tuple T0 , fun where T0 is the basic load value
     and fun the label of a space-dependent function, see remark 4 ff. on page 3-766. The
     actual load value is then given by

                                           T = T0 ∗ fun(x)

  6. The input value T resp. T0 is available for postprocessing by UCI command DEFAULT
     SET MODEL = VERIFICATION.

  7. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all temperature values of current data
     block are multiplied by the given value f actor.

  8. Trailing zeroes in data list may be omitted.

V 19.00.287                               PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                  3-813
                           (
                               p0           for nodes on / above fluid surface
                    pi =
                               p0 + g ρf hi for nodes below fluid surface

   with

                           pi     pressure value at node i
                           p0     constant pressure above fluid surface
                           g      gravity acceleration
                           ρf     fluid density
                           hi     distance of node i from fluid surface

   The generated pressure values are inserted as standard distributed load values of load-
   type PRESS, see e.g. page 3-611.

2. For one element and one load pattern only one pressure load definition by $DISLOAD,
   $DISLOADF, $DISLOADN, $DISLOADR, $DISLOADS or $DISLOADX is possible.

3. Hydrostatic pressure loads may be specified for elements (LDEF = ELEMENTS) or sur-
   faces (LDEF = SURFACE).

4. Hydrostatic pressure loads, specified for elements, are available for membrane, shell and
   load carrying membrane elements. Two data sets are possible. The (mandatory) first
   data set defines pressure at the upper side of the element where a positive pressure acts
   in the direction of the negative element normal. The (optional) second data set defines
   pressure at the lower side of the element where a positive pressure acts in the direction
   of the positive element normal.

5. Hydrostatic pressure loads, specified at surfaces, are available for membrane, solid, shell,
   load carrying membrane and gasket elements. The data set defines pressure at the
   specified surface where a positive pressure acts in the direction of the negative surface
   normal. The surface itself must be defined by elements, see data block $SURFACE.

6. The direction of gravity acceleration is given by the axis of a cartesian reference system
   rsys selected by parameter idof g (e.g. idof g = −3 means that the gravity acceleration
   vector points into the negative z-axis of reference system rsys).

7. The fluid surfaces are fixed by the reference point given by parameter PREF, and are
   perpendicular to the direction of gravity acceleration. If the surface reference point is
   specified by a node set, this node set must contain exactly one node. For geometric
   nonlinear analyses each node used as surface reference point must be connected to at
   least one finite element.

8. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, pressure values p0 as well as gravity
   acceleration g are multiplied by the given value f actor.

         name/text



16                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           V 19.00.287
                      grees of freedoms).
ACCE        name      Prescribed values are accelerations (only applicable for displacement
                      degrees of freedoms).
h            I≥0      Harmonic index. The default value is 1, see also remark 17.


Remarks:

    1. Definition of dynamic loads is only possible within a loading variant of a single or top
       component.




                                                                                                     Loading
    2. The degree of freedom type must be the same as of the connected load. This is important




                                                                                                       DAT
       e.g. in fluid structure coupled analyses.

    3. In frequency response analysis the real dynamic load is defined by

                              L(f, t) = Lc (f ) cos 2πf t + Ls (f ) sin 2πf t

      where f is the frequency and L contains a real amplitude vector depending on frequency.
      The amplitude vectors can be expressed as sums of products of constant load patterns
      P and amplitude spectra a(f ):
                                     X                X
                           Lc (f ) =   P cν aν (f ) +   P λ aλ (f ) cos ϕλ (f )
                                         ν                    λ
                                        X                     X
                            Ls (f ) =        P sµ aµ (f ) −        P λ aλ (f ) sin ϕλ (f )
                                         µ                     λ

      The phase spectra can be written as

                                        ϕλ (f ) = ϕ0λ + ϕ1λ f + pλ (f )

      where ϕ0λ and ϕ1λ are constant values.


    4. The corresponding dynamic load in complex notation is given by

                               L(f, t) = (Lc (f ) − i Ls (f )) exp(i 2πf t)

    5. Each data line defines one product of loading pattern and amplitude spectrum according
       to the amplitude type:


                                  Amplitude type              Type of product
                                  TOTAL                          P λ aλ (f )
                                  COSINE                         P cν aν (f )
                                  SINE                           P sµ aµ (f )


V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                            3-817
                                                                              degrees
                P a(f ) cos 2πf t            COSINE             a(f )              -
                P a(f ) sin 2πf t            SINE               a(f )              -
                P a(f ) cos(2πf t + ϕ(f ))   TOTAL              a(f )           ϕ(f )
                P a(f ) sin(2πf t + ϕ(f ))   TOTAL              a(f )        ϕ(f ) + 270

7. Complex dynamic loads of the form

                    L(f, t) = P (a1 (f ) + i a2 (f )) exp i (θ − 2πf τ ) exp(i 2πf t)

   may be defined by two data lines according to following table:

                          TYPE       AMPLITUDE             ϕ0         ϕ1
                                                        degrees     degrees
                          TOTAL           a1 (f )          θ         −360τ
                          TOTAL           a2 (f )        θ + 90      −360τ

8. All loads for frequency response analysis defined within one loading variant are accumu-
   lated into one dynamic load.

9. Each loading pattern lpat must be defined within current loading variant, either directly
   or within loading variants of connected subcomponents. The rules to define a loading
   pattern are the same as for static analysis with following restrictions:

      • Prescribed displacements are possible only in single or top components.
      • Initial strains and temperature loads leading to initial strains are not allowed.
      • For beam elements with distributed loads no element stresses or resultant forces are
        calculated.

0. If there are prescribed degrees of freedom, then for each prescribed degree of freedom
   at least one value must be defined by $PREVAL in any load pattern. In the remaining
   load patterns, contributions equal zero may be omitted.

1. For displacement degrees of freedom, prescribed values may be displacements, veloci-
   ties or accelerations, depending on parameter PRESCRIBED.

2. In the case of prescribed velocities or accelerations, in one load pattern, there can only
   be prescribed accelerations or velocities. Multiple definitions of prescribed accelerations
   or velocities within a single load pattern are also not possible. External loads cannot be
   definied in the same load pattern as prescribed velocities or accelerations.

3. Definition of phase is only meaningful for input of total amplitudes. Phase values and
   phase spectrum functions must be input in degrees.




18                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                  V 19.00.287
 15. Loads for frequency response analysis cannot be defined for temperature degrees of
     freedom.

 16. $FREQLOAD and $TRANSLOAD are mutually exclusive in the same loading variant.

 17. The harmonic index of the load. For direct and modal frequency response the harmonic
     index must be 1. For DIRECT HARMONIC BALANCE values between 0 and the maxi-
     mum number of harmonics in the DIRECT HARMONIC BALANCE command are allowed.

Remarks:

     1. Inertia forces may be defined for element sets. If no element set is specified (eset omitted
        on data line), the inertia force definition is valid for all elements of the component.

     2. Inertia force definitions must be unique, i.e. each load type ’linear acceleration’ (ACCEL-
        ERATION or GRAVITY), ROTATION and CORIOLIS may be defined only once for one
        element in one load pattern of one loading variant.

     3. Since gravity is a special case of linear acceleration, either ACCELERATION or GRAVITY
        may be used but not both for one element within one load pattern of one loading variant.

      or top component and is valid for whole configuration.

      MODAL TIMEhistory, MODAL FLuid TIMEhistory and MODAL FSCoupled TIMEhistory.

      atures or pressures, whereas parameter dof type specifies the degree of freedom type of
      the system where the initial values should be applied.

   4. Input of initial values is not possible for degrees of freedom which are declared as sup-
      pressed, prescribed or external, or used as dependent degrees of freedom im MPC’s.

   i.e. last column of result book is assumed.

9. If SOURCE = INPUT (default) is specified, input data may refer to a reference system
   given by parameter RSYS. If parameter RSYS is omitted, components of displacements
   etc. are referring to the (possibly rotated) local node coordinate system, RSYS = 0 means
   referring to component system. If the reference system rsys is a cylindrical or spherical
   one then input data refers to a local cartesian system which is generated according to the
   generation rules defined on page 1-11.

Remarks:

  1. In each component, one and only one load correction matrix may exist. The matrix is
     added to the stiffness matrix, therefore it is active for each load pattern.

  2. Load correction matrices describe linear load dependencies given by

                                                    R(r) = R0 + K R r


V 19.00.287                          PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                           3-835
   by all degrees of freedom of two nodes, one node for row, one (the same or another) node
   for column specification.

4. The highest nodal point degree of freedom of each submatrix dofR + ndofR − 1 or dofC +
   ndofC − 1 resp. must not exceed the maximum number of degrees of freedom at nodes.

5. A submatrix is defined by specifying row and column range by node id, first degree of
   freedom and number of degrees of freedom, which corresponds to a window definition
   with the upper left corner at dofR , dofC and the lower right corner at (dofR + ndofR −
   1), (dofC + ndofC − 1) within the complete submatrix:
                                        nid C
                                             dofC
                             nid R
                                                 ndofC
                                dofR    ndofR




   The submatrix element K(i, j) where i is the row index and j the column index contains
   the derivative of (generalized) force Fi with respect to (genearlized) displacement rj , i.e.

                                                            ∂Fi
                                                K(i, j) =
                                                            ∂rj

6. For all elements of a matrix either RSYS = ROTB (default) or RSYS = 0 must be valid;
   mixing of both specifications for elements of the same matrix is not possible.

7. The matrix elements of a submatrix must be input columnwise.

8. Trailing zeroes may be omitted.

marks:
1. Static load history definition is only possible within the loading variant of single or top
   components. It is applicable for all static analyses (i.e. STATIC, INERTIA, NLMATERIAL,
   NLINERTIA) and for nonlinear steady state heat transfer analysis (UCI command NLTEMP).

2. For contact analysis a static load history has to be defined as soon as friction with frictional
   coefficients 0.0 < µ < ∞ (≡ FIXED) is taken into account, see $CONTACT LOAD. In all
   other cases $NLLOAD is completely optional.

3. There may exist only one joined static load history definition within one loading variant,
   but the input may be split to more than one $NLLOAD data blocks.

4. If static load history definition is missing in a nonlinear static analysis, then the loading
   may contain only one load pattern.

5. The static load history definition refers to an artificial process time tp , i.e. the loading
   process is described with respect to an artificial time scale.

     with the loading patterns P i and the time-dependent amplitude function fi (t).

  7. Note that $NLLOAD builds up the load at time t by combining / scaling assembled load
     pattern vectors rather than combining / scaling the input values that defined those loads,
     e.g.

        • Initial gap width δ0 = δgeo +δU is scaled instead of the additive (input) gap width δU .




                                                                                                      Loading
        • Rotational inertia loads are scaled on base Ω2 instead of input rotational velocity Ω.




                                                                                                        DAT
        • For initial temperature strains the resulting strain εϑ = α (T −T0 ) is scaled / combined
          directly - corresponding to the scaling of releative temperatures (T − T0 ) with con-
          stant α (of course, α may depend on T for building up the load pattern vector).
        • For NLMATERIAL there exists one exception from this standard combination rule,
          see following remark 8.
        • An alternative approach is offered by $COMBINE LOADS.

  8. As an exception from the above standard combination rule, temperature loads in non-
     linear analyses (e.g. NLMATERIAL) are built up by directly combining / scaling the input
     temperatures rather than combining / scaling the corresponding temperature strains.
     Dependent on the DEFAULT switch NLSCALETEMP, the NLMATERIAL command builds
     the resulting temperature load at time t either absolute (always relative to zero) or relative
     to the reference temperature T0 .
                         P
      ABSTEMP: T = i fi T i
                               P
      RELTEMP: T = T 0 + i fi (T i − T 0 )
     As long as the sum of loading factors fi equals one, both settings lead to the same
     temperature loads.
     Example: resulting temperature loads for T1 = 100.0, T2 = 200.0, T0 = 20.0:
       f1      f2   ABSTEMP     RELTEMP
      0.0     0.0        0.0        20.0
      1.0     0.0      100.0       100.0
      0.0     1.0      200.0       200.0
      0.5     0.5      150.0       150.0
      2.0     0.0      200.0       180.0

  9. For the nonlinear static analysis (UCI command NLMATERIAL) there are some restric-
     tions until now:

        • The number of load patterns is limited to 1000 .

      • Care has to be taken for the combination of contact load property parameters GAP-

        any contact identifier or contact name holds the actual settings with all other contact
        loads using the ’neutral’ default definition GAPWIDTH = ABS (with δU = 0.0), NOR-
        MAL = FREE and FRICTION = FREE, respectively.
        However, for special purposes it is also possible to combine contact loads with arbi-
        trary GAPWIDTH, NORMAL or FRICTION parameter. For a description of sensible
        combinations and resulting contact parameters see page 4-2ff. of [um550].

1. For contact analysis the current gap width and contact status are continuous functions in
   ’time’, e.g. a slipping contact stays slipping as long as the current load does not fall under
   the ’regain-sticking-limit’ Fslip < µFnorm .
   However, if the load stays constant over a certain period (e.g. t2 > t1 with only one load
   active), then all slipping contacts regain sticking prior to the evaluation of the next load
   step with the frictional forces staying unchanged, i.e. a relaxation of all slipping contacts.

2. The UCI switch SET NLPLOT can be used to automatically generate a Postscript plot file
   to visualize the load history.

3. For more hints on how to use $NLLOAD in a contact analysis see $CONTACT LOAD and
   examples CA3, CA5 or NLS3 of the PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU) [um550].

Remarks:
  1. The introductory remarks from page 3-838 also apply for this type of $NLLOAD definition.

  2. If TIME is not specified, the standard generation rule TIME = 0.0, 1.0 is used.

  3. All $NLLOAD TABLE blocks are internally concatenated into one tabular definition.
     Therefore the sample times and corresponding amplitude values may be split to sev-
     eral blocks of $NLLOAD TABLE in order to allow a convenient and clear definition (e.g.
     avoiding line breaks for long data lines). E.g. the example inputs given below would build
     a joined load history if specified in the same loading variant.

  4. The parameter EXTRA defines the extrapolation rule to derive function values outside of
     the time range defined for each load pattern, i.e. for function values f (t) before tmin (lpat)
     or after tmax (lpat), respectively:

            • For the default option EXTRA = CONST a constant function value matching the
              first / last value defined for the corresponding load patttern is assumed from t=−∞
              up to tmin (lpat) and from tmax (lpat) to t=+∞.


V 19.00.287                      PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                            3-845
         for t < tmin (lpat) or the last two points for t > tmax (lpat), respectively.
      • EXTRA = NEXT0 is a smart option to fade in / out non-zero border values on the
        next specified time step without the drawback of discontinuous jumps.
      • For EXTRA = ZERO a zero function value is assumed from t=−∞ up to tmin (lpat)
        and from tmax (lpat) to t=+∞, respectively. Note that this causes discontinuous
        jumps before / after non-zero border values.

5. With EXTRA = lower, upper the user may specify different extrapolation rules for times
   t < tmin (lpat) and t > tmax (lpat), respectively (the default is to use the same extrapola-
   tion for both ends). However, currently not all combinations are supported:

                            EXTRA =      CONST       LIN    NEXT0      ZERO
                             CONST          ✔        ✔        ✔          –
                               LIN          ✔        ✔         –         –
                             NEXT0          ✔         –       ✔          ✔
                             ZERO            –        –       ✔          ✔

6. The extrapolation rule given for a certain LPAT always applies to t < tmin (lpat) and
   t > tmax (lpat) no matter whether the data points are given in one single $NLLOAD block
   or whether they are splitted over several $NLLOAD inputs (i.e. the extrapolation is not
   per $NLLOAD block but per LPAT). Moreoever, if the data points of one LPAT is split over
   several $NLLOAD blocks, then all blocks must have the same extrapolation parameters.

7. Within the same loading variant there may be only one unique amplitude value for a
   certain load pattern and sampling time. However, with the specification of a data pair or
   triple it is possible to define non-continuous jumps in the load history. With a data triple
   one can specify different values for f (< ti ), f (ti ) and f (> ti )) respectively – of course, two
   of those may also have identical values. If only a data pair is given, then the function value
   at jump time is the average value of both limit values, i.e. f (t) = 0.5 (f (< ti ) + f (> ti )).
   No jumps are allowed for the border times (first or last time per LPAT) if linear extrapolation
   is used.

8. Note that the dash symbol ’–’ neither means zero nor hold ! The dash indeed behaves
   like a nil entry of a $FUNCTION TABLE, i.e. its only purpose is to improve the readability
   of complex tables and free the user from the necessity of specifying intermediate function
   values for each time stamp and load pattern. If the concept of nil entries confuses you,
   simply use explicit values for all load patterns and all sampling times.

  3. If OVERLAP = ABS is specified, the interference is given by
                                               δ0 = δU

  4. If OVERLAP = ADD is specified, the interference δ0 is given by
                                            δ0 = δgeo + δU

     where δU is the user-defined overlap value and δgeo is the initial geometrical interference
     between the pressfit partners.

  5. Note that the pressfit overlap δU has to be a positive value to introduce a pressing geo-
     metric intersection. If – for some exotic reasons – a negative (tensile) overlap is needed
     then the user may scale a positive δU here with a negative scaling factor in $NLLOAD.

  6. Each data line defines one set of pressfit load properties for one loading case. They are
     assigned to all pressfit identifier/names specified in the corresponding data lines. For one
     pressfit identifier/name and one loading case and one node only one definition of pressfit
     load properties is possible.

  7. If node identifier/set nid/nset and function label funare omitted, the same pressfit overlap
     is assigned to all nodes belonging to the specified pressfit identifier/name.

  8. If a node identifier nid or node set nset is specified, then a corresponding pressfit load
     definition must be made for all nodes of the 2nd partner (or 1st partner for pressfit to
     ground) associated with the specified pressfit identifier/name.

     function value, i.e.
                                             δU ′ = δU ∗ f(x)
     The referred function may depend on the position in space or topological information, i.e.
     the following arguments are available:

0. If one special argument is selected via f arg then only that variable is passed as indepen-

   load functions with one independent variable only, e.g. f arg=z for sin(zn ). If f arg is a text
   string with a comma separated list of arguments then only that arguments are passed to
   the load function (in given sequence), e.g. f arg=’z,dg,nid’ or f arg=’(z,dg,nid)’.

m(s)      Type      Explanation

ef         I>0     Label (integer, name or text string) of pretension definition.
         name/text
          R≤ 0.0 Prescribed tightening, see remark 10.
          R< 0.0 Pretension force, see remark 7.


marks:

1. Definition of pretension load properties is only possible within a loading variant of a top or
   single component.

2. Each pretension load refers to a corresponding $PRETENSION PLANE or $PRETENSION
   THREAD definition made in the structure bracket.

3. If no pretension load property is given for a certain pretension definition respectively load
   pattern, the ’neutral’ default definition PREDIR = FREE is used, i.e. the pretension
   thread / area is not activated if no $PRETENSION LOAD is specified.

4. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all floating point values of the current
   data block are multiplied by the given value f actor, i.e. the same scaling applies to δ and
   Rp (if given).

5. Each data line defines one set of pretension load properties for one loading case. They
   are assigned to all pretension identifier / names specified in the corresponding data lines.
   For one pretension identifier / name and one loading case only one definition of pretension
   load properties is possible.

6. For PREDIR = FREE the guiding node is free to move in pretension direction. Although
   this means that the overall pretension force is zero this does not necessarily imply that all
   local forces between the copuling nodes are zero, too.
   Actually all local relative displacements will still be synchronized to attain the same (free)
   value. This is somewhat an equivalent to allowing a free rigid body movement while still
   coupling the shape of the coupling area, e.g. a global translation will not introduce forces,
   but a bending or torque will still be linked to the coupling partner.

7. If PREDIR = FORCE is specified the pretension thread / area is coupled and will con-
   stantly transmit the pretension force Rp as a sum of all coupling nodal point forces in
   pretension direction. The local force distribution may vary according to the local stiffness,



58                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          V 19.00.287
     a negative Rp here with a negative scaling factor in $NLLOAD.

  8. PREDIR = FORCE_LOCK works like PREDIR = FORCE if the corresponding load pat-
     tern is varied during the current time step, i.e. if this load pattern is scaled for the current
     time step in the non-linear load history.
     If the corresponding load pattern is kept constant (i.e. no change of this load pattern in
     the non-linear load history), then this works like PREDIR = LOCK.

  9. PREDIR = LOCK freezes the final shortage of a preceding load step. I.e. the short-
     age / elongation will not change due to further loads unless the LOCK is released (also
     changing a corresponding Rp force has no effect during LOCK state).




                                                                                                             Loading
     However, note that an explicit change of the prescribed distance δ will still affect a locked
     pretension! Those changes are re-compensated by PREDIR = LOCK with the help of




                                                                                                               DAT
     extra pretension forces to regain the former final / frozen distance. With this feature it is
     possible to add a prescribed change to an initially unknown state of pre-deformation, e.g.
     a prescribed re-tightening of a FORCE_LOCKed screw.
     Usually this is used in combination with a PREDIR = FORCE setting in the preceding load
     step for a standard pretension load (e.g. bolts). This feature requires the existence of a
     load history defined by $NLLOAD.

 10. If PREDIR = PRESCRIBE is specified, then the given tightening δ is used to prescribe a
     relative contraction between the pretension partners rather than prescribing the resulting
     cutting force. Note that the shortage value Rp has to be a negative value for the transmis-
     sion of a tensile force.*
     If - for some exotic reasons - a positive elongation value is needed, then the user may
     scale a negative δ here with a negative scaling factor in $NLLOAD.


Example:

Please refer to examples CA13 to CA13V5 and to example CA9 of [um550].

  $PRETENSION LOAD         LPAT = 7      PREDIR = FREE                   ! deactivated in LPAT 7
    SCREW2NUT

  ! apply force and lock resulting relative displacement
  $PRETENSION LOAD LPAT = 100 PREDIR = FORCE_LOCK
    SPREADER -4.E+06

  ! apply relative displacement
  $PRETENSION LOAD LPAT = 203 PREDIR = PRESCRIBE
    SCREW2NUT -0.1



* The $CONTACT LOAD analogon to a prescribed tightening is a positive gap with NORMAL = FIXED, i.e.   pre-
 scribing a pretension shortage is a synonym for the forced closure of an open contact gap.

Remarks:

  1. Prescribed degrees of freedom must be declared within the corresponding constraint vari-
     ant(s) by a $PRESCRIBE data block.
  2. Prescribed values must always be unique, therefore for one load pattern, one node and
     one degree of freedom only one value may be input.


V 19.00.287                     PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        3-861
   of freedom, starting with 1. Trailing zeroes may not be omitted.

5. If a scale factor is specified by parameter FACTOR, all prescribed values of current
   data block are multiplied by the given value f actor. The scaling factor is not available
   if SOURCE = RESULTS is specified.

6. Prescribed values for rotational degrees of freedom are expected to be in radians.

7. For DOFTYPE = POTE prescribed degree of freedom 4 (scalarpotential) is valid for the
   velocity-scalar potential φ̇, see page 3-375. Therefore all prescribed values are velocity-
   scalar potentials.

e following remarks are only valid for SOURCE = RESULTS.

e main use case is mapping of result values from a reference component onto the current
mponent as in example HT11 or in submodel technique, see examples LS15b, LS15c and
15d.

marks:

8. If SOURCE = RESULTS is specified, the prescribed values are determined by the re-
   sults of another analysis which is chosen by component name ref comp, situation name
   sitname and some additional specifications. The prescribed values at the specified no-
   des are interpolated from the nodal point results of the referred analysis, using the shape
   functions of the corresponding elements.

9. Prescribed values by result interpolation are available only for solid, shell and membrane
   elements.

0. If the referenced component ref comp is a subcomponent, then the name of its config-
   uration ref conf (the name of the corresponding top component) must be specified in
   addition.

1. The reference to the results of another situation must be unique for each load pattern of
   the current loading variant. That is, for one load pattern only one column/load pattern/time
   etc. from one situation in one component may be referenced for result interpolation.

2. For result interpolation, the number of prescribed degrees of freedom at the specified
   nodes must match the number of degrees of freedom at the corresponding nodes in
   the referenced component. Displacement degrees of freedom 7 (warping) and higher,
   however, are not taken into account, and cannot be prescribed by result interpolation.

3. If no application region is specified by the NODES option, all nodes inside the search
   volume defined by the reference component are considered.




 62                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         V 19.00.287
     but adjacent regions.

 15. MAXDIST is mandatory for twodimensional elements if SOURCE = RESULTS is speci-
     fied. With this parameter, a virtual search volume is built in positive and negative normal
     direction of 2D-elements. Meaningful values depend on the geometry of the model and
     on the selected unit of length.

 16. If SOURCE = RESULTS is specified, parameter OUTTOL is used to control the assign-
     ment of nodes outside of the search volume. Search volume is the volume of finite el-
     ements in case of solid elements, or the virtual search volume in case of 2D-elements,
     see remark 15. A node outside of the boundary is assigned, if the distance of the node to




                                                                                                   Loading
     the finite element is less than OUTTOL ∗LE where LE is a typical length of the element.
     OUTTOL is restricted to a maximum of 1.0, because the accuracy of the extrapolation




                                                                                                     DAT
     with element shape functions decreases rapidly outside the element. If not input, the
     default value defined by global system key OUTTOL is used.
