Remarks:

   1. Definition of loads for random response analysis is only possible within the loading variant




                                                                                                          Loading
      of a single or top component.




                                                                                                            DAT
   2. The load for random response analysis is given by the frequency dependent Hermitian
      spectral density matrix S(f ). Each element of that matrix may be defined in general by

                                             Sij (f ) = Rr,i ∗ Rc,j ∗ fun S,C (f )

        with Rr,i ,Rc,j as load values of degree of freedom i in the first load pattern patidr (row
        direction) and degree of freedom j in the second load pattern patidc (column direction)
        and fun S,C (f ) as complex spectral density function.
        Alternatively, the spectral density matrix may be defined directly for a set of loaded nodes,
        see remark 13.

   3. If due to input rules the second load pattern is not given, the first load pattern patidr is
      used for column direction too.

   4. Each load pattern may contain any external load or prescribed values but not both.

   5. The complex spectral density functions are always depending on frequency and may, in
      addition, depend on position in space, i.e. on the coordinates of the loaded nodes. So
      they may have one, three or seven independent variables:

                     fun S,C (f )                                frequency-dependent
                     fun S,C (f, nidx1 , nidx2 )                 frequency- and space-dependent
                     fun S,C (f, x1 , y1 , z1 , x2 , y2 , z2 )   frequency- and space-dependent

        where f is the frequency in cycles per second, and x1 , y1 , z1 and x2 , y2 , z2 are the coor-
        dinates of the nodes corresponding to degrees of freedom i and j in load pattern patidr
        and patidc, respectively. The coordinates refer to the component system. Instead of node
        coordinates, the nodal point identifiers nidx1 and nidx2 , delivered as floating point values.
        may be used as independent variables.

   6. Space-dependent spectral density functions may not be applied to loads on dependent
      degrees of freedom.



V 19.00.287                         PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          3-867
            ℑ(fun S,C (f, x2 , y2 , z2 , x1 , y1 , z1 )) = −ℑ(fun S,C (f, x1 , y1 , z1 , x2 , y2 , z2 ))

8. Either one-sided or two-sided spectral densities may be used, depending on parameter
   PSDTYPE, see $PARAMETER, page 3-852, but not both in the same loading variant.

9. Since spectral density functions are complex, they are defined as pairs of real general
   functions within a $FUNCTION data block, see page 3-1112. The meaning of the two
   functions is real and imaginary part or amplitude and phase in degrees, according to
   parameter DATTYPE. If one (but not both) function identifier is omitted or set to zero
   then the corresponding function value is set to zero. For DATTYPE = AP however, the
   amplitude function must always exist.

0. If KIND = AUTO is specified, then power spectral densities, i.e. diagonal values of the
   power spectral density matrix are defined. The power spectral density is the Fourier
   transform of the auto-correlation function and is always real.

      - First load pattern identifier patidr and first function label fun 1 must be specified.
      - The second load pattern identifier patidc may be omitted or must be equal patidr.
      - The second function label fun 2 may be omitted or must be equal zero.
      - The referenced load pattern may contain only nodal point loads, referring to the
        possibly rotated nodal point coordinate system, or prescribed displacements. Nodal
        point loads may not be applied on dependent degrees of freedom.
      - The corresponding spectral density matrix is a pure real, symmetric matrix. The
        imaginary part is equal zero.

1. If KIND = CROSS is specified, then cross spectral densities (in general off-diagonal val-
   ues) of the power spectral density matrix are defined. The cross spectral density is the
   Fourier transform of the cross-correlation function and is in general complex. Depending
   on the spectral density function there are two possibilities:

      • If the spectral density function depends only on frequency:
          – Two load patterns identifiers patidr and patidc must be specified. The load
            patterns may be different of identical.
          – If the correlation patidr, patidc is specified, the correlation patidc, patidr is in-
            cluded automatically and must not be specified.
          – If DATTYPE = RI is specified, then one function identifier may be zero but not
            both. Instead of setting the second function identifier equal to zero the function
            identifier may be omitted.
          – If DATTYPE = AP is specified, then the first function fun 1 must be given, and the
            second function fun 2 may be omitted.
          – According to the existence of real and imaginary part of the defined function,
            the corresponding spectral density matrix may be pure real, pure imaginary or
            complex.


68                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                         V 19.00.287
              – If DATTYPE = RI is specified, then one function identifier may be zero but not
                both. Instead of setting the second function identifier equal to zero the function
                identifier may be omitted.
              – If DATTYPE = AP is specified, then the first function fun 1 must be given, and the
                second function f id2 may be omitted.
              – According to the existence of real and imaginary part of the defined function,
                the corresponding spectral density matrix may be pure real, pure imaginary or
                complex.

 12. If KIND = BOTH is specified, then power spectral densities as well as cross spectral




                                                                                                      Loading
     densities are defined. Depending on the spectral density function there are two possibili-




                                                                                                        DAT
     ties:

        • If the spectral density function depends only on frequency:
              – First load pattern identifier patidr and first function fun 1 must be specified.
              – The second load pattern identifier patidc may be omitted or must be equal
                patidr.
              – The second function fun 2 may be omitted or must be equal zero.
              – The corresponding spectral density matrix is a pure real, symmetric matrix. The
                imaginary part is equal zero.
        • If the spectral density function is frequency- and space-dependent:
              – First load pattern identifier patidr must be specified.
              – The second load pattern identifier patidc may be omitted or must be equal
                patidr.
              – If DATTYPE = RI is specified, then one function identifier may be zero but not
                both. Instead of setting the second function identifier equal to zero the function
                identifier may be omitted.
              – If DATTYPE = AP is specified, then the first function f id1 must be given, and the
                second one fun 2 may be omitted.
              – According to the existence of real and imaginary part of the defined function,
                the corresponding spectral density matrix may be pure real, pure imaginary or
                complex.

 13. If KIND = MATRIX is specified, the complete spectral density matrix is provided by user
     supplied function SPDMATS (single precision) or SPDMATD (double precision), respec-
     tively, see remark 14, for all nodes of a certain set. Up to now, this is available for random
     pressure fields only:

        • First load pattern identifier patidr must be specified.
        • The second load pattern identifier patidc must be equal to patidr or may be omitted.




V 19.00.287                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          3-869
      • The pressure load at nodes must not depend on a load function (see page 3-694,
        remark 4).
      • Loads in subcomponents are not allowed.
      • All nodes loaded by load pattern patidr form the node set where the spectral density
        matrix must be supplied by user supplied function SPDMATS or SPDMATD, respec-
        tively.
      • From load pattern patidr and the first function fun 1 the power spectral densities for
        the loaded nodes (the diagonal of the spectral density matrix) are calculated. Of
        course, they may be overwritten in user supplied function SPDMATS or SPDMATD,
        respectively.
      • If the first function label fun 1 is missing, the function is replaced by 1.0 . The function
        fun 1 must not depend on space.
      • The second function label fun 2 may be omitted or must be equal zero.
      • The maximum distance for nodes taken into account for cross spectral density values
        must be specified by parameter USDMMAXDIST within data block $PARAMETER,
        see page 3-852. If the maximum distance is set to zero, cross spectral density values
        are not inserted.
      • Optionally, one or two data sets with user supplied data allocated to loaded nodal
        points may be accessed in the corresponding user supplied subroutines. npart1 and
        npart2 refer to data which must be input by $ALLOCATE USERDATA data blocks.

4. The corresponding subroutine call for execution in single precision is
      CALL SPDMATS (MODE,FREQ)
   or in double precision, respectively
      CALL SPDMATD (MODE,FREQ)
   with input arguments
     MODE     integer   initialization mode
                        = 0: initialized for diagonal values (power spectral density values)
                        = 1: initialized for coupling values (cross spectral density values)
     FREQ     real      excitation frequency in Hz

 CE       name     Absolute acceleration spectrum
 LO       name     Relative velocity spectrum

          I>0      Label (integer, name or text string) of spectrum function.
         name/text


marks:

1. Definition of spectra for response spectrum analysis is only possible within the loading
   variant of a single or top component.

2. A response spectrum is defined as the maximum absolute value S(f, ξ) of a response
   quantity of a single degree-of-freedom oscillator subjected to a prescribed base motion.
   It is always a function of frequency f and of modal viscous damping ratio ξ.



74                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       V 19.00.287
     corresponding modal viscous damping, and the function fun has only one independent
     variable, the frequency f in cycles per second.

  4. Spectrum functions are defined as general functions within a $FUNCTION data block,
     see page 3-1112 ff.

  5. Each spectrum type Sa (acceleration), Sv (velocity) or Sd (displacement) may be defined
     only once. If any spectrum is missing, it is approximated according to

                                           Sa = ωSv
                                            Sv = ωSd




                                                                                                  Loading
                                                                                                    DAT
     with circular frequency ω = 2πf .

  6. In response spectrum analysis, the excitation is assumed to be a prescribed base mo-
     tion. The base motion is one-dimensional, and its direction is given by the direction of
     prescribed displacements of the referenced load pattern patid.

  7. The referenced load pattern patid must fulfil the following requirements:

        • For all nodes which are fixed to the base, all translational degrees of freedom which
          are not perpendicular to the direction of the base motion must be prescribed.
        • The direction of the motion defined by the prescribed values must be the same for
          all nodes with prescribed values; the magnitude of the values itself is meaningless.
        • Translational degrees of freedom which are not perpendicular to the direction of the
          base motion may never be suppressed.
        • All other loads defined for that pattern are ignored in response spectrum analysis.

Example:

Please refer to Example DRX1 of [um550] on page 10-9 ff.

   $RSPECTRUM   LPAT=101
      TYPE=ACCE   FUNCTION=201
      TYPE=VELO   FUNCTION=202
      TYPE=DISP   FUNCTION=203

   $RSPECTRUM   LPAT=2 DOFTYPE=DISP
      FUNCTION=435   TYPE=DISP

Remarks:

   1. Rigid body motion definitions define velocity vectors for nodal points which are given for
      node n by
                                          v n = v + Ω × xn
         where velocity vector v and the rotational velocity vector Ω are defined by input, and xn
         is the nodal point position in space.

   2. Velocity states may be used to define direction and velocity magnitude for sliding friction,
      see $CONTACT LOAD.

   3. Velocity states must be unique, i.e. it may be defined only once for one node in one load
      pattern of one loading variant.

   4. By default, coordinates and velocity vector components refer to component system. Using
      parameter RSYS, a reference system may be specified for coordinates and velocity vector
      components. Reference systems are defined by data blocks $RSYS and figure F3-39 on
      following page.

   5. The meaning of the coordinates xi , yi , zi depends on the kind of reference system.

   6. If a reference system is specified, the components of translation velocity vector v refer
      to a local cartesian system generated using the generation rules for rotated node bases
      (see $ROTB) as defined on page 1-11.

   7. The axis of roation for rotational velocity is defined by two points P1 and P1 , where each
      point may be specified by its coordinates, a node or a node set containing only one node.

   8. The unit of input values for rotational velocity is defined by parameter XTYPE; the default
      is input of circular frequencies (angular velocities) in radians per unit time.

Remarks:

  1. Correlation of basic variables are defined in modification variants of single or top compo-
     nents only, and are used for reliability analysis.

  2. Correlation of basic variables may be defined for time-invariant as well as time-variant
     analyses. Nevertheless, the following restrictions are valid:

          • Time-independent basic variables may be correlated with other time-independent
            basic variables only.
          • Basic variables representing a stationary stochastic sequence may be correlated
            with other stationary basic variables only.
          • Basic variables representing random vector processes may never be correlated.

  3. A correlation between two basic variables may be input only once, i.e. if Cij is input, Cji
     must not be input.

  4. If only correlations between normal or lognormal distributed basic variables are present,
     the analytical Rosenblatt transformation is used from X-space to U-space and vice versa,
     else the Nataf transformation is selected automatically.

marks:

1. Definition a design constraint function is only possible in the modification variant of a
   single or top component. A DCFUNCTION is referenced by its identifier cstid or its name
   cstname.

2. Design constraint function identifiers and names must be unique within the modification
   variant. They also must differ from identifiers or names of $DCONSTRAINT and $DCLINK
   definitions.




92                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      V 19.00.287
  4. Only design constraints defined by $DCONSTRAINT in the current modification variant
     may be used as argument. Constraints defined by $DCLINK or by another $DCFUNCTION
     are not allowed.
  5. The value of any design constraint which is defined within a $DCONSTRAINT data block
     may be used as argument of a constraint function, and is accessed by its identifier cstid
     or name cstname. If design constraints are calculated in other components, the name
     name of the (sub-)component must be specified in addition.
  6. Design variables to be inserted as function arguments must not be stochastic design
     parameters,i.e. they must be deterministic design variables (not associated to any basic
     variable) or used as mean values of basic variables , see $BASVAR (see page 3-29 ff.).




                                                                                                  Modification
  7. Design variables of a design variable set are used as arguments in ascending order un-
     less an ordered set is defined, see $DSVSET (see page 3-92 ff.).




                                                                                                     DAT
  8. Each data line inserts at least element ind in the list of function arguments. If a design
     constraint delivers more than one value (e.g. stresses of an element set, amplitudes over
     a frequency range), than by nof val the number of result values may be specified which
     are inserted consecutively into the list of function arguments, starting at counter ind.
     If nof val is smaller than the number of delivered result values, the selection of values
     to be inserted for the specified design constraint is controlled by skey. Otherwise, the
     result values are first sorted by column (e.g. LPAT, MODE, FREQUENCY, TIME, ...) in
     ascending order, and then by node or element identifier (ascending order per column).
  9. Design constraints referred by a design constraint function are no longer used as design
     constraints, their bounds defined in the $DCONSTRAINT (see page 3-900 ff.) data block
     are ignored.
 10. Depending on parameter EQUALITY, two different types of constraints may be specified:
        • By EQUALITY = NO (default) one or two inequality constraints are defined:
          If UPPER = upper is specified, the constraint function is given by
                                                      !
                                                f (a) ≤ upper
          and if LOWER = lower is specified, the constraint function is given by
                                                      !
                                                f (a) ≥ lower
          Either UPPER or LOWER must be specified.
        • By EQUALITY = YES an equality constraint is defined:
                                                          !
                                                 f (a) = f val
          If f val is not specified, the equality constraint is given by
                                                              !
                                                   f (a) = 0


V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       3-893
2. Any design constraint function may be selected as design objective. For the design ob-
   jective, bounds as well as parameter EQUALITY are ignored.

ample:

  1 DCONSTRAINT : 8001
  2 DCONSTRAINT : 8005

marks:

1. Linked design constraints as function of other constraints are used to build linked con-
   straint equations for constraints, that are defined for multiple result values, e.g. several
   nodes or elements (rows) or several load patterns, time steps, frequencies (columns) and
   are referenced by its identifier cstid or its name cstname.

2. Design constraint link identifiers and names must be unique within the modification vari-
   ant. They must also differ from identifiers or names of $DCONSTRAINT and $DCFUNCTION
   definitions.

3. Only design constraints defined by $DCONSTRAINT in the current modification vari-
   ant may be used as argument. Constraints defined by $DCFUNCTION or by another
   $DCLINK are not allowed.

4. All independent constraints referred by a constraint link must be defined for the same set
   of result values, i.e. they must be defined for e.g. the same element or node set, same
   number of load pattern etc..

5. Constraint equations for the linked constraints are established according to following rules
   depending on the linking type:

       • TYPE = ITEM: The individual items of the independent constraints are arguments of
         the linked constraint equations, resulting in number of rows (nodes,elements) times
         number of columns (load patterns etc.) equations.
       • TYPE = ROW: The rows of the independent constraints are arguments of the linked
         constraint equations, resulting in one equation for each row (node/element) of the
         independent constraints.
       • TYPE = COLUMN: The columns of the independent constraints are arguments of the
         linked constraint equations, resulting in one equation for each column (load pattern
         etc.) of the independent constraints.

6. Functions are defined within a $FUNCTION data block, see page 3-1112 ff..

7. For each function referenced for design constraint linking the first derivative must be avail-
   able.

8. For each linked constraint, an upper and a lower bound may be defined. If a bound does
   not exist, NO instead of a bound value has to be inputted. If both values are given,


96                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           V 19.00.287
  9. Lower and upper bounds may be scaled and shifted according to

                                 cbound = scal ∗ (cbound,I + shif t)

     where scal and shif t are either constant values c1 and c2 , respectively, or function values
     of the time or frequency dependent functions fun 1 and fun 2 . Thus, the use of functions is
     restricted to constraints with column specification parameters TIME or FREQUENCY.
     In the equation above, cbound denotes the final bound used as constraint limit and cbound,I
     is the input value as defined in the data line. If the bounds are meaningless, i.e. if the
     constraint is used as design objective or as an argument of a design constraint function,




                                                                                                     Modification
     then the result values cres itself are modified by the inverse scaling and shift operations
     as described above:
                                                  cres




                                                                                                        DAT
                                       ccons =         − shif t
                                                  scal
     The modified value ccons is then used as design objective or as argument for the design
     constraint function.

 10. At most maxcst constraints are retrieved for each constraint linking definition. If maxcst is
     omitted, the default value is used, see parameter MAXCREG within data block $PARAMETER,
     page 3-992.

Example:

   $DCLINK TYPE = ITEM
     len_disp : 1001 : disp_x disp_y disp_z : NO 1.5E+07
   $DCLINK TYPE = COLUMN
     RF_10 : 1002 : F123_RF1         ! nodeset 123 x
    &               F123_RF2         ! nodeset 123 y
    &               F123_RF3         ! nodeset 123 z
    &      : NO 1.0E3
   $DCLINK TYPE = ROW
     safety : 1003 : SIG11 SIG22 SIG13 SIG12 SIG13 SIG23 : NO 1.0E+03

marks:

1. Design constraints may be defined for any component of a configuration with the excep-
   tion of global constraints which are related to configuration and therefore restricted to
   single or top components. They are referenced by its identifier cstid or its name cstname.

2. Design constraint identifiers and names must be unique within the modification variant.
   They also must differ from identifiers or names of $DCFUNCTION and $DCLINK defini-
   tions

3. Global constraints are valid for the whole configuration and the specified situation. There-
   fore, only one global constraint is possible for one result value (e.g. weight or one eigen-
   frequency etc.) and one situation.

4. Component constraints are valid for the current component, i.e. for each element or node
   resp. belonging to the component, and the specified situation. Only one component
   constraint is possible for one result value (e.g. displacement or stress component), one
   component and one situation.

5. Design model constraints are valid for the whole design model, i.e. for all elements or
   nodes assigned to any design element, and the specified situation. Only one design
   model constraint is possible for one result value and one situation.

6. Design element constraints are valid for only one design element and one situation, i.e.
   the specified result item is constraint for all elements or nodes assigned to the design
   element deid.

7. Set constraints are valid for all elements or nodes resp. belonging to the specified element
   set eset or node set nset and one situation.




00                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         V 19.00.287
     according to column specification. A range may be selected by specifiying a second value
     ([,val2]). Default, if applicable, is LPAT = ALL , i.e. valid for all load patterns of a (static)
     situation. Which column specification parameter is applicable depends on the analysis
     type of the corresponding situation.

 10. Result values at specified nodes and elements are selected by local identifier lid, which
     is the degree of freedom identifier for node related data and the component identifier for
     element related data. The local identifier must not be omitted.

 11. Any constraint may be selected as design objective. For the design objective, bounds are
     ignored.




                                                                                                         Modification
 12. For each constraint, an upper and a lower bound may be defined. If a bound does not
     exist, NO instead of a bound value has to be inputted. If both values are given, lower ≤
     upper must be true. A constraint definition without bounds may be useful only if it is used




                                                                                                            DAT
     for the design objective function or as argument of a design constraint function or design
     constraint linking.

 13. Lower and upper bounds may be scaled and shifted according to

                                  cbound = scal ∗ (cbound,I + shif t)

     where scal and shif t are either constant values c1 resp. c2 , or function values of the
     time or frequency dependent functions f id1 and f id2 . The use of functions is therefore
     restricted for constraints with column specification parameters TIME or FREQUENCY.
     In the equation above, cbound denotes the final bound used as constraint limit and cbound,I
     is the input value as defined in the data line. If the bounds are meaningless, i.e. if the
     constraint is used as design objective or as an argument of a design constraint function,
     then the result values cres itself are modified by the inverse scaling and shift operations
     as described above:
                                                    cres
                                        ccons =          − shif t
                                                    scal
     The modified value ccons is then used as design objective or as argument for the design
     constraint function.

 14. At most maxcst constraints per column (e.g. load pattern) are retrieved for each constraint
     definition. If maxcst is omitted, the default value is used, see parameter MAXCREG within
     data block $PARAMETER, page 3-992.

30                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                              V 19.00.287
Remarks:

  1. Each individual PERMAS element test (e.g. aspect ratio, Jacobi matrix etc.) is rep-
     resented by a continuous function, that increases towards 1.0 with decreasing element
     quality and exceeds 1.0 if the element will fail the test. The design constraint is the
     approximated envelope of the maximum element test values as a function of the node
     coordinates, see the red curve in the figure below.




                                                                                                Modification
                                                                                                   DAT
                                                 1.0
     1.0




                                                       Error value




     0.0                                         0.0
               OK       Warning     Error
                                                                     Coordinates

              Figure F3-40: Individual element test and DCONSTRAINT ELTEST
  2. All values less than 1.0 indicate acceptable elements.
     Due to the approximation, elements which are not yet erroneous may already exceed
     slightly the value of 1.0.

  3. To avoid degenerated elements in shape optimization, an upper limit lower than 1.0 is
     recommended, e.g. 0.8.

  4. Especially in freeshape optimization it should be avoided to start the optimization with
     element test constraints which are already violated. This may inhibit any shape changes.

  5. For checking purposes, the element test result may be generated after any analysis
     by GENerate ELement TEST and can be exported as ITEM ELement TEST, see page
     2-401. This does not require neither an optimization analysis nor optimization input.

rameter         Type      Value      Explanation

NSTRAINT                             Constraint(s) selected as design objective:
               I>0         cstid     Constraint identifier.
               name      cstname     Constraint name.
RGET           name                  Target of design objective function:
                          MIN        Target is minimization of objective function.
                          MAX        Target is maximization of objective function.
                         ABSMIN      Target is minimization of absolute value of objective func-
                                     tion.
                         ABSMAX      Target is maximization of absolute value of objective func-
                                     tion.


marks:

1. Definition of the design objective function is only possible in the modification variant of a
   single or top component.

2. The design constraints which are identified by cstid or cstname are selected as objec-
   tive function of the design optimization, and are minimized or maximized according to
   parameter TARGET.

3. Any design constraint which is defined within a $DCONSTRAINT (see page 3-900 ff.),
   $DCLINK (see page 3-897 ff.) or $DCFUNCTION (see page 3-893 ff.) data block of
   current modification variant may be used as objective function. If bounds are defined for
   the selected constraint they are ignored.

4. If multiple constraints are selected or the selected constraint is not uniquely specified, i.e.
   it refers to more than one element or node, load pattern, mode, frequency or time, the
   maximum value will be minimized (or vice versa, depending on the TARGET value).

                                                                                                        DAT
                                mark 3:
                    0           default: pure filter;
                    1           additional constraint on minimum member size;
                    2           additional constraint on minimum member and void size.
minwidth         R > 0.0        Minimum bead width for bead design.
maxratio      0.0 < R ≤ 1.0     Maximum bead ratio for bead design.

Remarks:

  1. Design variable filters may be defined only in modification variants of single or top com-
     ponents.
  2. A design variable filter with TYPE = TOPO allows to specify a minimum dimension size
     of the structure that will be approximately targeted. Its application is restricted to de-
     sign elements of type DTOPO (see page 3-71). On the one hand hand it is an alter-
     native to the checkerboard filter specified within the UCI-command TOPO and may be
     used to define different filter radii (i.e. minimum member size) for different design ele-
     ments. If both of them are specified, the respectively larger value is applied. On the
     other hand $DSVFILT TYPE = TOPO additionally allows the specification of a maximum
     member size.
  3. The setting with additional constraints only affect the topology optimization for default
     parameter TOPOVAR = NODAL, see STARTUP section command DEFAULT (see page
     2-66 ff.). In any other case only a pure filter is applied.
  4. The application of a design variable filter with TYPE = BEAD is restricted to design el-
     ements of type DBEAD (see page 3-62). The minwidth parameter specifies the mini-
     mum width of a crimp in at least one direction that will be approximately adopted in the


V 19.00.287                     PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       3-987
   tors in the $DVCOOR definition instead of inverting upper and lower design variable limits
   $DSVLIMIT.

5. The application of a design variable filter with TYPE = FREE is restricted to design ele-
   ments of type DFREE (see page 3-64).

ample:

 TYPE = TOPO please refer to examples TOPO1 and TOPO9 of [um550].

$DSVFILT TYPE = TOPO         ! minimum member size
  1001 25.0
  1002 50.0

 TYPE = BEAD please refer to example OP5V1 of [um550].

$DSVFILT TYPE = BEAD         ! maximum 50 % of nodes at upper limit
  101 120.0 0.5              ! minimum width of bead should be 120.0

Remarks:

  1. Design variable bounds may be defined only in modification variants of single or top com-
     ponents.

  2. Bounds have to be specified for each independent design variable, but may be omitted
     for design variables which are dependent due to design variable linking, see $DSVLINK.

  3. In general the lower bound of design variables must be > 0.0, i.e. the range for design
     variable values is strictly positive. However, design variables assigned to design nodes,
     see $DSVNODE, may also get zero or negative values, i.e. may have a lower (and also
     upper) limit ≤ 0.0, if an OPTIM command is executed.

Remarks:

  1. Variant names must be unique within one component and must not begin with DFLT.

  2. If parameter NAME is omitted the default variant name for the result variant is
     DFLTRES.

  3. Result variants are selected within the situation definition, see $SITUATION.

  4. Result variants of subcomponents are selected within a $SUBVAR data block of the direct
     hypercomponent.

  5. The result variant bracket is closed by an (optional) $END RESULTS line or by a new
     component input medium level bracket line or by any high level bracket line.

               name/text                 the sum of all result column contributions.

                                         $ENTER COMPONENT line, page 3-12, remark 6.

                                          TIME = t




Item(s)       Type      Explanation

name       name     Name of foreign situation.
patid      I>0      Input load pattern identifier.
t            R      Input time specifier.
c            R      Factor for load pattern contribution.
fun        I>0      Label (integer, name or text string) of function applied to load pattern
          name/text data.




V 19.00.287                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                               3-1001
2. Result column combination rules are used to generate new result columns. If LPAT = patidc
   is specifid on header line, the result column is assigned to new load pattern patidc , if
   TIME = tc is specifid on header line, the result column is assigned to time instance tc of a
   time-dependent result.

3. Result column combination rules are identified by their name, and are executed by the
   UCI-command COMBINE.

4. Result column combination rule names are unique only within the corresponding result
   variant.

5. Each $COMBINE RESULTS data block defines for the specified combination rule name
   the complete rule for exactly one combined result column. Any extension of the rule for
   that combined result column by another data block is not possible, whereas any number of
   further combined result columns defined by the same rule may be specified by new data
   blocks. All combined result columns of one rule, however, must be either load pattern or
   time steps

6. If no situation is specified on data line, the referred result column must belong to the
   current situation.
7. Result column combination rules may refer to result columns which are generated by itself
   by other result column combinations. But then the referred, already combined load pattern
   must belong to the current situation, and the combination rule must not be recursive.
   Reference to combined result columns of foreign situations is not possible.
8. The result column combination rule is defined as follows:
                                                    X
                         zk = fun 0 (yk ) ,    yk =      ci fun i (xk,i )
                                                          i

   with

                    xk,i    datum k of referred result column i
                    yk      sum of contribution k of all referred result columns
                    zk      datum k of new result column
                    fun 0   function applied to the sum of all contributions
                    ci      factor for all contributions of result column i
                    fun i   function applied to all data of result column i

9. As long as new load pattern results are linear combinations of results of linear analy-
   ses performed in situations with the same constraint, system, and, if initial strains are
   included, loading variants, they are valid solutions by itself, and all suitable subsequent
   result generation steps may be done. Otherwise further processing of the new load pat-
   tern results is possible only in some special cases. Data selection for output purposes is
   always available.


002                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         V 19.00.287
 11. If factor c is omitted, it is replaced by the value 1.0 .

 12. Functions can be defined as general functions within a $FUNCTION data block, see page
     3-1112. If the function identifier is omitted the function is replaced by the argument itself.

Example:

  $COMBINE RESULTS   RULE = Comb_Sym_Ant LPAT = 101
                       LPAT = 201            ! current situation with factor 1.0
    SITUATION = SYM    LPAT = 1 FACTOR = +2.0
    SITUATION = ANTI LPAT = 1 FACTOR = -2.0
  $COMBINE RESULTS RULE = Comb_Sym_Ant LPAT = 102




                                                                                                      Results
                       LPAT = 201 FACTOR = 3.0




                                                                                                       DAT
  !
  $COMBINE RESULTS RULE = EXTRACTION LPAT = 201 FUNCTION = 110
    SITUATION = SIT_1 LPAT = 100 FACTOR = 1.2 FUNCTION = 210
    SITUATION = SIT_1 LPAT = 200 FACTOR = 1.3 FUNCTION = 210
    SITUATION = SIT_1 LPAT = 300 FACTOR = 1.1 FUNCTION = 210
    SITUATION = SIT_1 LPAT = 400 FACTOR = 2.8 FUNCTION = 310
  !
  $COMBINE RESULTS RULE = COMB_LOAD TIME = 1.0
    SITUATION = TRANS TIME = 1.0
    SITUATION = STAT    LPAT = 200
  $COMBINE RESULTS RULE = COMB_LOAD TIME = 2.0

  $COMBINE RESULTS RULE = COMB_LOAD TIME = 3.0

    SITUATION = STAT    LPAT = 200

Remarks:

  1. Primary or secondary results may be input within a result variant of the corresponding
     component. For further processing that result variant has to be selected in the respective
     situation.

  2. Each situation contains, depending on the analysis type, only one kind of primary results.
     Consequently, only one kind of primary results can be inputted within one result variant.

  3. Data item type including type specification, column specification and quantity type define
     the generated data objects and their degree of freedom type. Data objects within one
     result variant must be unique, therefore existing data objects must not be generated by
     input, and missing data objects may be inputted only once.

  4. If TYPE = STATISTICS is specified, the statistical values generated by EVALuation with
     option STATISTICS are expected.

  5. The generated data objects are handled internally as if being results of an analysis with
     a type defined by the column specification according to following table:

                         Column specification   Analysis type          Quantity types
                         LPAT                   Static                 REAL
                         TIME                   Transient response     REAL
                         FREQUENCY              Frequency
                                                           response   -any-
                         MODE
                                                  Real eigenvalues     REAL
                         RBMODE
                         COLUMN                 -any-                  -any-




V 19.00.287                      PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          3-1007
7. The content of data objects must be unique. Consequently, each quantity may be inputted
   only once. Quantities in result books, which are not defined explicitly, are set to zero.

8. All data items available are described in detail on the following pages. Data item names
   starting with X_ signify data blocks which cannot be processed by input, so they are
   entirely skipped.

9. In list(lid) local identifiers, e.g. degrees of freedom for nodal point values, are specified;
   list(x), list(a) or list(a, ϕ), respectively, contain the corresponding values. If no local iden-
   tifiers are specified, the values must be ordered according to ascending local identifiers,
   and trailing zeroes may be omitted.

0. If parameter NCOL is specified, each data line must contain exactly ncol values or tuples.

1. Parameter ELTYPE must be specified if data format depends on element type.

Remarks:

   1. Rules for scaling of element results may be defined in result variants of any component.
      Their names rulename must be unique within the component.

   2. Each rule may be applied to stresses (for TYPE = STRESS) or to element forces (for
      TYPE = FORCE) but not both.

   3. Scaling of stress results is available for membrane, solid, shell, solid shell and load carry-
      ing membrane elements. Scaling of element forces (i.e. stress resultants) is available for
      beam and linear spring elements.

   4. Each rule may contain any number of element result scaling definitions, but within one
      rule, the scaling definition for any element (and loadcase if specified) must be unique.

   5. For scaling of element stresses (TYPE = STRESS), the elements are selected by mate-
      rial, i.e. a definition is valid for all elements referring to the specified material.
      For scaling of element forces (TYPE = FORCE), the elements are selected by property,
      i.e. a definition is valid for all elements referring to the specified geometrical data record,
      see $GEODAT.

   6. Scaling of element results by UCI-command ERSCALE is done in two steps:

           • For TYPE = STRESS: Calculation of maximum values for von Mises stresses and
             principal stresses for each element referring to the specified material.
             For TYPE = FORCE: Calculation of maximum values for normal and shear forces
             for each element referring to the specified geometrical data record. In addition, an
             equivalent force is calculated, see remark 7.
           • If limit values are specified, the element results are scaled, see remark 8. To do
             so, the limit stress values itself may be modified (scaled) if function fun v or fun p ,
             respectively, are given.



V 19.00.287                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          3-1029
   where for beam elements the maximum normal and shear forces are given by
                                                   q            
           Nm = max(Nn ) ; n = 1, 2 and Sm = max(     Sx2′ + Sy2′ ) ; n = 1, 2
                                                                                       n

   and for spring elements
                                                             q            
          Nm = max(Nx′ ,n ) ; n = 1, 2          and Sm = max(   Ny2′ + Nz2′ ) ; n = 1, 2
                                                                                           n

   If a function fun is specified, this function is used instead. It must be a function with two
   independent variables, i.e. it holds

                                           Fv,m = fun(Nm , Sm )

   The function must be given in a $FUNCTION data block, see page 3-1112 ff..
8. For each definition, i.e. for each property or material within one rule, limit values may be
   defined. Element results are then scaled according to following rules
      • If function fun v or fun p , respectively, are missing, von Mises equivalent stress σv
        and principal stress σp are scaled according to
                                                   σv                        σp
                                    (σv )sc =                  (σp )sc =
                                                σv,lim,0                   σp,lim,0
        using the input limit values σv,lim,0 or σp,lim,0 , respectively.
      • If function fun v or fun p , respectively, are input, the limit values itself are scaled first
        by
                        σv,lim = σv,lim,0 · fun v (σv )   σp,lim = σp,lim,0 · fun p (σp )
        using the stress value to be scaled as independent variable of the function, and so
        the scaling of stresses is done according to
                                            σv                                      σp
                       (σv )sc =                               (σp )sc =
                                   σv,lim,0 · fun v (σv )                  σp,lim,0 · fun p (σp )
        The functions fun v and fun p must be functions with one independent variable. If
        the function value fun v (σv ) or f idp (σp ) is equal zero, the corresponding stress value
        remains unchanged, i.e. it is not scaled.
   Element forces are scaled according to
                               Nm                            Sm                         Fv,m
                  (Nm )sc =                   (Sm )sc =                (Fv,m )sc =
                              Nm,lim                        Sm,lim                      Fv,lim
   with maximum normal force Nm , maximum shear force Sm and maximum equivalent force
   Fv,m .
   Either all (two or three) or only one limit value may be input. If a definition contains only
   one limit value (σv,lim or Nm,lim , respectively) or only one limit value with scaling rule
   (σv,lim and fun v (σv )), then this value is used for all stress or force values.


030                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                          V 19.00.287
     Load cases not specified are not scaled.

 10. If an element result scaling rule is applied to statistic data, e.g. in a modal timehistory
     analysis after executing the GENerate MODAL TIMEhistory STATISTICS command, then
     the columns with indices remain unscaled.

 11. If OPTIONAL is specified, the corresponding rule part is optional; i.e. it is skipped if
     execution is not possible (e.g. material not referenced). Referenced general functions,
     however, must be existing.

Example:

                                                                                                    DAT
  $ELRESRULE NAME = SCALE_STATIC TYPE = FORCE
    SHELL_P1, 110.0,110.0 21    SHELL_P2, 110.0,110.0            21
    SHELL_P1, 90.0,100.0 22     SHELL_P2, 90.0,100.0             22

  $ELRESRULE NAME = SCALE_AX       TYPE = STRESS
    MAT_1, 20.0,101

marks:

1. Failure functions are defined in the result variant of single or top components only. Their
   identifiers must be unique within the actual variant.
2. A failure function is established by a limit state function together with its arguments.
3. Each failure function g(Z, d) describes one mode of failure of the structure. Vector Z
   contains the state variables of the problem, which may be results of a finite element anal-
   ysis or basic variables used as direct parameters, whereas vector d contains additional


032                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         V 19.00.287
  4. The arguments of the limit state function may be the state variables, i.e. the elements of
     the associated z-vector (see the $ZVECTOR data block description), constant values or
     time. They must be defined on the data lines in the order of their occurrence in the limit
     state function.

  5. If ZVECTOR is specified within data list, then all elements of the associated z-vector are
     included.

  6. The argument list of each failure function must contain at least one z-vector element;
     argument lists with time and/or constant values only are not possible.

  7. Each z-vector element may be inserted into the argument list more than once.




                                                                                                  Results
  8. Each element of each z-vector must be referenced at least once.




                                                                                                   DAT
  9. Different failure functions may refer to the same z-vector.

 10. The limit state function itself is defined as general function within a $FUNCTION data
     block, see page 3-1112. The number of independent variables of the general function
     must be equal to the number of arguments of the limit state function.

Remarks:

   1. At least one fatigue load definition is required for a fatigue / durability analysis.

   2. One fatigue analysis refers to one specified fatigue load definition. An arbitrary number
      of fatigue loads may be defined, but only one may be defined without an explicit FLDEF
      label, i.e. the FLDEF labels for various fatigue load definitions must be disjoint.
      If no explicit FLDEF is given, the default name FLDEF = DFLT_FLDEF is used.

   3. Defining fatigue load collections is only possible within the result variant of a single or top
      component. It is applicable for all analyses with primary load pattern results, i.e. UCI
      commands STATIC or INERTIA (without a nonlinear load history from $NLLOAD).

   4. Each data line defines one load contribution of the load collective. A load contribution is
      the combination of a min / max scaled load pattern lpat with a number of repetition cycles
      ncyc.

   5. Scaling factors sl and su define the lower / upper load scaling per cycle. For, e.g. fully
      reversed load cycles, sl may be set to the value of −su .



V 19.00.287                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                            3-1035
7. The input type FLDEF yields a damage result by superimposing previously generated
   fatigue results without the additional cost of performing a rainflow analysis. E.g. this
   allows to define a load collective based on damage results from time history data.

ample:

ATIGUE COLLECTIVE     FLDEF = MY_UNITLOAD
101 0.0 1.0 1             ! load pattern 101, unscaled and only 1 cycle

ATIGUE COLLECTIVE FLDEF = MY_LP_COLLECTION_1
101   0.0 0.5    1000 ! 1000 times 50 % of load pattern 101
101 -1.2 1.2      200 ! 200 times 120 % of load pattern 101 (fully reversed)
102   0.0 3.0      50 !   50 times 300 % of load pattern 102

1. The assignment of S-N curves always applies to a specified fatigue load definition from

   Thus, ...

Remarks:

   1. At least one fatigue load definition is required for a fatigue / durability analysis.

   2. One fatigue analysis refers to one specified fatigue load definition. An arbitrary number
      of fatigue loads may be defined, but only one may be defined without an explicit FLDEF
      label, i.e. the FLDEF labels for various fatigue load definitions must be disjoint.
      If no explicit FLDEF is given, the default name FLDEF = DFLT_FLDEF is used.

   3. Defining a fatigue load is only possible within the result variant of a single or top com-
      ponent. It is applicable for all analyses with primary time history results, i.e. UCI com-
      mands STATIC, INERTIA, NLMATERIAL, or NLINERTIA (with a nonlinear load history
      from $NLLOAD) and DIRECTTIMEhistory or MODALTIMEhistory, respectively.


V 19.00.287                         PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                   3-1039
  bound,i.e. by using the dash symbol for tS . Multiple sections / intervals of the timehistory
  may be referenced, but is must be ensured that they do not overlap except for isolated
  points. At these points the arithmetic mean value of the scaling parameters are used.

5. Two mechanism are available to use a combination of stresses during a fatigue analysis.

    (a) A result combination rule may be referenced in the definition of the fatigue load. In
        this case, the result combination rule $COMBINE RESULTS, is applied during the
        fatigue analysis on-the-fly, i.e. this option uses minimal extra DMS space but does
        not allow to export the combined stresses.
    (b) An alternative is to use an in situ result combination via COMBINE. In this case, a
        combination rule must not be referenced in the fatigue load definition.

 1.0     - 10.0          ! assembly phase (history from start to 10.0)
 1.0 10.0 20.0           ! low load
10.0 20.0 30.0           ! high load
 1.0 31.0                ! end load       (history from 31.0 to end)

         name/text $FUNCTION, see remark 5.
         Symbol Dash symbol to mark an unlimited lower or upper bound.
tE         R       Time bounds for function, see remark 6.

marks:

1. At least one fatigue load definition is required for a fatigue / durability analysis.
2. One fatigue analysis refers to one specified fatigue load definition. An arbitrary number
   of fatigue loads may be defined, but only one may be defined without an explicit FLDEF
   label, i.e. the FLDEF labels for various fatigue load definitions must be disjoint.
   If no explicit FLDEF is given, the default name FLDEF = DFLT_FLDEF is used.
3. Defining fatigue load time lines is only possible within the result variant of a single or
   top component. It is applicable for all analyses with primary results with displacement
   degrees of freedom.
4. For the rainflow algorithm of the GENerate FATIGUE analysis the overall stress load his-
   tory (see remarks 5 and 6) is evaluated in the time range tstart ≤ t ≤ tend and sampled
   with time increment tinc (default 1.0).

     shifted by an extra time delay tD , i.e.:

marks:

1. Definition of excitation frequencies for frequency response analysis is only possible within
   a result variant of a single or top component.

2. The DOFTYPE must match the type of the performed analysis. For fluid-structure coupled
   models this will be DISP for pure mechanical, PRES for pure acoustic and MATH for FS
   coupled analysis.

3. Each data block defines one list of primary frequencies and, optionally, refinement rule
   and bounds for that list.

4. Each frequency value list is determined in three steps:

       • Definition of a list of primary frequencies by input or by selection of result frequen-
         cies.
       • Optional elimination of frequency values outside of corresponding boundaries.
       • Optional refinement of that list of primary frequencies. Values generated outside of
         corresponding boundaries are omitted.

5. All frequency values of all lists defined in one result variant are collected and sorted in
   ascending order. Duplicated or very close frequencies are eliminated.



046                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         V 19.00.287
                      f1 , f1 + ∆f, . . . , f1 + i ∆f, . . . , f1 + n ∆f ;          f1 + n ∆f ≤ f2

        • If PRIMARY = LOG is specified, a list of frequencies with logarithmic intervals is
          generated:

                                                                                              1    f2
                    fi = f1 exp((i − 1) α) ; i = 1, . . . , nl + 1           with       α=      ln
                                                                                              nl f1

  7. For the PRIMARY = EIGCLUS option, CLUSTER is expected to be specified. This op-
     tion is especially helpful, if sensitivities are needed, since the derivative at the eigenmode
     is not numerically stable and should be avoided.




                                                                                                                   Results
  8. If PRIMARY = FUNCTION is specified, all sampling points of a function are used as pri-




                                                                                                                    DAT
     mary frequencies. The function must be a tabular function with one independent variable,
     see page 3-1149.

  9. If PRIMARY = ROTSPEED is specified, then the excitation frequencies are given by
     the actual rotational speeds, specified by a $ROTSPEED data block, see page 3-1064,
     leading to a synchronous whirl analysis. Available only for modal frequency response
     analysis for displacement degrees of freedom, UCI-command MODAL FREQuency (see
     page 2-208 ff.). Refinement by options CLUSTER or GEOM as well as limitation by option
     BOUNDS are not provided.

 10. Each list of primary frequency values may be refined separately.

        • If CLUSTER is specified, frequency values with equidistant intervals are generated
          in the (close) environment of each primary frequency, i.e. in addition to each primary
          frequency fi in respective list 2 ndf frequency values

                                             fi ± i df ; i = 1, . . . , ndf

          are generated.
        • If GEOM is specified, the intervals between successive primary frequencies of re-
          spective list are subdivided symmetrically in geometrical progressions with common
          ratio s, leading to 2ns − 1 additional frequency values per interval, becoming closer
          and closer with approach to the primary frequencies, i.e. within each interval fi , fi+1
          of the sorted primary frequencies the values

                                   fi+1 − fi                       fi+1 − fi
                     fi + s(n−1)             ,     fi+1 − s(n−1)             ;        n = 1, . . . , ns
                                       2                               2
          are generated (The central value at (fi + fi+1 )/2 is generated only once).
          If bounds are specified not coinciding exactly with primary frequencies, F1 and F2
          are taken as central values of ’fictitious’ frequency intervals.

 11. Frequency values are input in cycles per second.

     mands NLMATERIAL, NLTEMP and DIRECT NLTEMP) and for stepwise linear contact
     analysis with a $NLLOAD load history (UCI command STATIC).

  2. The degree of freedom type must correspond to the analysis performed, i.e. DISP for
     mechanical and TEMP for thermal analyses.

  3. Each data block defines a list of points during the loading process. All lists defined within
     one result variant are collected, sorted, and define the steps where results are calculated
     and stored during the loading process.

  4. For nonlinear static and temperature analysis, the final result step is always stored. If




                                                                                                       Results
     STEPS = ALL is specified, results are calculated and stored for all steps in question
     (number and length of those steps are defined via the UCI-command and automatic




                                                                                                        DAT
     step length adaption). If STEPS = INTERVAL is specified, results are calculated and
     stored for all steps in question (number and length of those steps are defined via the
     UCI-command and automatic step length adaption) inside the declared time interval. If
     there are no result step definitions in the result variant, only the results of the final state
     are stored.

  5. If STEPS = PERIOD is specified for a DIRECT NLTIME analysis results are calculated
     and stored after each period of time. It should not be mixed up with the result request
     command STEPS = ALL . STEPS = PERIOD is ignored for all other analysis types.

  6. For a stepwise linear contact analysis (UCI command STATIC) no automatic time stepping
     is available. Therefore the result steps also define the time discretization of the loading
     process, i.e. evaluation times and result steps are identical and all result steps are stored.
     A set of default result steps is derived from the sampling times used for the $NLLOAD load
     history definition, i.e. if STEPS = ALL is specified (or if $NLRESULTS is omitted) results
     are calculated and stored for all sampling times given by $NLLOAD plus any additional
     result steps given herein (a $NLLOAD GENERAL without explicit bounds or sampling
     times will introduce time steps t = 0.0 and t = 1.0). Hence – for the stepwise linear contact
     analysis – $NLRESULTS may just be used to specify additional evaluation points.
     If STEPS = ALL is omitted, but at least one result step is given, then the highest result
     step specified also sets the maximum time value for the evaluation of the loading process
     (taking precedence over the maximum sampling time from $NLLOAD).

  7. If STEPS = EQUI is specified, a list of points is generated according to
                    r1 , r1 + ∆r, . . . , r1 + i ∆r, . . . , r1 + n ∆r ;   r1 + n ∆r ≤ r2

  8. If STEPS = LIST is specified, a list of points is expected, ordered according to ascending
     magnitude.

  9. If STEPS = INTERVAL is specified results are calculated and stored for all steps which
     are lying inside the given lower ts and upper te bound. It should not be mixed up with the
     result request command STEPS = ALL .

marks:

1. Parameter data sets for ply failure criteria may be defined in result variants of any com-
   ponent. Their names pf pname must be unique within the component.

2. Each parameter data set must contain all necessary parameters for an evaluation of the
   requested failure criterion from the UCI-command PLYFAILure.

3. Parameter data sets for ply failure criteria are applicable for elements with laminate ma-
   terial reference described by plies ($LAMINATE and $PLY), i.e. shell elements SHELL3
   and SHELL4.

4. The default setting for the parameters in direction normal to ply 1-2 plane are Zt = Yt and
   Zc = Yc assuming a transversely isotropic behavior.

5. If the selected ply failure criterion should consider interlaminar shear data the parameters
   S31 , S23 must be given. Otherwise only inplane shear data are considered.

6. The element and ply selection for ply failure criterion parameters is created automatically
   according to the input of the

      • i) laminate material name (lamname):
        all elements referring to the specified laminate material.
      • ii) homogeneous material name (matname):
        all plies containing the specified homogeneous material.

7. If the ply failure criterion parameters should be used for the complete laminate material
   definition then the option "ALL" must be specified. Otherwise local ply identifiers can

     axial material tests. These parameters are sufficient for global tensor polynomial failure

                         -1 Minimal values.

                      100 List of values, see remark 8.

          I>0        Label (integer, name or text string) of function.
         name/text


marks:

1. Result item extraction rules are defined in the result variant of single or top components
   only. They may refer to result items in any component of a configuration.

2. Result item extraction rule identifiers must be unique within the actual variant.

3. Result item extraction rules are mainly used within sampling (see UCI-command SAMPLING)
   to extract a specified number of data from result items selected within $RSLITEM data
   blocks. The result data are collected over the task loops and, at the end, are available as
   xy-data sets over the sample counter.

4. Result item extraction rules can only be used with UCI-commands SAMPLING, OPTIM
   and TOPO and are ignored in all other solution procedures.

5. If ITEM is specified, then each rule extracts nof val result values from the corresponding
   result item selection. The use of ALL instead of nof val in combination with the selec-
   tion of ALL result columns in $RSLITEM extracts a maximum of MAXREXT values, see
   $PARAMETER.

6. If FUNCTION is specified, then each rule extracts the specified number of result values
   from each corresponding result item selection, and transfer the data in that order as in-
   dependent variables to function fun. The function value is then available as xy data sets
   over the sample counter.

7. The selection of result values to be extracted out of all result values available for the
   specified result item is controlled by skey.

8. Selection skey = 100 means that nof val values are taken in the sequence as stored
   in the data object, starting with the first one. This selection is available up to now only
   for complex eigenvalue extraction by $RSLITEM CFREQ (see page 3-1081 ff.) or by
   $RSLITEM CAMPBELL (see page 3-1075 ff.).

Data lines:
If PRIMARY = LIST is specified (default):


                list(fi )




If PRIMARY = EQUI is specified (only one data line per data block):


                f1    f2    ∆f




If PRIMARY = LOG is specified (only one data line per data block):


                f1    f2    nl




No data lines allowed if PRIMARY = EIG is specified.




V 19.00.287                       PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                    3-1065
                          mark 7.
                R>0       Last rotational speed for generation with f2 > f1 . For negative
                          values see remark 7.
f               R>0       Rotational speed interval.
                I>0       Number of logarithmic intervals.


marks:

1. Definition of rotational speed values for analyses of rotating systems is only possible
   within a result variant of a single or top component.
2. Each data block defines one list of primary rotational speeds and, optionally, refinement
   rule and bounds for that list.
3. Each rotational speed value list is determined in three steps:
      • Definition of a list of primary rotational speeds by input or by selection of result values
        (eigenfrequecies).
      • Optional elimination of rotational speed values outside of corresponding boundaries.
      • Optional refinement of that list of primary rotational speeds. Values generated out-
        side of corresponding boundaries are omitted.
4. All rotational speed values of all lists defined in one result variant are collected and sorted
   in ascending order. Duplicated or very close rotational speeds are eliminated.
5. Lists of primary rotational speed values may be generated.
      • If PRIMARY = EQUI is specified, a list of equidistant rotational speeds is gener-
        ated:

                    f1 , f1 + ∆f, . . . , f1 + i ∆f, . . . , f1 + n ∆f ;          f1 + n ∆f ≤ f2
      • If PRIMARY = LOG is specified, a list of rotational speeds with logarithmic intervals
        is generated:
                                                                                           1    f2
                  fi = f1 exp((i − 1) α) ; i = 1, . . . , nl + 1           with       α=     ln
                                                                                           nl f1
6. Each list of primary rotational speed values may be refined separately.
      • If CLUSTER is specified, rotational speed values with equidistant intervals are gen-
        erated in the (close) environment of each primary rotational speed, i.e. in addition to
        each primary rotational speed fi in respective list 2 ndf rotational speed values
                                           fi ± i df ; i = 1, . . . , ndf
         are generated.


066                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                     V 19.00.287
           each interval fi , fi+1 of the sorted primary rotational speeds the values

                                   fi+1 − fi                     fi+1 − fi
                     fi + s(n−1)             ,   fi+1 − s(n−1)             ;   n = 1, . . . , ns
                                       2                             2
           are generated (The central value at (fi + fi+1 )/2 is generated only once).
           If bounds are specified not coinciding exactly with primary rotational speeds, F1 and
           F2 are taken as central values of ’fictitious’ rotational speed intervals.

  7. Rotational speeds may have negative values if they are specified by list with PRIMARY
     = LIST or generated with equidistant intervals by PRIMARY = EQUI. In addition, for
     negative rotational speeds neither bounds nor refinements are allowed. Furthermore,




                                                                                                            Results
     negative rotational speeds are not allowed if FRICTION = MATRICES is specified in the




                                                                                                             DAT
     $CONTLOCK data block (see page 3-32), e.g. for brake squeal analysis.

  8. The unit of input values is defined by parameter XTYPE; the default is input of frequency
     values in cycles per unit time (i.g. cycles per second). Of course, the selected type of
     input values is valid for bound and cluster definition values too.

Example:

  ! list of rotational speeds in revolutions per minute
  $ROTSPEED XTYPE = RPM
    1000.0 1500.0 2000.0 2500.0 2800.0

  ! rotational speeds in the range 10 to 100 rad/s, step 2 rad/s
  $ROTSPEED PRIMARY = EQUI XTYPE = OMEGA
    10.0 100.0 2.0

  ! rotational speeds at eigenfrequencies plus
  ! clusters with constant steps 0.1/0.01
  $ROTSPEED PRIMARY = EIG CLUSTER = 4,0.1
  $ROTSPEED PRIMARY = EIG CLUSTER = 4,0.01

Please refer to examples DEVX4, DEVX6, DEVX7, DRA5, DRA6 and DRA12 of [um550].

   single or top components. They are referenced by its identifier rstid or its name rstname.

2. Up to now, result item selections are available for sampling (UCI-command SAMPLING),
   optimization (UCI-command OPTIM and TOPO) and reliability analysis (UCI-commands
   MCS RELIABILITY ANalysis, RELIABILITY ANalysis and OPTREL), and must be speci-
   fied in the result variants belonging to the situations for sampling or reliability analysis.

3. Result item selection identifiers and names must be unique within the result variant.

4. Global results are valid for the whole configuration and the specified situation. Therefore,
   only one global result item selection is possible for one result value (eg. one eigenfre-
   quency etc.) and one situation.

5. Component results are extracted for the current component, i.e. for each element or node
   resp. belonging to the component, and the specified situation. Only one component result
   item selection is possible for one result value (eg. displacement or stress component),
   one component and one situation.

6. Design model results are extracted for the whole design model, i.e. for all elements or
   nodes assigned to any design element, and the specified situation. Only one design
   model result item selection is possible for one result value and one situation.

7. Design element results are extracted for only one design element and one situation, i.e.
   the specified result item selection is valid for all elements or nodes assigned to the design
   element deid.

8. Set results are extracted for all elements or nodes resp. belonging to the specified ele-
   ment set eset or node set nset and one situation.

9. Direct results are valid for one specific result value at one node nid or element eid and
   one situation.

0. Result item selections may be valid for all or restricted to one particular load pattern, time
   step etc. according to column specification. Default, if applicable, is LPAT = ALL , i.e.
   valid for all load pattern of a (static) situation. Which column specification parameter is
   applicable depends on the analysis type of the corresponding situation.

1. Result values at specified nodes and elements are selected by local identifier lid, which
   is the degree of freedom identifier for node related data and the component identifier for
   element related data. The local identifier must not be omitted.

pending on element type, there are different stress formats available to define element stress
ults:


         All elements with uniaxial stress state, i.e. 3D and axisymmetric flange elements.
         All 3D elements where averaged nodal point stresses are available, i.e. all 3D
         solids and membranes with the exception of shear panel SHEAR4. Stress com-
         ponents refer to component system.
         Homogeneous shell elements with stress output at lower and upper surface. For
         Tresca equivalent stress only plane shear stress is taken into accoint, i.e. it does
         not necessarily deliver the actual maximum shear stress. Principal stresses are
         only available for real arithmetic and belong to the plane stress state at surface.
         Axisymmetric solids. Stress components refer to component system.
         Beam elements with standard cross-sections. Only normal stresses are taken
         into account, shear stress contributions are ignored completely.

rameter   Type         Value        Explanation

ND        name       ABS            Steps are defined as actual values of total time.
          name      RATIO           Steps are defined as fraction of total time.
FTYPE     name     dof type         Degree of freedom type. For default see description
                                    of $ENTER COMPONENT line, page 3-12, remark 6.




                   h        i   h                          i
          t   ∆t       tG           NLSOLV = solvname




em(s)          Type         Explanation
               R            Time t at which the time step increment ∆t shall be done.
t             R> 0          Time step increment, ∆t > 0.
               R            Time gate tG at which the time step increment ∆t shall end.
lvname        name          Abbreviation name of solution method:
                            NR/MNR/SNM/QNM/THOMAS.




102                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        V 19.00.287
     NLMATERIAL, NLTEMP and DIRECT NLTEMP).

  2. Each data block defines a pair of time/time increments/time gate/solution method dur-
     ing the loading process. All lists defined within one result variant are collected, sorted,
     and define the times/time step increment/time gate/solution method during the loading
     process.

  3. If a time gate tG is specified, the given time increment ∆t is used and held constant for
     all following time steps from time t as long as the time is less or equal the time gate.

  4. If no time gate tG is specified, the given time increment ∆t is used once at time t. After-




                                                                                                    Results
     wards the automatic time incrementation is applied if no other user time requests exist.




                                                                                                     DAT
  5. The global solution method given in the UCI command by NLSOLV = xxxx can be over-
     written by the definition of the name in NLSOLV = NR/MNR/SNM/QNM/THOMAS. The
     solution method declared here is used from time t as long as no other solution method is
     defined. The solution method is never automatically switched back to the given solution
     method in the UCI command.

  6. The maximum number of pairs for time/time increments within one result variant is re-
     stricted to 250.

  7. For contradictions between the requested time steps and other time stepping information
     see $NLRESULTS.

  8. If KIND = ABS is specified, then the points during the loading process are defined as
     actual values of the process itself, i.e. the input values must satisfy 0 ≤ r ≤ T EN D where
     0 represents the beginning and TEND the end of the loading process as declared in the
     UCI command.
     It must not be mixed up with KIND = RATIO in the same result variant.

  9. If KIND = RATIO is specified, then the points during the loading process are defined as
     fraction of the loading process itself, i.e. the input values must satisfy 0 ≤ r ≤ 1 where 0
     represents the beginning and 1 the end of the loading process.
     For a stepwise linear contact analysis (UCI command STATIC) KIND = RATIO is not
     applicable, since all result steps must be specified explicitly with absolute ’process time’
     values according to the $NLLOAD load history.

marks:

1. Discrete values of design or basic variables are used to perform analyses several times
   with different values for design or basic variables. They are not suited for optimization
   or reliability analyses, and must not be confused with possible discrete values of design
   variables input by data block $DSVVAL.
2. Discrete values of design or basic variables must be specified within the result variant of
   single or top components.
3. Within one result variant, discrete values may be aligned to design variables or to basic
   variables but not to both; so, in a corresponding task loop, the loop is done either over
   design variables or over basic variables.


106                        PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                  V 19.00.287

     values for each design or basic variable, i.e. by
                                                    Y

                                                          i

     where nv,i is the number of discrete values specified for design or basic variable i.

  7. If INPUT = EQUI is specified, a list of equidistant values is generated:

                  x1 , x1 + ∆x, . . . , x1 + i ∆f, . . . , x1 + n ∆x ;          x1 + n ∆x ≤ x2
