                                                                                         n l x1

  9. If INPUT = FUNCTION is specified, the function must be a tabular function with one
     independent variable, see page 3-1149. The values of the independent variable of the
     function are used for sampling.

 10. Limits of design variables given by a $DSVLIMIT data block are ignored, restrictions like
     the admissible range of design variables (e.g. positive for geometrical data) or the re-
     stricted domain of probability density functions of basic variables must be taken into ac-
     count in the definition of $VPARVAL.

Remarks:

  1. Z-vectors are defined in the result variant of single or top components only. Their identifier
     must be unique within the actual variant.
  2. Each element of each z-vector must be referenced at least once by a failure function
     definition, see $FAILFUNCTION data block.
  3. Z-vectors contain the state variables of reliability analyses. State variables may be result
     items of the finite element analysis or basic variables used as state function parameters
     directly.
  4. The length of a z-vector is defined implicitly by the highest index zvindmax . Within the
     z-vector, all elements 1 ≤ zvind ≤ zvindmax must be defined.
  5. Two or more z-vector elements may refer to the same result item or basic variable.
  6. Each z-vector must contain at least one result item.
  7. Result items to be inserted into z-vectors are defined within a $RSLITEM data block
     and accessed by its identifier rstid or name rstname. If result items are calculated in
     subcomponents, the name name of the subcomponent must be specified in addition.
  8. All result items to be inserted into one z-vector must belong to the same load pattern. If
     the load is a stochastic one, then the referred load pattern must be the combined load
     pattern describing the stochastic load.
  9. Basic variables to be inserted into z-vectors must be declared as state function parame-
     ters at their definition, see $BASVAR data block.
 10. Each data line inserts at least element zvind of the z-vector. If a result item contains more
     than one value (e.g. displacements of a node set), than by nof val the number of result
     values may be specified which are inserted consecutively into the z-vector, starting at
     index zvind. The selection of result values to be inserted out of all result values available
     for the specified result item is controlled by skey.

  2. Only one data line per data block is allowed.
  3. The parameter NVAR is used to specify the number of independent variables of the as-
     sembled function, not the number of independent variables of the top level primary func-
     tion. If parameter NVAR is not specified then nof var = 1 is assumed.
  4. Functions used to define assembled functions must be primary functions, i.e. they may
     be defined as library, tabular or user-supplied functions, and must not be assembled
     functions by itself.
  5. Definitions of assembled functions may not be recursive.

     corresponding primary functions. Second derivative is available in addition for assembled
     functions with only one independent variable.

                                   n−1

2. Given three points P0 , P1 and P2 the two orthogonal unit-length direction vectors D1 , D2 ∈
   R3 are computed as:
                                 P1 − P0
                         D1 =                     and       D2 = N × D1
                                kP1 − P0 k

   where N is the unit length normal vector

                                        (P1 − P0 ) × (P2 − P0 )
                                N =
                                       k(P1 − P0 ) × (P2 − P0 )k

   of the plane spanned by P0 , P1 and P2 .

3. By defining trimming parameters tmin and tmax , the original definition range t ∈ Ω (see
   remarks above) may be further restricted to:

                                      t ∈ Ω ∩ [tmin , tmax ]

4. If an offset vector D = (dx dy dz )T is specified, an offset with constant distance kDk is
   added to the original space curve:

                                                             D × f ′ (t)
                             f (t)   ←      f (t) + kDk ·
                                                            kD × f ′ (t)k

   The curve function must be continuously differentiable, otherwise the offset is undefined.
   Furthermore, to be well defined the offset vector D should not be parallel to the tangent
   vector of the space curve f ′ (t) in the definition range t ∈ Ω.

The formula syntax follows the general known math notation (e.g. f (x, y) = (x+y)ˆ2.0). First the
user must enter the name of the function (e.g. f ), followed by the list of variables of the function
in brackets (e.g. (x, y)). After the equality sign =, a formula expression may be defined, using
the mathematical operations and constants defined in the tables below, numbers and previously
defined variables. In addition, brackets () may be used. All numbers may be integer or floating
point numbers (1, 2., 3.0, −3.62E − 5 etc.).
For all formula functions, first and second derivatives are available. All formula functions are
threadsafe and may be used in a parallel environment. Performance wise, formula functions
are slower compared to standard library functions. So if the function evaluation is critical for
performance, standard library functions should be used.

marks:

1. By $FUNCTION FOURIERSRS a Fourier transformation is done for an existing tabular
   function fun, defined for a period T .

2. Since the Fourier transform of a real function is a complex one, two new tabular func-
   tions fun 1 and fun 2 are generated. If DATTYPE = RI (default) is specified, function fun 1
   contains the real part and function fun 2 the imaginary part of the Fourier transform, for
   DATTYPE = AP function fun 1 contains the amplitude and function fun 2 the phase in de-
   grees. The values of the new tabular functions are the coefficients ck of a complex Fourier
   series of order K which may be written as real series for DATTYPE = RI by
                                      K
                                      X
                             x(t) =     (ℜ(ck ) cos ωk t − ℑ(ck ) sin ωk t)
                                      k=0

    or, if DATTYPE = AP is specified, by
                                               K
                                               X
                                      x(t) =         ĉk cos(ωk t + ϕk )
                                               k=0

    with
                           ωk = 2πk
                                 T                 Circular frequency
                                p
                           ĉk = ℜ(ck )2 + ℑ(ck )2 Amplitude
                           ϕk = arctan ℑ(c k)
                                       ℜ(ck )               Phase angle

3. According to parameter METHOD, a discrete Fourier transformation (DFT) or a fast
   Fourier transformation (FFT) is performed. If not specified, the method is selected in-
   ternally.

4. The function to be transformed must be a tabular function in the time domain, i.e. the
   independent variable is assumed to represent the time. It is given by N0 + 1 tuples
   (x(tn ), tn ), n = 0, 1, . . . , N0 ; extrapolation is not taken into account. The period of the
   function is defined as difference between first and last time value:

                                               T = tn − t0



128                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           V 19.00.287
                                                                               N
     In some cases, the values of the function in the time domain cannot be used directly:

        • If fast Fourier transformation is requested, N must be a power of 2. Therefore N is
          determined according to




                                                                                                    Function
                      N = 2M       with     2M −1 < (N0 − 1) ≤ 2M ,      M integer




                                                                                                     Data
        • If the function values are not equidistant or if N is not equal N0 − 1, the function is
          evaluated at N equidistant points to prepare the input for Fourier transformation.

  6. The order of the generated Fourier series can be specified by parameter LIMIT, directly
     by mf or by upper frequency limit f req. The highest possible order, however is given by
     N/2 corresponding to a frequency of N/(2T ).

  7. If a threshold is defined, all terms of the Fourier series with amplitudes less than the
     threshold value are removed from the generated function.

  8. Tabular functions generated by Fourier transformation may be used as primary functions
     for the definition of assembled functions.

  9. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.

 10. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
     any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component, and
     are valid and accessible for all components.

Example:

   $FUNCTION FOURIERSRS LABEL = 2101,2102          DATTYPE = RI
     FUNCTION = 1115 METHOD = DFT

   $FUNCTION FOURIERSRS LABEL = 2201,2202 DATTYPE = AP
     FUNCTION = 1112 METHOD = FFT LIMIT = 200.0

Please refer to example DRA11 of [um550].

Remarks:

     1. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.

     2. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
        any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component and
        are valid and accessible for all components.

     3. Only one data line per data block is allowed.

     4. At least one function coefficient must be different from zero.

     5. Since in some cases input values are considered as integer values, floating point as well
        as integer values are accepted on the data line.

     6. The maximum number of coefficients for library functions is restricted to 2000.

     7. Trailing zeros in list of coefficients may be omitted. Exception: function type TRINOMIAL.

     8. First derivatives are available for all library functions, second derivatives only for library
        functions with one independent variable and for polynomials of type WSUMLIN, WSUMQUARE,
        SUMSQDIFF, FRACLINXY and TRINOMIAL.

     9. Arguments of trigonometric functions are expected to be in radians.

    10. Results of inverse trigonometric functions are in radians.

    11. For function type POWERLIN the argument x must be greater than zero.

    12. If for function type POWEREXPCOS the exponent c2 and the factor c1 are both different
        from zero, then the argument x must be greater than zero.

    13. For function type FRACPOLYPOLY the number of coefficients must be always greater
        than 2, and the denominator must be always nonzero.

    14. Since for functions type WSUMLIN and WSUMQUARE the number of coefficients deter-
        mine the number of independent variables, at least 2 coefficients must be specified.


V 19.00.287                     PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       3-1133
   least one of the coefficients a and b must be unequal zero.

7. For function type SUMSQDIFF the number of coefficients must be always be odd and
   greater than 2, and all di must be non-zero.

8. For function type TRINOMIAL the number of coefficients must always match the corre-
   sponding maximum polynomial degree specified in the first coefficient. It is not possible to
   omit coefficients, e.g. for a maximum polynomial degree of 2 there must be 10 polynomial
   coefficients otherwise an error will be returned. The maximum polynomial degree is 20,
   resulting in 1772 coefficients.

9. The zero function does always return zero. Sometimes it is useful to exchange a function
   for zero for testing purposes for example.

  2. Only one data line per data block is allowed.

  3. If parameter NVAR is not specified, then nof var = 1 is assumed.

  4. Functions used to define assembled functions must be primary functions, i.e. they may be
     defined as library, tabular or user-supplied functions and must not be assembled functions
     by itself.

  5. Definitions of assembled functions may not be recursive.

  6. First derivatives are available for all assembled functions, if the derivatives exist for all
     corresponding primary functions. Second derivative is available in addition for assembled
     functions with only one independent variable.

  7. Arguments of trigonometric functions are expected to be in radians.

  8. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.

  9. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
     any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component, and
     are valid and accessible for all components.

Remarks:

    1. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.

    2. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
       any other variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component
       and are valid and accessible for all components.

    3. Only one data line per data block is allowed.
    4. First and second derivatives are available for all SURFACE functions.
    5. TYPE = PLANE defines a plane surface with parametric equation for f (u, v) and a defi-
       nition range (u, v) ∈ Ωu × Ωv as follows:

                          f (u, v) = P0 + u · D1 + v · D2 ,    (u, v) ∈ (−∞, +∞) × (−∞, +∞)

          The direction vectors D1 and D2 are derived from the points P0 , P1 and P2 specified in
          the corresponding data line as described in remark 14.
    6. TYPE = CYLINDER defines a cylindrical surface with parametric equation for f (u, v) and
       a definition range (u, v) ∈ Ωu × Ωv as follows:

                                 f (u, v) = P0 + r · (cos(u) · D1 + sin(u) · D2 ) + v · D3


V 19.00.287                            PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      3-1145
7. TYPE = SPHERE defines a spherical surface with parametric equation for f (u, v) and a
   definition range (u, v) ∈ Ωu × Ωv as follows:

             f (u, v) = P0 + r · cos(v) · (cos(u) · D1 + sin(u) · D2 ) + r · sin(v) · D3

                                (u, v) ∈ (−∞, +∞) × [−π/2, +π/2]
   The direction vectors D1 , D2 and D3 are derived from the points P0 , P1 and P2 specified
   in the corresponding data line as described in remark 14.

8. TYPE = CONE defines a conical surface with parametric equation for f (u, v) and a def-
   inition range (u, v) ∈ Ωu × Ωv as follows:

         f (u, v) = P0 + (r + v · sin(α)) · (cos(u) · D1 + sin(u) · D2 ) + v · cos(α) · D3

                                 (u, v) ∈ (−∞, +∞) × (−∞, +∞)
   The direction vectors D1 , D2 and D3 are derived from the points P0 , P1 and P2 specified
   in the corresponding data line as described in remark 14.

9. TYPE = TORUS defines a toroidal surface with parametric equation for f (u, v) and a
   definition range (u, v) ∈ Ωu × Ωv as follows:

        f (u, v) = P0 + (r1 + r2 · cos(v)) · (cos(u) · D1 + sin(u) · D2 ) + r2 · sin(v) · D3

                                 (u, v) ∈ (−∞, +∞) × (−∞, +∞)
   The direction vectors D1 , D2 and D3 are derived from the points P0 , P1 and P2 specified
   in the corresponding data line as described in remark 14.

0. TYPE = EXTRUSION defines a surface by linear extrusion of a space curve with para-
   metric equation for f (u, v) and a definition range (u, v) ∈ Ωu × Ωv as follows:

                     f (u, v) = fc (u) + v · D1 ,      (u, v) ∈ Ωc × (−∞, +∞)

   Here fc (u) denotes the parametric equation of the function defining the space curve with
   (optionally trimmed) definition range Ωc (see $FUNCTION CURVE3D). The direction
   vector D1 is derived from the points P0 and P1 specified in the corresponding data line as
   unit length vector:
                                               P1 − P0

                                              kP1 − P0 k

   with parametric equation for f (u, v) and a definition range (u, v) ∈ Ωu × Ωv as follows:

         f (u, v) = fc∗ (v) + ( fc (v) − fc∗ (v) ) · cos(u) + D1 × ( fc (v) − fc∗ (v) ) · sin(u)

                                         (u, v) ∈ (−∞, +∞) × Ωc

Remarks:

  1. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.

  2. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
     any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component, and
     are valid and accessible for all components.

  3. At least two function values have to be input.




V 19.00.287                        PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)           3-1151
5. If JUMPS = YES is specified, jumps, that means two data pairs with the same argument
   (xi+1 = xi ) are allowed, but not at the end points. The function value at jump points is the
   average value, i.e. fun(x) = 0.5 (fun(xi ) + fun(xi+1 )).
   If a jump is defined by three data pairs with the same argument (xi−1 = xi = xi+1 ), then
   the function value at jump point is given by the middle one, i.e. fun(x) = fun(xi ).
   If JUMPS = YES is specified, parameters XGEN or GRID cannot be used.
6. If parameter XGEN is specified, the values of the function are input for equidistant values
   of the independent variable x. The equidistant values are generated automatically, where
   the first value is xA and the increment per step is ∆x. If n function values are input the
   last one belongs to x = xA + (n − 1)∆x.

7. If parameter GRID is specified, the values of the function are input for a regular grid
   in up to three dimensions. The number of points nxj for each dimension (i.e. inde-
   pendent variable) must be input, and for each dimension one data line with coordinate
   values in ascending order is expected. At least two values are expected for each inde-
   pendent variable in question. The function values itself are input on nx2 ∗ nx3 data lines,
   and each line contains all function values belonging to one pair x2 , x3 , i.e. nx1 values
   fun(x1,i , x2,j , x3,k ), i = 1, nx1 . The data lines with function values must be given in as-
   cending order of x3 , and for equal values x3 in ascending order of x2 .
   For grids with two or only one dimension this scheme is reduced accordingly. Generation
   (parameter XGEN) or jumps (JUMP = YES) are not available for grids.

8. Linear interpolation is used for calculation of function values within the defined range
   of the tabular function with one independent variable. For functions with two or three
   independent variables, bilinear and trilinear interpolation is used, respectively.

9. First and second derivatives are available for all tabular functions without jumps, if not
   JUMP = YES is specified. Due to linear interpolation the second derivative of tabular
   functions with one independent variable is always zero, except for option
   INTERPOLATE = SMOOTH, see remark 10.
0. Interpolation of function values may be improved if INTERPOLATE = SMOOTH is se-
   lected. This option is only available if JUMPS = NO is selected and the function values
   dependent on one independent variable only. In this case the second derivative is non-
   zero and the first derivative is improved. This option can be used in a TIMEHISTORY sim-
   ulation, where some nodes have a predescribed displacement given by a tabular function.
   If consistent mass is used, an additional force term f = −Mü can be taken into account
   because of the non-zero second derivative.

1. Sometimes data is given in a log-log or lin-log diagram. In this case, a line in the di-
   agram is actually a power function (log-log) or an exponential function (lin-log). If the
   data is supposed to be interpolated as in the diagram the option SCALE = LOGLOG or
   SCALE = LINLOG must be selected. This option is only available if JUMPS = YES is
   selected and the function values dependent on one independent variable only. No deriva-
   tives are available.


152                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          V 19.00.287
     If no extrapolation rule is selected, then the value of the function outside of the definition
     region is zero.
     If constant extrapolation is selected, then the value of the function outside of the definition
     region is equal to the function value at the first point for x < xmin or at the last point for
     x > xmax , respectively.




                                                                                                       Function
     If linear extrapolation is selected, then the function value outside of the definition region
     is determined by a linear extrapolation using the first two points for x < xmin or the last




                                                                                                        Data
     two points for x > xmax , respectively.

 13. Tabular functions may be used as primary functions for the definition of assembled func-
     tions.

                           NO       User subroutine FNUSRF: returns only value of

            list(c)




156                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        V 19.00.287
list(c)        R/I   List of function coefficients.




                                                                                                      Function
Remarks:




                                                                                                       Data
   1. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.

   2. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
      any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component, and
      are valid and accessible for all components.

   3. The user function itself is defined by a Fortran subroutine the user has to supply.

   4. If parameter NVAR is not specified, then nof var = 1 is assumed.

   5. If DER = NO (default) is specified, the user function returns only the value of the function
      fun(xi ). The corresponding subroutine call is

          CALL FNUSRF (IDFNCX,NOC,DATA,X, F )
           Input:
           IDFNCX Integer     Function identifier fun, only integer possible!
           NOC     Integer(*) Integer parameters:
                              (1): number of coefficients noc
                              (2): number of independent variables nof var
           DATA    Real(*)    Array with NOC function coefficients
           X       Real(*)    Array with nof var independent variables xi
           Output:
           F       Real       Value of function fun(xi )


          If DER = YES is specified, the user function returns the value of the function fun(x) and
          the first and second derivatives. The corresponding subroutine call is

          CALL FNUSRD (IDFNCX,NOC,DATA,X, F , F D , F D D )




V 19.00.287                     PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        3-1157
                             (2): number of independent variables nof var
    DATA        Real(*)      Array with NOC function coefficients
    X           Real(*)      Array with nof var independent variables xi
    Output:
    F           Real         Value of function fun(xi )
    FD          Real(*)      Value of first derivative(s)
    FDD         Real(*)      Value of second derivative(s)

   The sequence of the first derivatives in array FD must be according to
                                       ∂fun   ∂fun          ∂fun
                                                     ...
                                       ∂x1    ∂x2           ∂xn
   The sequence of the second derivatives in array FDD must be according to
   ∂2 fun    ∂2 fun           ∂2 fun     ∂2 fun    ∂2 fun           ∂2 fun           ∂2 fun        ∂2 fun
                       ...                                  ...              ...
    ∂x21    ∂x1 ∂x2          ∂x1 ∂xn      ∂x22    ∂x2 ∂x3          ∂x2 ∂xn         ∂xn−1 ∂xn        ∂x2n

6. Only one data line per data block is allowed.

7. If parameter NCOEF is not specified then noc = 0 is assumed.

8. If the number of coefficients noc is zero, no data line is allowed.

9. Floating point as well as integer values are accepted on data line. In the subroutine call,
   however, integer values are always available as floating point values.

0. Trailing zeros in list of coefficients may be omitted.

1. User supplied functions may be used as primary functions for the definition of assembled
   functions.

2. For THREADSAFE = YES the user supplied function must be thread-safe and so it must
   not have any internal state. In the simplest case, the output parameters of the subroutine
   depend only on input parameters, and constant data is specified within the subroutine.

3. By means of two system variant parameters FNUSRFID and FNUSRFNOFID, see data
   block $PARAMETER, page 3-549, it is possible to access internally provided functions
   as user supplied function. If the function identifier fun lies within the range defined by
   those two parameters, subroutine FNUSRF (if not replaced by the user) calls a subroutine
   FNUSRFXX with the same list of parameters. If subroutine FNUSRFXX is not replaced, it
   calls an internally provided function for the calculation of cutting forces of machine tools.
   A call to subroutine FNUSRFXX is possible only within an active situation.

4. If a user defined function has a name or text as label, then the name of the user defined
   function can be accessed in the Fortran subroutine by

Remarks:

  1. Material names must be unique. No default exists.
     As sole exception, PERMAS accepts repeated input of identical material definitions. That
     is, material name and material properties must be identical in this case.

  2. For definition of degree of anisotropy types see material description, page 8-1.

  3. The degree of anisotropy is a basic property of the material to be defined. Therefore all
     subsequent data blocks must contain data lines according to the degree of anisotropy
     selected.

  4. Material definition bracket is closed by an (optional) $END MATERIAL line or by a new
     material definition bracket line or by any high level bracket line.

2. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
   of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167.
3. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotro-
   pic behavior for 1-D, 2-D and 3-D elements. Nevertheless in any case all heat conductivity
   matrices which can be derived from input data are build up.
4. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1173, is
   recommended.
5. If the material is not isotropic the orientation of the material axes has to be defined by a
   material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527.

                                                              
                                                               ∂T
                         (q̇λ )1      λ11    λ12 λ13   ∂x1 

8. Temperature-dependent heat conductivity is available only in single or top components.
9. If a linear analysis is performed, temperature-dependent material data are evaluated at
   the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER COMPTEMP.
0. Material porosity is the fraction of the volume of voids over the total volume, 0.0 ≤ p < 1.0.
1. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line deter-
   mines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
2. Temperature- and/or porosity-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
   interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
   are used outside the table definition range.
3. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
   more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

                                     12.

Remarks:

  1. Only one definition of creep behavior by a $CREEP data block is allowed within the defi-
     nition of one material.

  2. Creep behavior as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in
     single or top components.

  3. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
     of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
     only isotropic material is actually supported for nonlinear material behavior.

  4. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of aniso-
     tropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
     which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
     can be found in the element description.

  5. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1184, is
     recommended.

  6. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line deter-
     mines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.

  7. For isotropic material the creep behavior is defined by

                                             εcr = f(σef f , T, t)

      where

                                     εcr       =    Creep strain
                                     σef f     =    Effective stress
                                     T         =    Temperature
                                     t         =    Time

  8. The creep behavior may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis with nonlinear
     material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DISLOAD etc,


V 19.00.287                 PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       3-1181
9. Time-, stress- and temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
   interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
   are used outside the table definition range.

0. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
   more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

1. The creep behavior may be described by a user supplied function, i.e. by a FORTRAN
   subroutine. The subroutine call is given by

   CALL MUCREP (MATNAM,NOFDEP,ZVEC,NODATA,IDRREQ,DATA,DERIV,IRC)

    Input:
    MATNAM      Character∗(∗)    Material name
    NOFDEP      Integer          Number of actual dependencies
    ZVEC        Real(∗)          Array with state variables. Values for all dependencies
                                 defined by input for actual material property, sorted ac-
                                 cording to internal sequence of dependencies (see be-
                                 low).
    NODATA      Integer          Number of expected data
    IDRREQ      Integer(∗)         (1) Derivative request etc.
                                        0 No derivatives requested
                                        1 Derivatives requested, must be returned
                                   (2) not used
                                   (3) External element identifier
    Ouput:
    DATA        Real(∗)          Array with NODATA material data
    DERIV       Real(∗)          Array with NODATA∗NOFDEP derivatives.
    IRC         Integer          Return code
                                      0 Material data returned
                                     -1 Error(s) occurred
                                  -200 Material data not available
   Meaning and number of material data correspond to input described for tabular func-
   tion (of course without values of independent variables), depending on material property
   type and degree of anisotropy.
   The sequence of state variables and, correspondingly, the sequence of material data
   derivatives is determined by the internal sequence of independent variables, which for
   creep behavior description is given by




182                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        V 19.00.287
     If a dependency is not defined by parameter DEP, it is omitted and NOFDEP is reduced
     accordingly.




                                                                                                  Homogen.
                                                                                                   Material
 12. For THREADSAFE = YES the user supplied function must be thread-safe and so it must
     not have any internal state. In the simplest case, the output parameters of the subroutine
     depend only on input parameters and constant data specified within the subroutine.

 13. The user may specify a complete isotropic nonlinear material model by user-supplied
     subroutines, please refer to examples MNL15 and MNL15V1 of [um550].
     By setting THREADSAFE = YES those subroutines may be declared as thread-safe.

 14. If plastic behavior is specified by user-supplied subroutines (INPUT = UMAT), then creep
     behavior, if input, must be specified by user-supplied subroutines too, and vice versa.

  2. Structural damping is understood as a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not depend
     on the degree of anisotropy of the material.




                                                                                                      Homogen.
                                                                                                       Material
  3. Structural damping within material description yields complex elemental stiffness matrices
     of the form
                                      K̄ E = (1 + igE (f ))K E
     with the (optional) frequency-dependent elemental damping factor gE (f ).

  4. Elemental structural damping may be used for direct or modal frequency response analy-
     sis and any other analysis in frequency domain. For use in time domain, e.g. for transient
     response analysis, it is converted to equivalent viscous damping by

                                                  gE (fE )
                                         Dg,E =            KE
                                                   2πfE

     The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by pa-
     rameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.

  5. Material porosity is the fraction of the volume of voids over the total volume, 0.0 ≤ p < 1.0.

  6. Frequency- and/or porosity dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
     interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
     are used outside the table definition range.

  7. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line deter-
     mines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.

  8. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
     more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

  $MATERIAL NAME=STA_325
    $DAMPING
       0.02
  $END MATERIAL
  $MATERIAL NAME=A2390
    $DAMPING INPUT=TABLE         DEP=FREQ
       0.02 : 0.0
       0.03 : 10.0
       0.05 : 20.0
  $END MATERIAL

   CALL MUELAS (MATNAM,NOFDEP,ZVEC,NODATA,IDRREQ,DATA,DERIV,IRC)

    Input:
    MATNAM      Character∗(∗)    Material name
    NOFDEP      Integer          Number of actual dependencies
    ZVEC        Real(∗)          Array with state variables. Values for all dependencies
                                 defined by input for actual material property, sorted ac-
                                 cording to internal sequence of dependencies (see be-
                                 low).
    NODATA      Integer          Number of expected data
    IDRREQ      Integer(∗)         (1) Derivative request etc.
                                        0 No derivatives requested
                                        1 Derivatives requested, must be returned
                                   (2) Seletion at jumps
                                        0 or 1 Right-hand side of a jump
                                             -1 Left-hand side of a jump
                                   (3) External element identifier
    Ouput:
    DATA        Real(∗)          Array with NODATA material data
    DERIV       Real(∗)          Array with NODATA∗NOFDEP derivatives.
    IRC         Integer          Return code
                                      0 Material data returned
                                     -1 Error(s) occurred
                                  -200 Material data not available

   Meaning and number of material data correspond to input described for tabular function
   (of course without values of independent variables), depending on material property type
   and degree of anisotropy.
   The sequence of state variables and, correspondingly, the sequence of material data
   derivatives is determined by the internal sequence of independent variables, which for
   stress - plastic strain relation is given by

              Internal No.   Mnemo     No. of Items   Data Items    Content
                   1         TEMP           1         T             Temperature
                   2         PORO           1         p             Porosity

9. For THREADSAFE = YES the user supplied function must be thread-safe and so it must
   not have any internal state. In the simplest case, the output parameters of the subroutine
   depend only on input parameters and constant data specified within the subroutine.

           $ELCONDUCT                mattype

Parameter     Type           Value      Explanation

mattype       name                      Material property type.
                            GENERAL     General case.
                             PLANE      Plane analysis.



Data lines:


              list(x)




 Item(s)           Type        Explanation
 list(x)                R      List of data describing electric conductivity behavior.


Remarks:

  1. Only one definition of electric conductivity behavior by an $ELCONDUCT data block is
     allowed within the definition of one material.

  2. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
     of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167.

  3. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of an-
     isotropic behavior for 1-D, 2-D and 3-D elements. Nevertheless in any case all electric
     conductivity matrices which can be derived from input data are build up.

  4. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1223, is
     recommended.

  5. If the material is not isotropic the orientation of the material axes has to be defined by a
     material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527.

2. Only one definition of the hardening type ratio is allowed within the definition of one ma-
   terial.

3. If not defined, pure isotropic hardening is assumed.

4. Hardening as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single or
   top components.

5. Hardening type ratio is understood as a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not de-
   pend on the degree of anisotropy of the material.

6. The hardening type ratio m with 0.0 ≤ m ≤ 1.0 describes the relation of isotropic harden-
   ing to total hardening by
                                        isotropic hardening
                                  m=
                                          total hardening
   and, consequently, for the relation of kinematic hardening to total hardening it follows

                                            kinematic hardening
                                1.0 − m =
                                               total hardening

   m = 0.0 means pure kinematic, m = 1.0 pure isotropic hardening.


7. If linear kinematic hardening is applied (i.e. m < 1.0 and no $NLKINHARD specified) the
   yield curve in the $PLASTIC data block should be linear, see its remark 18.

8. The hardening type ratio may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis with non-
   linear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DISLOAD
   etc), then the temperatures to evaluate temperature-dependent material data are taken
   from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element temperature state is
   defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP and system variant
   parameter COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.

9. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is
   used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside
   the table definition range.

0. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
   more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

Remarks:

  1. Data block $HOMOGENIZE allows for establishing material property data of a homoge-
     neous material by Mōri-Tanaka type mean-field homogenization.
  2. The volume fraction of the fiber(inclusion) material can be input elementwise with $ELSTATE VOLFFRA
     on page 3-445. In this case, the value in the material block will be ignored for the cor-
     risponding elements.

  3. If FIBER_MATRIX is specified as homogenization type, then the material consists of uni-
     directionally spheroidal or spherical (depends on ldr) inclusions and an isotropic matrix
     material. The homogenized material is therefore (transversely) isotropic (depends on
     value of ldr), where the orientation of the inclusions coincides with the first material di-
     rection. If it is defined as orthotropic and the corresponding fiber orientation distribution


V 19.00.287                 PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         3-1235
      • The homogenized material must be declared as transversely isotropic or orthotropic,
        see 3-1167.
      • For fibers (inclusions) as well as for the matrix an isotropic material must be input.
      • Actually, only elasticity and density data may be established by homogenization. To
        do so, fiber as well as matrix material must contain the corresponding property with
        constant data. Any dependency is not allowed.
      • With the exception of plasticity data and yield limit with CRITERION = GENANISO
        for TYPE = TRANS, no other properties may be input for that material up to now.
      • If plasticity data are not specified for the main material but are given for fiber (inclu-
        sion) or matrix material, then dummy data are generated internally for plasticity and
        yield limit to assure a formal correct processing on element level.
      • For orthotropic material the input of the structure tensor of fiber orientation distri-
        bution per element by a $ELSTATE STCTENS data block (see page 3-437) is nec-
        essary. Only (transverse) isotropy can be considered if it is not given, despite of
        TYPE = ORTHO.
      • If the length to diameter ratio of fiber ldr is given as 1.0, any anisotropy will vanish, it
        results in an isotropic material stiffness despite of input by TYPE on the $MATERIAL
        line, see page 3-1167.

4. If any property of a material used for homogenization (i,e, fiber (inclusion) or matrix ma-
   terials) is given by a user supplied function, then this function must be thread-safe.

5. Since the homogenized material is always considered as anisotropic, the orientation of
   the material axes has to be defined by a material reference system or element structure
   tensor within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527 or $ELSTATE STCTENS
   on page 3-437.




owing material stiffness data are derived:
 C      Stiffness matrix of general 3-D case, dimension 6x6.

ase refer to examples MNL17V1 of [um550].

  1. Only one definition of hyperelastic behavior by a $HYPERELASTIC data block is allowed
     within the definition of one material.
  2. Hyperelastic behavior as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only




                                                                                                   Homogen.

                                                                                                    Material
  3. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
     of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
     currently only isotropic material is supported for this nonlinear material.
  4. The $HYPERELASTIC data block describes the complete elastic behavior of the material,
     so elastic data must not be specified by an $ELASTIC data block. Furthermore, the
     material properties for nonlinear material behavior specified by data blocks $CREEP,
     $HARDENING, $NLELASTIC, $NLKINHARD, $PLASTIC, $VISCOELASTIC and $YIELD
     are meaningless and must not be specified.
  5. Parameter SPTYPE specifies the type of strain energy potential form.
  6. If INPUT = FITTING is specified, then the hyperelastic property data are derived from
     measured stress over strain data, which must be input in a $MEASUREMENT data block
     (see page 3-1244 ff.) with data type STRESS_STRAIN. The requested type of strain
     energy potential form generated by fitting must be given by parameter SPTYPE.
  7. Measured stress over strain data used for fitting may not be temperature-dependent.
  8. The range of measured stress over strain data may be limited by parameter RANGE, i.e.
     only stress data within the range eps1 ≤ ε ≤ eps2 are taken into account for fitting.
  9. The polynomial strain energy potential is defined in terms of the invariants of the right
     Cauchy-Green tensor C = FT F, where F is the deformation gradient. In order to split
     the strain energy potential into an isochoric and a volumetric part the Jacobi determinant
     J = detF, the isochoric deformation gradient F̄ = J −1/3 F and the isochoric right Cauchy-
     Green tensor C̄ = F̄T F̄ are introduced. The isochoric invariants are defined as I¯1 = trC̄
     and I¯2 = (1/2) (IP ¯2 − tr(C̄2 )). The strain energy potential reads
                          1                                 P
     W (I1 , I2 , Jel ) = ni+j=1 Cij (I¯1 − 3)i (I¯2 − 3)j + ni=1 D1i (Jel − 1)2 i .
         ¯   ¯
     Here Jel is the elastic Jacobi determinant which is defined in terms of the total Jacobi
     determinant via Jel = J/(1 + ǫth )3 and ǫth is the thermal strain. The Cij parameters
     describe the shear behavior of the material while the Di parameters describe its com-
     pressibility. Note that the small strain shear and bulk modulus for the material are given
     as µ0 = 2 (C10 + C01 ) and k0 = 2/D1 .
 10. The reduced polynomial strain energy potential is equivalent to the polynomial strain en-
     ergy potential with Cij = 0 if j 6= 0 such that the potential does not depend on the second
     invariant I¯2 , see remark 9.
 11. The Neo-Hookean strain energy potential is equivalent to the reduced polynomial strain
     energy potential with n = 1, see remark 10. Hence, it does not depend on the second
     invariant I¯2 .


V 19.00.287                 PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        3-1241
   potential with n = 3, see remark 10. Hence, it does not depend on the second invariant
   I¯2 .

4. The Ogden strain energy potential is defined in terms of the three isochoric principal
   stretches λ̄i , which are the P    square roots of the eigenvalues of the isochoric right Cauchy-
   Green tensor C̄, i.e. C̄ = 3i=1 λ̄2i Ni ⊗ Ni , compare remark 9. Ni are the orthonormal
   vectors in the direction of principal stretch in the initial configuration. The strain energy
   potential is split intoP    an isochoric and a volumetric part
                                                                Pas
   W (λ̄1 , λ̄2 , λ̄3 , Jel ) = i=1 α2 (λ̄1 + λ̄2 + λ̄3 − 3) + ni=1 D1i (Jel − 1)2 i .
                                n   2 µi  αi    αi     αi
                                      i
   The parameters µi and αi describe the shear behavior of the material while the Di pa-
   rameters describe its compressibility.    P Note that the small strain shear and bulk modulus
   for the material are given as µ0 = ni µi and k0 = 2/D1 .

Remarks:

  1. Only one definition of nonlinear elastic material behavior by a $NLELASTIC data block is
     allowed within the definition of one material.

  2. To complete the description of elastic behavior, the corresponding linearized elastic be-
     havior for vanishing elastic strains must be input by $ELASTIC (see page 3-1202 ff.).

  3. Nonlinear Elastic behavior as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available
     only in single or top components.

  4. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
     of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
     only isotropic material is actually supported for nonlinear material behavior.

  5. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of aniso-
     tropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
     which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
     can be found in the element description.

  6. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1250, is
     recommended.

  7. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line deter-
     mines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.

  8. For isotropic material the nonlinear elastic behavior is defined by

                                             σ = f(εel , T )

      where

                                       σ     =   Stress
                                       εel   =   Elastic strain
                                       T     =   Temperature

  9. The stress must be given as engineering stress, i.e. the ratio of the applied force to the
     original (undeformed) cross section area. The strain must be given as engineering strain,
     i.e. the ratio of the length change to the original length.




V 19.00.287                 PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       3-1247
1. The nonlinear elastic behavior may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis with
   nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DIS-
   LOAD etc, see page 3-581 ff.), then the temperatures to evaluate temperature-dependent
   material data are taken from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element
   temperature state is defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP,
   see page 3-440, and system variant parameter COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.
2. If the nonlinear elastic behavior is temperature-dependent, the linearized elastic behavior
   defined by $ELASTIC must be temperature-dependent too.
3. Input may be done as tabular function. Linear interpolation is used within the table to
   determine function values, and boundary values are used outside the table definition
   range.
4. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
   more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
5. The nonlinear elastic behavior may be described by a user supplied function, i.e. by a
   FORTRAN subroutine. The subroutine call is given by


   CALL MUNLEL (MATNAM,NOFDEP,ZVEC,NODATA,IDRREQ,DATA,DERIV,IRC)

    Input:
    MATNAM      Character∗(∗)    Material name
    NOFDEP      Integer          Number of actual dependencies
    ZVEC        Real(∗)          Array with state variables. Values for all dependencies
                                 defined by input for actual material property, sorted ac-
                                 cording to internal sequence of dependencies (see be-
                                 low).
    NODATA      Integer          Number of expected data
    IDRREQ      Integer(∗)         (1) Derivative request etc.
                                        0 No derivatives requested
                                        1 Derivatives requested, must be returned
                                   (2) not used
                                   (3) External element identifier
    Ouput:
    DATA        Real(∗)          Array with NODATA material data
    DERIV       Real(∗)          Array with NODATA∗NOFDEP derivatives.
    IRC         Integer          Return code
                                      0 Material data returned
                                     -1 Error(s) occurred
                                  -200 Material data not available

  2. Only one definition of the nonlinear kinematic hardening is allowed within the definition of

  3. Nonlinear kinematic hardening as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is avail-

  4. The description of nonlinear kinematic hardening is extracted from the plasticity data (see
     $PLASTIC (see page 3-1268 ff.)) using the maximum plastic strain εpl,max . If plasticity
     data are given as tabular function, εpl,max should coincide with the maximum plastic strain
     of that table, if plasticity data are given by user supplied function, εpl,max should be the

marks:

1. Only one definition of stress - plastic strain behavior by a $PLASTIC data block is allowed
   within the definition of one material.

2. To complete the plastic deformation behavior description of the material, yield behavior
   (data block $YIELD, see page 3-1305 ff.) must and hardening (data block $HARDENING,
   see page 3-1229 ff.) may be defined in addition. If hardening type is not defined explicitly,
   then pure isotropic hardening is assumed. For transversly isotropic material, Poisson’s
   ratio for plastic deformation may be input by data block $PLSPOISSON, see page 3-1277
   ff..

3. Plasticity as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single or
   top components.

4. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
   of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
   only isotropic or transversely isotropic material is actually supported for nonlinear plastic
   material behavior.

5. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of aniso-
   tropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
   which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
   can be found in the element description.

6. If the effective stress depends on the plastic strain, then the dependency on εpl ≥ 0.0
   must always be specified. For pressure modified v.Mises or cast iron yield condition (see
   $YIELD (see page 3-1308 ff.)) and isotropic material, the dependency εpl ≤ 0.0 may
   be different, and must be specified in addition with a jump at εpl = 0.0. Note that the
   compression yield stress must be greater than the tension yield stress for any state, i.e.
   |σef f (−εpl , T )| > σef f (εpl , T ) for each effective plastic strain εpl ≥ 0.0 and temperature T .

7. If for transversely isotropic material the dependencies for positive and negative plastic
   strain are different, all functions describing the transversely isotropic plasticity must be
   input with jumps as requested in remark 6.

6. If strain-dependency is omitted (INPUT = DATA specified or only temperature-dependent

   should represent the material behavior in an average sense within the expected range of
   plastic strain.

     plied function, i.e. by a FORTRAN subroutine. The subroutine call is given by


     CALL MUPLAS (MATNAM,NOFDEP,ZVEC,NODATA,IDRREQ,DATA,DERIV,IRC)

      Input:
      MATNAM      Character∗(∗)    Material name
      NOFDEP      Integer          Number of actual dependencies
      ZVEC        Real(∗)          Array with state variables. Values for all dependencies
                                   defined by input for actual material property, sorted ac-
                                   cording to internal sequence of dependencies (see be-
                                   low).
      NODATA      Integer          Number of expected data
      IDRREQ      Integer(∗)         (1) Derivative request etc.
                                          0 No derivatives requested
                                          1 Derivatives requested, must be returned
                                     (2) Seletion at jumps
                                          0 or 1 Right-hand side of a jump
                                               -1 Left-hand side of a jump
                                     (3) External element identifier
      Ouput:
      DATA        Real(∗)          Array with NODATA material data
      DERIV       Real(∗)          Array with NODATA∗NOFDEP derivatives.
      IRC         Integer          Return code
                                        0 Material data returned
                                       -1 Error(s) occurred
                                    -200 Material data not available

     Meaning and number of material data correspond to input described for tabular function
     (of course without values of independent variables), depending on material property type
     and degree of anisotropy.

              Internal No.   Mnemo     No. of Items   Data Items    Content
                   1         TEMP           1         T             Temperature
                   2         EPSP           1         εpl           Plastic strain

   If a dependency is not defined by parameter DEP, it is omitted and NOFDEP is reduced
   accordingly.

3. For THREADSAFE = YES the user supplied function must be thread-safe and so it must
   not have any internal state. In the simplest case, the output parameters of the subroutine
   depend only on input parameters and constant data specified within the subroutine.

4. The user may specify a complete isotropic nonlinear material model by user-supplied
   subroutines, please refer to examples MNL15 and MNL15V1 of [um550].
   By setting THREADSAFE = YES those subroutines may be declared as thread-safe.

   top components.

   recommended.

     more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

marks:

1. Only one definition of thermal expansion behavior by an $THERMEXP data block is al-

2. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
   of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167.

3. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of aniso-
   tropic behavior for 1-D, 2-D and 3-D elements. Nevertheless in any case all thermal
   expansion matrices which can be derived from input data are build up.

4. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1293, is
   recommended.

5. If the material is not isotropic the orientation of the material axes has to be defined by a
   material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527.

6. The general three dimensional thermal expansion matrix α is defined by
                                                  
                                  ε1              α1
                                ε              α 
                                2              2 

                                                  
                                ε5 = γ23       α5 
                                  ε6 = γ31 ϑ      α6

7. The two dimensional thermal expansion matrix for plane analysis α2d is defined by
                                                         
                          ε1              α2d
                                           1               α1
                                                         
                         ε2        =  α2d
                                           2  ∆T =  α2  ∆T
                          ε4 = γ12        α2d
                                           3               α4
                                       ϑ




288                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       V 19.00.287
                             εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )
     with T0 as the (element) temperature where the thermal strain is zero. The element
     temperatures T0 are defined within the loading variant for each loading case with thermal




                                                                                                      Homogen.
                                                                                                       Material
     loads by $REFVAL TEMP data blocks, see page 3-872, and loading variant parameter
     REFTEMP, see page 3-852.
     Loading variant parameter REFTEMP must not be mixed up with parameter REFTEMP
     on header line.

  9. Material porosity is the fraction of the volume of voids over the total volume, 0.0 ≤ p < 1.0.

 10. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line deter-
     mines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.

 11. Temperature- and/or porosity-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
     interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
     are used outside the table definition range.

 12. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
     more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

 13. The thermal expansion behavior of isotropic material may be described by a user sup-
     plied function, i.e. by a FORTRAN subroutine. The subroutine call is given by

    NOFDEP      Integer          Number of actual dependencies
    ZVEC        Real(∗)          Array with state variables. Values for all dependencies

   Meaning and number of material data correspond to input described for tabular function
   (of course without values of independent variables), depending on material property type
   and degree of anisotropy.
   The sequence of state variables and, correspondingly, the sequence of material data
   derivatives is determined by the internal sequence of independent variables, which for
   thermal expansion is given by

              Internal No.   Mnemo     No. of Items   Data Items    Content
                   1         TEMP           1         T             Temperature
                   2         PORO           1         p             Porosity

4. For THREADSAFE = YES the user supplied function must be thread-safe and so it must
   not have any internal state. In the simplest case, the output parameters of the subroutine
   depend only on input parameters and constant data specified within the subroutine.

ta line:
alue on one logical line.

marks:

1. Only one definition of viscoelastic material behavior by an $VISCOELASTIC data block is
   allowed within the definition of one material.

2. Viscoelastic behavior is specified by a scalar time constant τ . The viscous damping part
   of viscoelastic elements is then given by τ k where k is the corresponding elastic stiffness
   matrix. For isotropic material, the damping constant is given by D = τ E where E is
   Young’s modulus.

3. Viscoelastic behavior constant is always a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not
   depend on the degree of anisotropy of the material.

ample:

ase refer to examples DRA20 and DRA20V1 of [um550].

$MATERIAL NAME=RUBBER
  $VISCOELASTIC
     0.033514
$END MATERIAL

V 19.00.287                          PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      3-1301
2. To define the complete viscoplastic behavior, plasticity data (see $PLASTIC (see page
   3-1268 ff.)) must be specified in addition.

3. Viscoplastic behavior is described by a power–law viscoplastic model
                                            "        1.     #
                                         1.     σ      ε
                                    γ̇ =                  − 1.
                                         µ     σef f

   where the strictly positive material constants µ and ε are the viscosity and rate–sensitivity
   parameters and σ and σef f are the effective and yield stress (σef f = f (εpl , T )), respec-
   tively.

4. The viscoplastic properties may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis with
   nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DIS-
   LOAD etc, see page 3-581 ff.), then the temperatures to evaluate temperature-dependent
   material data are taken from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element
   temperature state is defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP
   (see page 3-438 ff.), and system variant parameter COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.

5. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is
   used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside
   the table definition range.

6. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
   more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

marks:

1. Only one definition of yield behavior by a $YIELD data block is allowed within the definition
   of one material.

2. The definition of yield limit by a $YIELD data block is necessary if plastic deformation
   behavior as defined by a $PLASTIC data block (see page 3-1265 ff.) is taken into account.

3. Yield behavior as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single
   or top components.

4. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
   of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
   only isotropic material is actually supported for nonlinear material behavior.

5. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of aniso-
   tropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
   which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
   can be found in the element description.

6. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1309, is
   recommended.

7. If the material is not isotropic the orientation of the material axes has to be defined by a
   material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527.

           $SANDWICH       NAME = name          TYPE = type




Parameter     Type        Value       Explanation

NAME          name      name          Name of material.
TYPE          name       type         Degree of anisotropy.




                                                                                                 Sandwich
                                                                                                  Material
                         ISO          Isotropic.
                       ORTHO          Orthotropic.
                     MONOCLINIC       Monoclinic.
                       ANISO          General anisotropic, input of matrix elements instead
                                      of engineering constants.


Remarks:

  1. Material names must be unique. No default exists.
     As sole exception, PERMAS accepts repeated input of identical material definitions. That
     is, material name and material properties must be identical in this case.

  2. For definition of degree of anisotropy types see material description, page 8-1.

  3. The degree of anisotropy is a basic property of the material to be defined. Therefore all
     subsequent data blocks must contain data lines according to the degree of anisotropy
     selected.

  4. Material definition bracket is closed by an (optional) $END MATERIAL line or by a new
     material definition bracket line or by any high level bracket line.

Example:

Please refer to example LA4 of [um550].

         $END       SANDWICH




marks:

1. $END lines are always optional.

                                                              

                         (q̇λ )1      λ11    λ12 λ13   ∂x1 

6. Temperature-dependent heat conductivity is available only in single or top components.

7. If a linear analysis is performed, temperature-dependent material data are evaluated at
   the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER COMPTEMP.

8. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is
   used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside
   the table definition range.

9. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
   more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

Data lines:
 If INPUT = DATA is specified (default):                        1 value on one logical line.
 If INPUT = TABLE is specified:                                 1 value and corresponding frequency
                                                                per logical line.


                   h            i
              gE       :    f




 Item(s)           Type             Explanation
 gE                    R            Structural damping factor of sandwich material.
 f                     R            Frequency in cycles per seconds.




V 19.00.287                          PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                   3-1323
2. Structural damping is understood as a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not depend
   on the degree of anisotropy of the material.

3. Structural damping within material description yields complex elemental stiffness matrices
   of the form
                                    K̄ E = (1 + igE (f ))K E
   with the (optional) frequency-dependent elemental damping factor gE (f ).

4. Elemental structural damping may be used for direct or modal frequency response anal-
   ysis and any other analysis in frquency domain. For use in time domain, e.g. for transient
   response analysis, it is converted to equivalent viscous damping by

                                               gE (fE )
                                      Dg,E =            KE
                                                2πfE

   The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by pa-
   rameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.

5. Frequency-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is used
   within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside the
   table definition range.

6. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
   more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

ample:

$SANDWICH NAME=STA_325
  $DAMPING
     0.02
$END SANDWICH
$SANDWICH NAME=A2390
  $DAMPING INPUT=TABLE        DEP=FREQ
     0.02 : 0.0
     0.03 : 10.0
     0.05 : 20.0
$END SANDWICH

5. Since the core material carries only shear loads the corresponding thermal expansion

6. If data are temperature-dependent, total thermal expansion coefficients are expected de-
   scribing thermal expansion from reference temperature Tref , which is defined by param-
   eter REFTEMP on header line, to actual temperature T . The thermal strain is than calcu-
   lated according to
                          εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )
   with T0 as the (element) temperature where the thermal strain is zero. The element
   temperatures T0 are defined within the loading variant for each loading case with thermal
   loads by $REFVAL TEMP data blocks, see page 3-872, and loading variant parameter
   REFTEMP, see page 3-852.
   Loading variant parameter REFTEMP must not be mixed up with parameter REFTEMP
   on header line.

   T . Linear interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary
   values are used outside the table definition range.

   more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

Parameter     Type       Value        Explanation

NAME          name       name         Name of laminated material.
DESTYPE       name                    Type of material description.
                         PLY          Description by plies.
                        MATRIX        Description by matrices (integrated values).
TYPE          name      type          Degree of anisotropy.
                     MONOCLINIC       Monoclinic.


Remarks:

  1. Material names must be unique. No default exists.
     As sole exception, PERMAS accepts repeated input of identical material definitions. That
     is, material name and material properties must be identical in this case.

  2. There are two ways available to describe a laminated material

        • If DESTYPE = PLY is specified, the laminate is defined by the complete description
          of each ply, see data block $PLY, page 3-1353 ff.. The properties of the laminate
          are derived internally according to an extension of classical laminate theory.Material
          damping, however, may be input for the laminate.
        • If DESTYPE = MATRIX is specified, integrated values are expected describing the
          laminate properties. Consequently, ply-dependent results, e.g. stresses within one
          ply, are not available.
        • A mixture of PLY and MATRIX description for one material is not possible.

  3. Laminates are always handled as anisotropic with monoclinic behavior (see page 8-1),
     even if the material itself is isotropic. Therefore a material reference system must be
     defined for all elements with laminated material by a $MATREF data block, see page
     3-527 ff..

                                                                                                     Laminated
     specified, damping is derived from the description of the ply materials.




                                                                                                      Material
  3. Structural damping is understood as a scalar quantity. Nevertheless since laminated
     material is always handled as anisotropic, the orientation of the material axes has to be
     defined by a material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on
     page 3-527.

  4. Structural damping within material description yields complex elemental stiffness matrices
     of the form
                                      K̄ E = (1 + igE (f ))K E
     with the (optional) frequency-dependent elemental damping factor gE (f ).

  5. Elemental structural damping may be used for direct or modal frequency response anal-
     ysis and any other analysis in frquency domain. For use in time domain, e.g. for transient
     response analysis, it is converted to equivalent viscous damping by

                                                  gE (fE )
                                         Dg,E =            KE
                                                   2πfE

     The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by pa-
     rameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.

  6. Frequency-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is used
     within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside the
     table definition range.

  7. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
     more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

  3. The general stiffness relation of the extended classical laminate theory is given by:
                                                              
                                    N          A B              ε0
                                                              
                                   M = B D               κ 

     with


                 N     =   {Nx Ny Nxy }      Membrane forces per unit length
                 M     =   {Mx My Mxy }      Moments per unit length
                 S     =   {Nyz Nzx }        Transverse shear forces per unit length
                 A     =   [Aij ]            Symmetric membrane stiffness
                 B     =   [Bij ]            Symmetric coupling stiffness
                 D     =   [Dij ]            Symmetric bending stiffness
                 G     =   [Gij ]            Symmetric transverse shear stiffness
                 ε0    =   {ε0x ε0y ε0xy }   Membrane strains
                 κ     =   {κx κy κxy }      Curvatures
                 γ     =   {γyz γzx }        Transverse shear strains

 name              name       Name of homogeneous material.
 t                   R        Ply thickness, must be ≥ 0.0, see remark 6 .

                              material reference system to ply direction.

V 19.00.287                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      3-1353
2. Each data line describes one ply of the laminate, starting at lower surface. According
   to the specified treatment as shell, membrane or shear-carrying core, the referenced
   material must be capable to deliver the material stiffness matrix for plane stress analysis
   Q and/or the transverse shear stiffness matrix C ts , see page 3-1203.

3. If ASYM is specified, the laminate is assumed to be asymmetric, and each ply has to be
   described.

4. If SYM or ANTI is specified, a symmetric or antisymmetric resp. laminate is assumed,
   and only the lower half of the laminate has to be described whereas parameter NPLY
   must contain the total number of plies. For an even number of plies nof ply/2 data lines
   are expected, for a symmetric laminate with an odd number of plies (nof ply + 1)/2 data
   lines, including the description of the middle ply.

5. The resulting laminated material contains all material properties which are defined for
   each homogeneous material referenced in the ply description. Dependency of ply mate-
   rial on temperature or frequency is not yet supported.

6. The thickness of the laminate is the sum of all ply thicknesses, and must be greater than
   zero. Single plies with thickness = 0 may be used to evaluate interlaminar shear stresses.

7. The stiffness of each ply may be reduced to membrane or transverse shear stiffness only.
   The complete laminate, however, must be able to carry all kind of loads.

ample:

$PLY ASYM     NPLY=3
   CFRP_1     2.0   0.0
   CFRP_1     3.0 90.0
   CFRP_2     1.0   0.0

$PLY SYM     NPLY=3
   EPE_10      1.0     0.0   :   PLANE
   FOAM_2      6.0     0.0   :   CORE

3. The thermal expansion matrix is defined according to
                                             
                                     α11 α12
                                             
                        "    #  α21 α22  "                   #
