   eter REFTEMP on header line, to actual temperature T . The thermal strain is than calcu-
   lated according to
                          εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )
   with T0 as the (element) temperature where the thermal strain is zero. The element
   temperatures T0 are defined within the loading variant for each loading case with thermal
   loads by $REFVAL TEMP data blocks, see page 3-872, and loading variant parameter
   REFTEMP, see page 3-852.
   Loading variant parameter REFTEMP must not be mixed up with parameter REFTEMP
   on header line.

   T . Linear interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary

     isotropic behavior. For gasket material, however, only transversely isotropic material is

  4. The material system axes are defined by the element geometry, i.e. the first material
     direction is given by the normal to the mean plane of the element. Therefore, a material
     reference system must not be defined.

  5. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line deter-
     mines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.

  6. Loading behavior of gasket elements is valid only for deformation in the first material
     direction (the normal to the mean plane of the element), therefore it is a scalar function.
     It is described as pressure on the gasket material for the loading process, depending on
     deformation and, optionally, on temperature. The relation is given by

                                             pL = f(dn , T )

     where

        pL    =   Pressure ( = −σN ) during loading
        dn    =   Deformation (compression) in element normal direction (in units of length)
        T     =   Temperature

     If loading and unloading behavior are different, the corresponding unloading behavior
     must be defined within a $GSKUNLOAD data block, see pages 3-1377 ff. . Furthermore,
     the corresponding elastic behavior for the remaining material directions must be defined
     within a $ELASTIC data block, see pages 3-1369 ff. .

  7. If by parameter FACTOR a scaling factor is specified, then the pressure input values pL
     are scaled by factor fs .

  8. Reaching the maximum deformation (dn )max , no further compression of the gasket mate-
     rial is possible; internally it is handled as a closed contact, see figure F3-42. If, however,
     MAXDEFX is not specified, the maximal given deformation value is used.

   3-549.

     scribing thermal expansion from reference temperature Tref , which is defined by param-
     eter REFTEMP on header line, to actual temperature T . The thermal strain is than calcu-
     lated according to
                            εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )
     with T0 as the (element) temperature where the thermal strain is zero. The element
     temperatures T0 are defined within the loading variant for each loading case with thermal
     loads by $REFVAL TEMP data blocks, see page 3-872, and loading variant parameter
     REFTEMP, see page 3-852.
     Loading variant parameter REFTEMP must not be mixed up with parameter REFTEMP
     on header line.

  7. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions of the actual temperature
     T . Linear interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary
     values are used outside the table definition range.

  8. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
     more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

V 19.00.287                       PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                3-1421
le                 I>0      Label of transformation rule $TRULE.
                  name/text
tex1 , vertex2     I>0      Labels of edge bounding $VERTEX.
                  name/text
 2                  R       Curve parameter values associated with vertices.
tex                I>0      Vertex of singular edge.
                  name/text
 dg                R>0      Tolerance for edge representations, see remark 6.


marks:

1. Edge labels must be unique within one geometry.

2. An edge (if not degenerated, see remark 5) is a parametric space curve C(t) ∈ R3 that is
   bounded by vertex1 and vertex2 with coordinates V1 , V2 ∈ R3 and corresponding param-
   eter values t1 6= t2 . The tangential vectors C ′ (t) establish the orientation of the edge.

3. TYPE = PARAMETRIC defines an edge with a general parametric space curve fc3d ,
   optionally subject to a coordinate transformation defined by rule trule :

                                  fc3d (t) −→ C(t) ,   t ∈ [tS , tE ]

     where tS := min{t1 , t2 } and tE := max{t1 , t2 }. The parameters t1 and t2 must lie in the
     possibly trimmed (see $FUNCTION CURVE3D, remark 13) definition range Ω of fc3d (t).
     Additionally, for periodic curves (i.e. circles and ellipses) the range |t2 − t1 | must not
     exceed the period length 2π. To form a closed edge, both vertices must be the same (and
     not only have the same coordinates), but with different curve parameters. To be a valid
     parametric edge, the relations

                         kC(t1 ) − V1 k ≤ tol1   and kC(t2 ) − V2 k ≤ tol2

     must be fulfilled, where tol1 and tol2 are the corresponding vertex representation toler-
     ances (see $VERTEX, remark 3) or the tolerance given by the global TOLGEO parameter.

4. TYPE = LINE defines an edge with a straight line between the vertices:

                               C(t) = V1 + t · (V2 − V1 ) ,   t ∈ [0, 1]

     The vertices vertex1 and vertex2 must be different.

5. TYPE = DEGENERATE defines an edge, that degenerates to a singular vertex vertex
   with coordinates V , that is
                                 C(t) = V
     for arbitrary values of t. A degenerated edge has no orientation and resides e.g. on the
     apex of a cone, the pole of a sphere or any other surface singularity.


422                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        V 19.00.287
     larged tolerance may be defined in its data line. The tolerance value for an edge should
     not exceed the tolerance value of its vertices. Otherwise the smallest vertex tolerance
     value will be used for the edge.

4. TYPE = TRIANGLE defines a triangle face

                S(u, v) = V1 + u · (V2 − V1 ) + v · (V3 − V1 ) ,   (u, v) ∈ D

  where V1 is the common vertex of edge3 and edge1 , V2 the common vertex of edge1 and

                         D := {(u, v) | 0 ≤ u, v ≤ 1 ∩ u + v ≤ 1}

V 19.00.287                         PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                              3-1427
         name/text


marks:

1. Shell labels must be unique within one geometry.

2. All faces of the shell must be connected, that is, starting with the first face, each must
   must be visitable by crossing edges ($EDGE) adjacent to two faces.

3. The set of faces must be a manifold, that is, each edge must not be referred by more then
   two faces.

4. The set of faces must be orientable, that is, it must be possible to define a common
   frontside for all faces of the shell without any contradiction between to adjacent faces. For
   iorient = 1 the frontside of the shell coincides with frontside (see $FACE, remark 2) of the
   first face (or single face for RULE = ALL) in the dataline, otherwise this is the backside.

5. If all edges referred by faces of a shell are adjacent to exactly two faces (or two times in
   opposite direction to the same face for seam edges), the shell is closed. Closed shells
   may be referred by a $SOLID.

6. Faces (and also their edges and vertices) may be referred by an arbitrary number of
   shells.

7. The COLOR parameter defines a default color for visualization purposes. For details on
   color values please refer to remark 5 on page 3-207.

Remarks:

  1. Solid labels must be unique within one geometry.

  2. Shells referred by a solid must be closed (see $SHELL, remark 5) and must not intersect
     itself or each other. Different shells used for one solid definition must not share any face.
  3. The enclosure of the first closed shell in the dataline defines an outer bound, while the
     enclosure of optional remaining shells define inner bounds. Points between inner and
     outer bound and the bounds itself are the material region, all other are void.
  4. Shells must not be multiply used by the same or different solids, but solids may be con-
     nected by faces, edges or vertices with other solids, if the different shells do so.

Remarks:




                                                                                                  Misc
  1. $ECHO lines may appear anywhere and as often as needed in the data input stream.




                                                                                                  DAT
  2. If ECHO is set to OFF printout of lines is suppressed.

  3. If ECHO is set to HEADER only header and bracket lines are printed.

  4. If ECHO is set to ON all input lines are printed.

  5. If ECHO is set to GEN all generated lines are printed in addition.

  6. The default may be set by the default parameter ECHO (see page 2-68).

  7. If an error is detected during the input the erroneous line is printed in any case. If the
     erroneous line is a data line and ECHO is set to OFF, the corresponding data block header
     line is printed in addition.

  8. In some cases the error message may appear before the echo-print of the erroneous line.
     This is not possible if ECHO is set to ON or GEN.

  9. $ECHO lines cannot have any continuation lines, they are always restricted to one physi-
     cal line.

V 19.00.287                PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                    3-1443
   physical line and its continuation line.

2. Input variables used within a $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket must be defined before the
   $LOOP statement.

3. Input variables with fixed integer index (e.g. VARNAM(3)) may be used, after its definition,
   anywhere in the current data input stream as constant items but not in the logical input
   line immediately after its definition.

4. If generation is selected, the variable values of type integer, real or double precision are
   generated according to
                                      x(i) = xS + (i − 1) ∗ xI
   For name and text values, an integer value is generated according to

                                      k(i) = kS + (i − 1) ∗ kI

   and appended to the constant name part cpname, i.e. the generated name/text is given
   by
                             name(i) =< cpname >< k(i) >
   without blanks etc. between name part and number. In case of text variables, cpname
   must be given in quotation marks.

5. $DEFVAR lines may have any number of continuation lines.

6. If KEEP = NO is specified, input variable definitions by $DEFVAR are valid only for the
   current data input stream, including, however, data files added by a $INCLUDE (see
   page 3-1444 ff.)-statement.

7. If KEEP = AUTO is specified (default), the $DEFVAR definition is kept global like KEEP=YES
   as long as the definition is globally unique. However, if the same name is used in other
   $DEFVAR statements with a different definition then KEEP=NO is applied (but identical
   duplicates are still kept globally).

8. If KEEP = YES is specified, the $DEFVAR definition is global and valid for all subsequent
   PERMAS data and UCI input streams. In addition, it may be used in corresponding UCI-
   commands by the help of self expanding format strings like ’%(defvar[name])’ (if the
   same name is used in other $DEFVAR statements with a different definition an error will
   be issued).

9. Gobal $DEFVAR definitions may be included, with identical definition, in all subsequent
   PERMAS data and UCI input streams.

       ! create a (infinite) list of integer values: 1,4,7,10,...

       ! create a (infinite) list of names and ensure global scope:
       ! MOD_FREQ_11, MOD_FREQ_12, MOD_FREQ_13,...
       $DEFVAR SIT_NAME TYPE=NAME     GEN=MOD_FREQ_,11,1   KEEP=YES

Please refer to examples LS14, LS17V2, LS17V3, DEVX1V1 et al. of [um550].

V 19.00.287               PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)              3-1445
         $LOOP    lpvar = iS , iE




rameter    Type    Value   Explanation

ar         name            Name of loop variable (max. 12 significant characters).
           I>0      iS     Start value of loop variable.
           I>0      iE     Last value of loop variable, iE ≥ iS .


marks:

1. Each $LOOP line initializes a new data generation loop with a unique loop variable lpvar.

2. Each data generation loop must be closed by a $ENDLOOP line.

3. Data generation loops may be defined within the $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket of a higher
   level data generation loop; up to 25 loop levels are supported.

4. $DEFVAR lines may not appear within a $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket.

5. A loop is executed iE − iS + 1-times where the loop variable is incremented by one at
   each execution, i.e. the value of the loop variable in cycle k is iS + k − 1.

6. $LOOP lines cannot have any continuation lines, they are always restricted to one physi-
   cal line.

ample:

      ! create a list of integer values: 10000, 10001...
      $DEFVAR NODEID    GEN=10000,1
      ! create a list of real values: 0.0, 1.0, 2.0 ...
      $DEFVAR NODCOOR TYPE=REAL GEN=0.0, 1.0

      $COOR       ! create 4 nodes
      $LOOP J=1,4
        NODEID(J) NODCOOR(J)    0.0       0.0
      $ENDLOOP

ase refer to examples LS14, LS17V2, LS17V3, DEVX1V1 et al. of [um550].




446                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      V 19.00.287
           $ENDLOOP



Remarks:

  1. Each $ENDLOOP line terminates innermost data generation loop.

  2. Each data generation loop must be closed by a $ENDLOOP line.

V 19.00.287              PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)        3-1447
         $IF ( A lop B ) THEN




rameter         Type        Value    Explanation

           R/I/name/text             First operand, see remark 5.
                                     Logical operator, see remark 7.
           R/I/name/text             Second operand, see remark 5.


marks:

1. A $IF line starts an IF . . . ENDIF construct.
2. Each IF . . . ENDIF construct must be closed by a $ENDIF line.
3. If the logical expression on the $IF line is false, all input lines between $IF- and $ENDIF
   lines are skipped.
4. IF . . . ENDIF constructs must not be nested.
5. The operands A and B may be input variables defined by a $DEFVAR (see page 3-1447
   ff.) command or constant values. In any case, the type of the second operand, may be
   R, I, name or text, must match the type of the first one. Comparing of single and double
   precision values is allowed. Constant text operands must be given in quotes.
6. Outside of a loop, input variables must have a fixed integer index. Within a loop, the loop
   counter may be an index expression, see $DEFVAR (see page 3-1447 ff.) command.
7. The possible logical operators are listed in the following table:

                                <        Less condition
                               <=        Less or equal condition
                               ==        Equal condition
                               /=        Not equal condition
                               >=        Greater or equal condition
                                >        Greater condition

   For name or text operands only equal or not equal conditions are available. Comparison
   of names is always done in uppercase representation.
8. $IF lines cannot have any continuation lines, they are always restricted to one physical
   line.

FLA2           2 Noded Straight Flange (Rod) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   4-8

FLA3           3 Noded Straight Flange (Rod) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-15




                                                                                                     Elements
The flange elements are displacement models that are fully compatible with the membrane ele-




                                                                                                      Flange
ments QUAM and TRIM. Their main application is thus the modelling of enforcements (flanges,
stringers, prestressing cables) in membrane shells and in plane stress problems.

Both elements have their cross section centroids aligned along a straight axis z’, on which the
elements nodes are also located.

Flange elements can carry loads only along their axis (no bending, torsion, or shear stiffness).
If a more general load-carrying capacity is needed, beam elements must be used instead.
Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the flange
elements may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed explicitly.

When flange elements are combined with other elements it is important that elements of the
same order are coupled:

   • FLA2 elements are compatible with the edges of HEXE8, PENTA6, PYRA5, QUAD4,
     QUAM4, SHEAR4, TET4, TRIA3 and TRIM3.

   • FLA3 elements are compatible with straight edges of HEXE20, HEXE27, PENTA15,
     PENTA18, TET10, QUAM8, QUAM9 and TRIM6 if the inner node of the edge is at mid-
     point position.

Flange elements may have, according to their nature, only homogeneous isotropic material,
therefore a homogeneous material has to be defined with TYPE = ISO (default). The appropri-
ate material property type is GENERAL, but SHELL and PLANE, if existent, are accepted in
addition. All applicable material input options for flange elements are summarized in the follow-
ing table:

The membrane elements are displacement models that are, straight element edges assumed,
fully compatible with the flange elements FLA.

Membrane elements can carry loads only within their reference plane (no bending). Quadri-
lateral elements are mapped into that plane, therefore corner nodes don’t have to be exactly




                                                                                                 Membrane
                                                                                                 Elements
coplanar. When a more general load-carrying capacity is needed, shell elements must be used
instead. Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the
membrane elements may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
explicitly.

When membrane elements are combined with flange elements it is important that elements of
the same order are coupled:

   • FLA2 elements are compatible with the edges of TRIM3 and QUAM4.

   • FLA3 elements are compatible with straight edges of QUAM8, QUAM9 and TRIM6, if the
     inner node of the edge is at midpoint position.

The local element system for triangular elements is defined as follows:

  1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.

  2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.

  3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.

For quadrilateral elements the local element system is defined in the following way:

  1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
     plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.




V 19.00.287                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      4-21
3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
   the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
   rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.

4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
   the reference surface.

The solid elements can be classified with respect to their geometry or the order of their shape
functions. In terms of geometry there are four types of elements:




                                                                                                     Elements
                                                                                                       Solid
   • The Brick elements HEXE8, HEXFO8 HEXE20 and HEXE27.

   • The Wedge elements PENTA6, PENTA15 and PENTA18.

   • The Tetrahedron elements TET4, and TET10.

   • The Pyramid element PYRA5.

Although tetrahedron elements are sufficient to mesh any geometry, better results are obtained
when brick elements are used whenever possible, restricting the use of wedges, tetrahedrons
and pyramids to those parts of the mesh where they cannot be avoided.

In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified:

   • Elements with linear shape functions: HEXE8, HEXFO8, PENTA6, TET4 and PYRA5.

   • Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: HEXE20 and PENTA15.

   • Elements with quadratic shape functions: HEXE27, PENTA18 and TET10.


V 19.00.287                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          4-73
solid elements carry 3 displacement degrees of freedom per node. At times it may be phys-
ly meaningful to combine solid elements with other elements (e.g. FLA, TRIM or QUAM),
ng into account that at the connections there may be severe discontinuities resulting in
orted stress patterns.

 the combination of solid and shell elements a volume shell transition using interpolation
ions is recommended (see page 3-150, 3-155 or 3-163 ).

all solid elements, the positive face normal is directed outwards and does not depend on
sequence of corner nodes of the face.

BECOS          2 Noded Straight Solid Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-172

BECOC          2 Noded Straight Thin-Walled Tube . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-178

BETAC          2 Noded Straight Tapered Thin-Walled Tube . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-184

BECOP          2 Noded Straight Thin-Walled Open Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-190

BETOP          2 Noded Straight Tapered Thin-Walled Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-196

BEAM2          2 Noded Straight General Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-202

BEAM2W         2 Noded Straight General Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-209

FSCPIPE2       2 Noded Straight or Curved Fluid-Filled Pipe . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-216




The beam elements BECOS, BECOC, BETAC, BECOP and BETOP are formulated as equilib-
rium models, based on engineering theory of bending and St. Venant torsion. In addition, shear
effects in bending (BECOC, BETAC, BETOP) and torsion-bending (BECOP, BETOP) may be
included.
The beam elements BEAM2 and BEAM2W are Timoshenko beams with St. Venant torsion and
shear effects in bending, BEAM2W including torsion-bending in addition.
With the exception of the fluid filled pipe element FSCPIPE2, all beam elements have their
cross section centroids G aligned along a straight axis, and may have excentric nodes, i.e. off-
set vectors from node Pi to the corresponding centroid Gi .

                   Definition of local element system for beam elements


1. The z ′ -axis coincides with the beam axis (neutral axis), pointing from the center of gravity
   G1 at node P1 to G2 at node P2 . For beam elements without offset the z ′ -axis is running
   from node P1 to node P2 .

2. The z ′ x′ -plane is spanned by the z ′ -axis and the vector from centroid G1 to the reference
   point P0 .

3. The x′ -axis, lying in the z ′ x′ -plane perpendicular to the z ′ -axis, is directed towards the
   reference point P0 .

4. The y ′ -axis forms a right hand system with the z ′ - and the x′ -axis.

Stress Resultants


If no information about the geometry of the beam cross-sections is available, only stress resul-
tants instead of stresses are calculated. They are referred to the local beam coordinate system
(x′ y ′ z ′ ), and are calculated at the end cross-sections of the beam, containing the following
components:


 N            Normal force in direction of beam axis z ′ . Positive if beam is elongated.

 Sx′          Shear force in x′ -direction, acting at shear center of cross-section. Positive at
              node P1 if pointing into negative x′ -direction, and at node P2 if pointing into posi-
              tive x′ -direction.

 Sy ′         Shear force in y ′ -direction, acting at shear center of cross-section. Positive at
              node P1 if pointing into negative y ′ -direction, and at node P2 if pointing into posi-
              tive y ′ -direction.

 Mx′          Bending moment about x′ -axis. Positive at node P1 if anti-parallel to x′ -axis, and




                                                                                                        Elements
              at node P2 if parallel to x′ -axis.




                                                                                                          Beam
 My′          Bending moment about y ′ -axis. Positive at node P1 if parallel to y ′ -axis, and at
              node P2 if anti-parallel to y ′ -axis.
 T            Twisting moment about z ′ -axis (beam axis). Positive at node P1 if anti-parallel to
              z ′ -axis, and at node P2 if parallel to z ′ -axis.

 B            Bimoment (only for BECOP, BETOP and BEAM2W).

 pi           Pressure of inner fluid (only for FSCPIPE2).

analogy to the stress resultants, the initial strains which can be specified for beam elements
 integrated quantities. They are able to produce virtual work on the stress resultants, and
 be understood as initial deformations referring to the local beam coordinate system:


          Elongation of the beam along z ′ -axis.

 ,1       Bending deformation of the beam axis at node P1 about x′ -axis.

 ,2       Bending deformation of the beam axis at node P2 about x′ -axis.

,1        Bending deformation of the beam axis at node P1 about y ′ -axis.

,2        Bending deformation of the beam axis at node P2 about y ′ -axis.

          Total initial twist of the beam axis.

          Initial twist of the beam axis at node P1 .

          Initial twist of the beam axis at node P2 .
                                dθ
          Initial rate of twist dz ′ at node P1 (only BECOP, BETOP and BEAM2W).

                                dθ
          Initial rate of twist dz ′ at node P2 (only BECOP, BETOP and BEAM2W).

                                 Definition of initial deformations



The initial elongation δ is positive if the beam is stretched. The initial bending deformations
φ can be interpreted as the initial slopes at the ends of a simply supported beam. They are
positive if produced by a pair of positive bending moments. The initial twist deformation θ is




                                                                                                        Elements
the initial relative angle of twist and positive, if produced by a pair of positive twisting moments.



                                                                                                          Beam
The sign conventions for the initial deformations thus are in agreement with those for the stress
resultants.

finition of Element System:
  For straight elements (curvature 1/R = 0) the standard local element system for
  beam elements is used, defined by the beam axis (neutral axis) and reference point
  P0 , see page 4-160.
  For curved elements (curvature 1/R > 0) it is assumed that the element lies within
  the plane defined by element nodes P1 , P2 and the reference point P0 , and the
  reference point is inside of the curvature on the opposite side of the straight line
  connecting the element nodes.




16                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       V 19.00.287

neral Description:
  Circular tube with constant ring cross section, filled with a compressible internal
  fluid. The ends of the tube may be connected to other tubes, closed or open. Equi-
  librium model for tension, bending (Timoshenko beam), St.Venant torsion, trans-
  verse shear. Longitudinal stresses/strains due to internal pressure are included.
  Linear interpolation for displacement of internal fluid along pipe axis. If the internal
  fluid is omitted, the corresponding degree of freedom has to be suppressed.
  The mass of the inner fluid is split up between the translational degree of freedom
  of the fluid and the translational degrees of freedom of the structure normal to the
  pipe axis. If an outer fluid is present, no degree of freedom is associated with that
  fluid, but its mass is added to the translational degrees of freedom of the structure
  normal to the pipe axis.

For the combination of solid and shell elements a volume shell transition using interpolation
regions is recommended (see page 3-150, 3-155 or 3-163 ).

The local element system for triangular elements is defined as follows:

  1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.

  2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.

  3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.

For quadrilateral elements the local element system is defined in the following way:

  1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
     plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.

  2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
     pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
     rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
     corner node).

  3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
                                                                                                     Elements
     the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
                                                                                                       Shell

     rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.

  4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
     the reference surface.

neral Description:
  Plane element with bilinear displacement field for membrane, linear bending mo-
  ment along element edges and constant transverse shear forces. Warped elements
  are handled by transformation into a plane reference configuration. Separation of
  membrane and bending stiffness is possible. Suited for thin and thick shell appli-
  cations. Artificial (small) stiffness for in-plane rotations. Optionally with rigid lever
  arms from nodal point to corner of element middle surface.
  Two additional formulations are available. Setting
        DEFAULT SET LQUADSHAPE = QUAD4N
  yields a formulation with modified membrane and bending stiffness whereas with
        DEFAULT SET LQUADSHAPE = QUAD4R
  a formulation is applied where the in-plane rotations are coupled to the membrane
  displacement field.

ntrol of Stiffness Calculation
  The parameter sep in the geometrical data input allows for separation of membrane
  and bending stiffness:
           sep = 0     Complete stiffness matrix is calculated (default).
           sep = 1     Only bending and shear stiffness is calculated.
           sep = 2     Only membrane stiffness is calculated.
  The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
  element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by

                                   Kϕz ′ = (0.01 + c)KB

  where KB is a mean bending stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by default
  equals zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.01 means no
  artificial stiffness.
  Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
  freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
  plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least
  at one nodal point. This is no longer true if the modified formulation ’QUAD4R’ is
  selected.

ethod:                    Calculated at center of element

                       (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ ) in lower surface
                       isotropic material: referred to element system
                       anisotropic material: referred to material system

General Description:
     Plane element with bilinear displacement field for membrane, linear bending mo-

     by transformation into a plane reference configuration. Separation of membrane
     and bending stiffness is possible. Suited for thin and thick shell applications. Artifi-
     cial (small) stiffness for inplane rotations. Optionally with rigid lever arms from nodal

     and bending stiffness:
              sep = 0     Complete stiffness matrix is calculated (default).
              sep = 1     Only bending and shear stiffness is calculated.

                                      Kϕz ′ = (0.01 + c)KB

                                                                                                     Shell




V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        4-243
neral Description:
  Plane element with linear displacement field for membrane, linear bending moment
  along element edges and constant transverse shear forces. Separation of mem-
  brane and bending stiffness is possible. Suited for thin and moderate thick shell
  applications. Artificial (small) stiffness for inplane rotations. Optionally with rigid
  lever arms from nodal point to corner of element reference surface. Laminate mid-
  dle surface and element reference surface may be separated.

ntrol of Stiffness Calculation
  The parameter sep in the geometrical data input allows for separation of membrane
  and bending stiffness:
           sep = 0     Complete stiffness matrix is calculated (default).
           sep = 1     Only bending and shear stiffness is calculated.
           sep = 2     Only membrane stiffness is calculated.
  The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
  element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by

                                        Kϕz ′ = (0.01 + c)KB

  where KB is a mean bending stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by default
  equals zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.01 means no
  artificial stiffness.
  Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
  freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
  plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least at
  one nodal point.

esses:
ethod:                        Calculated at center of element.
                              Available only for laminate description by plies.
ored in book SIG.DISP: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ σy′ z ′ , σx′ z ′ ) in the middle surface of each ply,
                       referred to material system
inted element stresses: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ σy′ z ′ , σx′ z ′ ) in the middle surface of each ply,
                        referred to material system
eraged nodal stresses: Element ignored (no contribution)

                                  referred to material system
    Printed stress resultants: Membrane forces (Nx′ x′ , Ny′ y′ , Nx′ y′ ), transverse shear forces
                               (Ny′ z ′ , Nx′ z ′ ) and bending moments (Mx′ x′ , My′ y′ , Mx′ y′ ),

 62                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       V 19.00.287
General Description:
     Plane element with linear displacement field for membrane, incomplete quartic dis-
     placement field for bending (Kirchhoff bending theory) and constant transverse
     shear forces. Separation of membrane and bending stiffness is possible. Suited
     only for thin shell applications. Artificial (small) stiffness for inplane rotations. Op-
     tionally with rigid lever arms from nodal point to corner of element middle surface.

Control of Stiffness Calculation
     The parameter sep in the geometrical data input allows for separation of membrane
     and bending stiffness:
              sep = 0     Complete stiffness matrix is calculated (default).
              sep = 1     Only bending and shear stiffness is calculated.
              sep = 2     Only membrane stiffness is calculated.
     The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
     element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by

                                      Kϕz ′ = (0.01 + c)KB

     where KB is a mean bending stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by default
     equals zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.01 means no
     artificial stiffness.
     Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
     freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
     plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least at
     one nodal point.

QUAMS4         4 Node Quadrilateral Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-280

QUAMS8         8 Node Quadrilateral Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-286

QUAMS9         9 Node Quadrilateral Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-292

TRIMS3         3 Node Triangular Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-298

TRIMS6         6 Node Triangular Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-304




The solid shell elements can be classified with respect to their geometry and order of their
shape functions. In terms of geometry there are two types of elements:

   • The quadrilateral elements QUAMS4, QUAMS8 and QUAMS9.

   • The triangular elements TRIMS3, TRIMS6.

In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified :

   • Elements with linear shape functions: QUAMS4, TRIMS3.

   • Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: QUAMS8.

   • Elements with quadratic shape functions: QUAMS9, TRIMS6.

The element with the same order of shape function are fully compatible with each other when-
ever they match face to face. When the faces do not match completely (e.g. when two triangles
are mated with a quadrilateral), the full kinematic compatibility is lost.

All solid shell elements carry 7 degree of freedoms per node. Linear solid shell elements can
be combined with the linear shell elements TRIA3 and QUAD4.

For the combination of solid and shell elements a volume shell transition using interpolation
regions is recommended (see page 3-150, 3-155 or 3-163).

Lower and upper surface of solid shell elements are defined by the shell director which points
from the lower to the upper element surface. The shell director forms a right hand system
with the axes of the reference surface in the initial configuration at the nodal points. The shell
director varies over and is not necessarily perpendicular to the axes of the reference surface.
When common shell directors at the nodal points are used (DEFAULT SET CSHDIR = ON), the
shell directors of adjacent solid shell elements should have approximately the same direction.
The allowable kink angle is specified by DEFAULT SET CSHDIRKINK.

General Description:
     Element with straight edges, bilinear displacement field on reference surface and
     linear displacement field across the thickness. Suited for thin and thick shell appli-
     cations. Artificial (small) stiffness for inplane rotations.

Control of Stiffness Calculation
     The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
     element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by

                                    Kϕz ′ = (0.001 + c)Krot

     where Krot is a mean rotational stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by
     default equal zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.001
     means no artificial stiffness.
     Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
     freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
     plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least at
     one nodal point.

Stresses:
 Method:                    Calculated at Gauss points on reference surface and at Lobatto
                            points through the thickness. Extrapolated to corner nodes.
 Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx )
                          at all nodes with five layers through the thickness
                          first layer belongs to upper surface
                          third layer belongs to the reference surface
                          fifth layer belongs to lower surface

 Printed element stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx )
                           at all nodes with five layers through the thickness
                           first layer belongs to upper surface
                           third layer belongs to the reference surface
                           fifth layer belongs to lower surface

 Averaged nodal stresses: Element ignored, no contribution.

 06                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           V 19.00.287
General Description:
     Element with curved edges, quadratic displacement field on reference surface and
     linear across the thickness. Suited for thin and thick shell applications. Artificial
     (small) stiffness for inplane rotations.

Control of Stiffness Calculation
     The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
     element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by

                                    Kϕz ′ = (0.001 + c)Krot

     where Krot is a mean rotational stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by
     default equal zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.001
     means no artificial stiffness.
     Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
     freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
     plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least at
     one nodal point.

Stresses:
 Method:                    Calculated at Gauss points of reference surface and at Lobatto
                            points through the thickness. Extrapolated to corner nodes.
 Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx )
                          at all nodes with five layers through the thickness
                          first layer belongs to upper surface
                          third layer belongs to the reference surface
                          fifth layer belongs to lower surface

 Printed element stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx )
                           at all nodes with five layers through the thickness
                           first layer belongs to upper surface
                           third layer belongs to the reference surface
                           fifth layer belongs to lower surface

 Averaged nodal stresses: Element ignored, no contribution.

Three–dimensional Gasket Elements are used to model sealing components between struc-
tural components. The through–the–thickness behavior is uncoupled from membrane and
transverse shear behavior and is defined by a non–linear pressure/closure curve known from
test data. The nonlinearity can be elastic or plastic. Membrane and transverse shear behaviour
is linear elastic. There is no thermal expansion in through–the–thickness direction.

With the default settings (GSKSOLV = CONTACT) the gasket model corresponds to a mem-
brane with decoupled non-linear springs.


                                                                  γ




                               Schematic of a gasket element

The midsurface behaves like a membrane element with material parameters E and ν. Decou-
pled springs act in through-the-thickness direction at element edges with a nonlinear gasket
loading curve. The shear behavior of the springs corresponds to a shear modulus G with
τ = G tan γ.

Element specific results are GASKET CLOSURE and GASKET PRESSURE, which are cre-
ated automatically.




V 19.00.287                 PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         4-311
 • The Wedge elements GKPNT6, GKPNT15 and GKPNT18.

erms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified:

 • Elements with linear shape functions: GKHEX8 and GKPNT6.
 • Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: GKHEX20 and GKPNT15.
 • Elements with quadratic shape functions: GKHEX27 and GKPNT18.

ments with the same order of shape function are fully compatible with each other whenever
y match face to face. When the faces do not match completely (e.g. when two triangles are
ted with a quadrilateral), the full kinematic compatibility is lost.

Gasket elements carry 3 displacement degrees of freedom per node.

 default the through–the–thickness direction of the Gasket elements is orthogonal to the
 surface between element faces 1 and 6 for the brick elements and element faces 1 and 5
the wedge elements. For brick elements also another midsurface can be chosen by defining
element system $ELSYS (see page 3-97 and remark 3) in the structure bracket. Then the
ough–the–thickness is orthogonal to the midsurface which is orthogonal to the z’ axis of the
ment system.

 all Gasket elements, the positive face normal is directed outwards and does not depend on
 sequence of corner nodes of the face.

Typically gasket elements are connected to adjacent parts by a fixed coupling ($MPC ISURFACE
or common nodes) on bottom, respectively top side. The opposite side is connected by a
contact boundary condition ($CONTACT) with the gasket element nodes as second contact
partner.

If necessary, local element systems for spring elements are defined using three points R1 , R2
and R3 as follows:

  1. The xR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .

  2. The yR -axis is perpendicular to the xR -axis, pointing to the third point R3

  3. The zR -axis forms a right hand system with the xR - and yR -axis.

  4. The local element system (x′ , y ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (xR , yR , zR ) with
     its origin at the first element node.

lated for both nodes, referring to the local element coordinate system (x y z ), and can be
easily interpreted as the forces acting on the element in order to produce the elastic deforma-
tions. The latter are represented by the difference of total element deformations and element
initial deformations. For SPRING1, SPRING3, NLSTIFF and NLSTIFFR elements correspond-
ing stress resultants at both nodes are antivalent (equal magnitude, opposite direction), with




                                                                                                       Elements
positive values at the second node for positive elastic elongations ∆ui = ui,P 2 − ui,P 1 .




                                                                                                        Spring
In analogy to the stress resultants, the initial strains which can be specified for spring elements
are initial deformations, referring to the local element coordinate system:


 δ1           Elongation along the x′ -axis.

 δ2           Elongation along the y ′ -axis.

 δ3           Elongation along the z ′ -axis.

 δ4           Twist about the x′ -axis.

 δ5           Twist about the y ′ -axis.

 δ6           Twist about the z ′ -axis.

When all degrees of freedom at the first element node P1 are suppressed, a positive elongation
will move the second element node P2 in the direction of the corresponding local coordinate
axis, and a positive twist will rotate node P2 in a positive sense of rotation around the respective
local coordinate axis.

General Description:
     Discrete equilibrium model with nonlinear force/deflection characteristic for elonga-
     tion along the spring axis:




                                                                                                    Elements
                         Fx′ = f (∆u′ )       with      ∆u′ = u′P 2 − u′P 1




                                                                                                     Spring
     No stiffness with respect to transverse displacements or rotations. The nonlinear
     force is split up into a linear and a nonlinear part according to

                                       Fx′ = k ∆u′ + fnl (∆u′ )

     where the constant value k is determined by the derivation of the nonlinear function
     for ∆u′ = ulin
                                          dFx′
                                    k=
                                         d(∆u′ ) ∆u′ =ulin
     and included in the stiffness matrix, whereas the nonlinear part

                                       fnl (∆u′ ) = Fx′ − k ∆u′

     is added to the right-hand side of the dynamic equation in transient response anal-
     ysis. Consequently, in statics, eigenmodes and frequency response analysis only
     the linear part is taken into account.
     Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the
     element may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed ex-
     plicitly.

Stresses:
     No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

                            ment system.

General Description:
     Discrete equilibrium model with nonlinear moment/rotation characteristic for twist
     about the spring axis:

                         Mx′ = f (∆ϕ′ ),      with     ∆ϕ′ = ϕ′P 2 − ϕ′P 1

     ysis. Consequently, in statics, eigenmodes and frequency response analysis only
     the linear part is taken into account.
     Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the
     element may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed ex-
     plicitly.

Number of Nodes: 2
Coordinates:      Necessary for node P1 and P2 , may be identical.
Discretisation:   Constant stiffness between two specified translational degrees of freedom at
                  different nodes.
D. O. F. Types:   DISP


Definition of Element System:
     Stiffness acts in the direction of the (rotated) basis at the element nodes. Element
     force results are stored in the local element system which is assumed to coincide
     with the (possibly rotated) basis at node P1 .

Remarks:

  1. If the element nodes have different coordinates, and the specified degrees of freedom are
     not collinear, then an additional elastic constraint is introduced which may e.g. destroy
     rigid body motion.

  2. Element force results are stored in the element system which can differ from the rotated
     basis at node P2 .

  3. Since the element has no temperature degrees of freedom, it is ignored in thermal anal-
     ysis.

                                                                                                             Mass
If necessary, local element systems for mass elements are defined using three points R1 , R2
and R3 as follows:

  1. The xR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .

  2. The yR -axis is perpendicular to the xR -axis, pointing to the third point R3

  3. The zR -axis forms a right hand system with the xR - and yR -axis.

  4. The local element system (x′ , y ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (xR , yR , zR ) with
     its origin at the first element node.

X2DAMP6        Scalar Viscous Damper at Two Nodes with Six Degrees of Freedom . . . 4-437



All available damper elements have viscous damping, i.e. their element forces depend on the
time derivative of the element deformations. Element structural damping, however, may be




                                                                                                           Elements
                                                                                                           Damper
represented using any type of linear ’stiffness’ element with material property $DAMPING.


If necessary, local element systems for damper elements are defined using three points R1 , R2
and R3 as follows:

  1. The xR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .

  2. The yR -axis is perpendicular to the xR -axis, pointing to the third point R3

  3. The zR -axis forms a right hand system with the xR - and yR -axis.

  4. The local element system (x′ , y ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (xR , yR , zR ) with
     its origin at the first element node.

cous damper elements do not refer to any material property, therefore no material has to be

ess Resultants and Initial Deformations


 viscous damper elements only stress resultants are available. They are calculated for both
des, referring to the local element coordinate system (x′ y ′ z ′ ), and can be easily interpreted
the forces acting on the element in order to produce the element deformation velocity. For
MP1, DAMP3, NLDAMP and NLDAMPR elements corresponding stress resultants at both
des are antivalent (equal magnitude, opposite direction), with positive values at the second
de for positive element deformation velocity ∆u̇i = u̇i,P 2 − u̇i,P 1 .

Discretisation:   Nonlinear force/velocity characteristic in direction of the damper axis.
                  No damping with respect to transverse displacements and rotations.
D. O. F. Types:   DISP


Definition of Element System:
      Damper axis and local x′ -axis are always identical.
      If the element nodes have different locations in space, the damper axis points from
      node P1 to node P2 .
      If the element nodes have identical coordinates, the local element system has to be
      defined using three points, see page 4-411.


Remarks:

  1. The element does not refer to any material property.

  2. The nonlinear part of the element force is restricted to direct or modal transient response
     analysis. For any other kind of linear analysis only the linearized element characteristic
     (constant viscous damping coefficient) is taken into account.

  3. Since the element has no temperature degrees of freedom, it is ignored in thermal anal-
     ysis.

General Description:
     Discrete equilibrium model with nonlinear force/velocity characteristic for elongation
     along the spring axis:

                         Fx′ = f (∆u̇′ )    with       ∆u̇′ = u̇′P 2 − u̇′P 1

     The nonlinear force is split up into a linear and a nonlinear part according to

                                    Fx′ = du ∆u̇′ + fnl (∆u̇′ )

     where the constant value du is determined by the derivation of the nonlinear function
     for ∆u̇′ = u̇lin
                                           dFx′
                                    du =
                                          d(∆u̇′ ) ∆u̇′ =u̇lin
     and included in the viscous damping matrix, whereas the nonlinear part

                                    fnl (∆u̇′ ) = Fx′ − du ∆u̇′




                                                                                                    Elements
     is added to the right-hand side of the dynamic equation in transient response anal-




                                                                                                    Damper
     ysis. Consequently, in frequency response analysis only the linear part is taken into
     account.
     No damping with respect to transverse displacements or rotations.

Stresses:
     No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

                            ment system.

neral Description:
  Discrete equilibrium model with nonlinear force/velocity characteristic for twist about
  the spring axis:

                      Mx′ = f (∆ϕ̇′ ),    with      ∆ϕ̇′ = ϕ̇′P 2 − ϕ̇′P 1

  The nonlinear moment is split up into a linear and a nonlinear part according to

                                 Mx′ = dϕ ∆ϕ̇′ + fnl (∆ϕ̇′ )

  where the constant value dϕ is determined by the derivation of the nonlinear function
  for ∆ϕ̇′ = ϕ̇lin
                                       dMx′
                                 dϕ =
                                      d(∆ϕ̇′ ) ∆ϕ̇′ =ϕ̇lin
  and included in the viscous damping matrix, whereas the nonlinear part

                                 fnl (∆ϕ̇′ ) = Mx′ − dϕ ∆ϕ̇′

  is added to the right-hand side of the dynamic equation in transient response anal-
  ysis. Consequently, in frequency response analysis only the linear part is taken into
  account.
  No damping with respect to translations or rotations perpendicular to element axis.

esses:
  No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

                          ment system.

HEXVE8         8 Noded Viscoelastic Solid Hexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-444

HEXVR8         8 Noded Viscoelastic Solid Hexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-448




Viscoelastic elements represent a Maxwell model, i.e. elastic and viscous part in series. The
submatrices of the elastic part are identical to the matrices of the corresponding solid elements,
i.e. for the HEXVE8 element the matrices of the HEXE8 element etc.. To achieve a general-
ized Maxwell or Biot model, one or more viscoelastic solid elements are added to one standard
(basic) solid element, forming a so-called Prony series. The standard translational degrees of
freedom of all those viscoelastic elements belonging to one basic element must be coupled,
either by identical element node lists (HEXVR8 elements) or coupled by MPCs (HEXVE8 ele-
ments). The non-standard degrees of freedom of HEXVE8 elements, representing the viscous
part, remain uncoupled.


For all viscous solid elements, the positive face normal is directed outwards and does not
depend on the sequence of corner nodes of the face.

LOADA4         4 Node Quadrilateral Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . 4-457




                                                                                                    Mem
                                                                                                      L
LOADA8         8 Node Quadrilateral Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . 4-460

LOADA9         9 Node Quadrilateral Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . 4-463

LOADA3         3 Node Triangular Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-466

LOADA6         6 Node Triangular Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-469

The load carrying membrane elements can be classified with respect to their geometry and
order of their shape functions. In terms of geometry there are two types of elements:

   • The Quadrilateral elements LOADA4, LOADA8 and LOADA9.

   • The Triangular elements LOADA3, LOADA6.

In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified :

   • Elements with linear shape functions: LOADA3, LOADA4.

   • Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: LOADA8.

   • Elements with quadratic shape functions: LOADA6, LOADA9.

The element with the same order of shape function are fully compatible with each other when-
ever they match face to face. When the faces do not match completely (e.g. when two triangles
are mated with a quadrilateral), the full kinematic compatibility is lost.

All load carrying membrane elements have three degree of freedoms per node. They are used
solely for the definition of surface loads which act on solid elements. In addition they are able
to calculate the stresses on the boundary of solid elements, plain stress conditions assumed.
Hence evaluation of stresses on surfaces loaded by out-of-plane loads will give wrong results,
since the effect of stresses normal to the surface is ignored. In any case the material property
of the elements must be identical to the underlying solid elements. They do not contribute to
stiffness, damping or mass matrix.

   • LOADA3 elements are compatible with the surfaces of TET4, PYRA5 and PENTA6.

   • LOADA4 elements are compatible with the surfaces of PYRA5, PENTA6 and HEXE8.

   • LOADA6 elements are compatible with the surfaces of TET10, PENTA15 and PENTA18.

   • LOADA8 elements are compatible with the surfaces of PENTA15 and HEXE20.

   • LOADA9 elements are compatible with the surfaces of HEXE27.

   Definition of local element systems, element corner nodes Ci and element edges Ei for
                        triangular and quadrilateral membrane elements

For the print–out of stresses the local element system for triangular elements is defined as
follows:

  1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.

  2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.

  3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.

For the print–out of stresses the local element system for quadrilateral elements is defined in
the following way:

  1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
     plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.

  2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
     pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
     rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
     corner node).

  3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
     the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
     rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.

  4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
     the reference surface.

If necessary, local element systems for special elements are defined using three points R1 , R2
and R3 as follows:

  1. The xR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .

  2. The yR -axis is perpendicular to the xR -axis, pointing to the third point R3

  3. The zR -axis forms a right hand system with the xR - and yR -axis.

  4. The local element system (x′ , y ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (xR , yR , zR ) with
     its origin at the first element node.

General Description:
     Discrete force generator with nonlinear force acting in the direction of element axis.
     The element force is defined by




                                                                                                      Elements
                        Fx′ = f (xi ),    i = 1, n    with      1 ≤ n ≤ 18




                                                                                                       Special
     where up to 18 of the element nodal point displacements or corresponding velocities
     may be used as independent variables. Rotated node bases are taken into account,
     i.e. displacements and velocities used as independent variables refer to local node
     bases. A positive element force Fx′ acts at the first element node P1 in positive
     x′ -direction, and at the second element node P2 in negative x′ -direction. The third
     element node is used to carry degrees of freedom and may be located anywhere in
     space.
     Furthermore, for Harmonic Balance, there may be forces acting on the third node,
     defined by the field HYSTFUN. In this case the DOFs of the third node may act as
     internal variables of a hysteresis law, for example. Since the element has no linear
     stiffness, it will introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
     explicitly unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary condi-
     tions.

Stresses:
     No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

                              ment system.

 Printed stress resultants: (Nx′ , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0) at both element nodes

     No distributed loads available.

marks:

1. The element may introduce nonlinear or linear, optionally frequency or speed dependent
   forces or any combination of it.

2. At least one of the field pairs FUNCTION and VAR, STIFFLIN and STIFFKND or DAMPLIN
   and DAMPKND must be defined.

3. Repetition = 15 means that up to 15 fields VAR may be used to declare independent
   variables for the functions defining the nonlinear element characteristics as well as fre-
   quency and speed dependency. The sequence of VAR-fields defines the sequence of
   independent variables, i.e. the i-th field VAR belongs to the i-th variable, and the se-
   quence is valid for all nonlinear force functions in field FUNCTION.

4. For elnid > 0, fields VAR declare displacements or velocities at the element nodes P1 to
   P3 as independent variables of the functions.




82                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        V 19.00.287
                  1   Actual time
                  2   Time step counter
                  3   Frequency in cycles per unit time (cycles per second)
                  4   Rotational speed in cycles per unit time (cycles per second)
                  5   Rotational speed in radians per unit time (radians per second)




                                                                                                    Elements
                                                                                                     Special
                  6   Rotational speed in revolutions per minute

  6. Nonlinear force function identifier f id = 0 or omitting trailing function identifiers means
     that the corresponding nonlinear natural force is equal zero. Stiffness and damping con-
     tribution for that degree of freedom, if defined, are nevertheless included.

  7. Natural stiffness and viscous damping matrices of dimension (6,6) referring to local el-
     ement coordinate system may be input where the matrix kind is specified by stf knd or
     dmpknd resp. according to:

                                 kind      Meaning          No.of values
                                    0      Diagonal              6
                                    1      Symmetric            21
                                    2      Quadratic            36

     The matrix input is done columnwise, for diagonal matrices only the diagonal, for sym-
     metric matrices only the upper triangle is input. Trailing zeroes may be omitted. The
     symmetric part of the stiffness matrix must be positive (semi-)definite.

  8. The structural damping matrix is established by multiplying each element of the stiffness
     matrix by the corresponding structural damping factor. Therefore, the following rules must
     be fulfilled:

        • Input of structural damping factors is possible if and only if the constant stiffness
          matrix is specified.
        • The kind of the structural damping matrix (diagonal, symmetric or quadratic) is al-
          ways the same as the kind of the stiffness matrix, i.e. it is given by stf knd.

     For analyses in time domain, e.g. for time history analysis, structural damping is con-
     verted to equivalent viscous damping by
                                                       1             
                                        (dequ )ij =          (gij kij )
                                                      2 π fE

     The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by pa-
     rameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.

  9. For static analysis or real eigenvalue calculation, only the symmetric part of the constant
     stiffness matrix in field STIFFLIN is taken into account.



V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         4-483
      • Field STIFFFUN with stiffness function identifiers may be specified if and only if
        constant stiffness matrix is given in field STIFFLIN.
      • Field DAMPFUN with viscous damping function identifiers may be specified if and
        only if constant viscous damping matrix is given in field DAMPLIN.
      • Field GFUN with structural damping factor function identifiers may be specified if and
        only if constant stiffness matrix is given in field STIFFLIN. Field G, however, may be
        missing.
      • The sequence of function identifiers in fields STIFFFUN, DAMPFUN and GFUN cor-
        responds to the sequence of matrix elements in fields STIFFLIN and DAMPLIN, i.e.
        the i-th function identifier in field STIFFFUN replaces the i-th matrix element in field
        STIFFLIN etc.. Function identifiers equal zero are ignored.
      • Stiffness and viscous damping functions may be frequency and/or speed dependent,
        structural damping factor functions only frequency dependent. The independent vari-
        ables frequency and rotational speed must be declared by means of fields VAR.
      • If a field VAR specifies frequency as independent variable, all specified stiffness,
        viscous damping and structural damping factor functions must be frequency depen-
        dent. If a field VAR specifies rotational speed as independent variable, all specified
        stiffness and viscous damping functions must be speed dependent. The sequence
        of frequency and speed specification by fields VAR fixes the sequence of those inde-
        pendent variables for stiffness and viscous damping functions, and all other indepen-
        dent variables declared in the remaining fields VAR are ignored for those functions.

1. For time history analysis, the nonlinear force functions in field FUNCTION determine the
   complete natural element forces. If, for any natural degree of freedom, no nonlinear force
   function is defined, then the corresponding natural force is calculated from stiffness and
   damping matrices, if those matrices are input.

2. If frequency is specified as independent variable, the value is determined according to
   following rules:

      • If the UCI-command provides the specification of a reference frequency, the refer-
        ence frequency is specified by the command.
      • For time history analysis, the reference frequency must be input in the aligned result
        variant by parameter RFREQTHA, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-1055.
      • For analyses in the frequency domain where the solution procedure performs a loop
        over excitation frequency, the actual excitation frequency is used.

3. If rotational speed is specified as independent variable, its value must be input within the
   aligned result variant by a data block $ROTSPEED (see page 3-1066 ff.) with one value.
   If, however, the solution procedure performs a loop over rotational speeds (e.g. MODAL
   ROTATING (see page 2-231 ff.)), then the actual rotational speed is used instead.

V 19.00.287                PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)              4-485
neral Description:
  The element provides three different modes:

     • Discrete force generator with six natural forces in linear or nonlinear time his-
       tory analysis.
     • Frequency and/or rotational speed dependent stiffness and viscous as well as
       structural damping, possibly unsymmetric, for other dynamic analyses.
     • Symmetric stiffness for linear static and real eigenvalue analysis.

  For time history analysis, three nonlinear natural forces acting in the direction of
  element system axis and three nonlinear natural moments acting around them are
  given by
                                          
                   FN,x            fx (xi )
                 F             f (x ) 
                   N,y         y i 
                                          
                 FN,z          fz (xi ) 
        FN =             =                 , i = 1, n   with     1 ≤ n ≤ 15
                 MN,ϕx         fϕx (xi ) 
                                          
                 MN,ϕy         fϕy (xi ) 
                  MN,ϕz            fϕz (xi )

  where up to 15 element nodal point displacements, corresponding velocities or
  node-independent data may be used as independent variables. Rotated node bases
  are taken into account, i.e. displacements and velocities used as independent vari-
  ables refer to local node bases.
  For frequency response analysis, the natural forces may be frequency dependent,
  i.e. they are given by

              F N = kN (f, Ωref ) ̺N + dN (f, Ωref ) ̺˙ N + hN (f, Ωref ) ̺˙ N

  with the structural damping contribution
                                         
          hN (f, Ωref ) = hN,ij (f, Ωref ) , hN,ij (f, Ωref ) = gij (f ) kN,ij (f, Ωref )

  where f is the excitation frequency and Ωref a fixed rotational speed.
  For analyses with a loop over rotational speed, the natural forces depending on
  speed are calculated for the actual speed value.
  For other dynamic analyses, including time history analyses where nonlinear force
  functions are missing, frequency and/or speed dependent matrices are evaluated
  for fixed reference values. If necessary (e.g. in time domain), structural damping is
  replaced by equivalent viscous damping.
  Optionally with rigid lever arms from nodal points to elastic center. If the offset is not
  defined, the elastic center is always at the first element node.
  A positive element force Fx′ acts at the first element node P1 in positive x′ -direction,

 96                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                      V 19.00.287

      ....0   Current controller omitted, replaced by internal connection.
      ....1   Current controller included.

  3. According to the selection of controller functions, the input values for a cascade controller
     must fulfill the following conditions:

        • If the position controller is included, its proportional factor KP d must be greater than
          zero.
        • The velocity controller must be always included, and its proportional factor KP v must
          be greater than zero.
        • If the integral response part of the velocity controller is included, the reset time TN v
          must be greater than zero.
        • If the current controller is omitted, it is replaced by an internal connection without
          any influence.
        • If the current controller is included, its equivalent time constant TE must be greater
          than zero.
        • Mass m used for normalization must be greater than zero.
        • If nominal velocity is requested, the proportional factor of velocity feedforward Kvv
          must be greater than zero, if field CSCADD is specified, else Kvv is set to 1.0.
        • A proportional factor for velocity feedforward Kvv > 0 is possible only if nominal
          velocity is requested.
        • First order delay of nominal displacement is only possible if position controller is
          included and nominal displacement is requested.
        • If specified, the time constant TSd for first order delay of nominal displacement must
          be greater or equal zero where zero means no delay.
        • If specified, the time constant Tdif f for first order delay of actual velocity must be
          greater or equal zero where zero means no delay.
        • For a low pass filter, the eigenfrequency f0 and the damping ratio D or DB resp.
          must be greater than zero.
        • For a band stop filter, the center frequency f0 and the pass bandwidth DB must be
          greater than zero whereas the stop bandwidth BZ must be greater or equal zero.

  4. There are different filters available in the cascade controller, which may be selected by
     the corresponding filter type selection switch f ltreq:




V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           4-497
         • Two low pass (PT2 ) or band stop (notch) filters for the nominal velocity, input values
           given in fields VNFILTER.
         • Two low pass (PT2 ) or band stop (notch) filters for the nominal current, input values
           given in fields CNFILTER.

  For a low pass filter the eigenfrequency f0 and the damping ratio D are requested whereas
  for a band stop filter the center frequency f0 , the pass bandwith B and the stop bandwidth
  BZ (bandwith of the numerator term) are expected.

neral Description:
  The element is intended to represent a linearized formulation of any controller in
  state space. To this end, a quadratic stiffness matrix as well as a quadratic damping
  matrices are defined by calling a user supplied function, i.e. a FORTRAN subrou-
  tine. The expected matrices of dimension (30,30) refer to the following vector of
  local element degrees of freedom

       ̺′ = { u′1 z1 z2 z3 u′2 z4 z5 z6 u′′3 z7 z8 z9 · · ·
              u′′4 z10 z11 z12 u′′′
                                5   z13 z14 z15 u′′′
                                                 6   z16 z17 z18 · · ·
              u0 z19 z20 v0 z21 z22 }

  It is intended that the element force is acting on the element x′ -axis between no-
  des P1 and P2 . The nominal displacement or velocity values u0 or u̇0 resp may
  be given (e.g.prescribed) at degree of freedom 11 of nodes P7 or P8 . The actual
  displacement or velocity values may be extracted e.g. by

                                       u = u′′4 − u′′3

  where u′′3 and u′′4 are the displacements at nodes P3 and P4 in x′′ -direction, and

                                      u̇ = u̇′′′   ′′′
                                             6 − u̇5

  where u̇′′′
           5 and u̇6 are the velocities at nodes P5 and P6 in x -direction.
                   ′′′                                         ′′′

  The internal degrees of freedom z1 to z22 may be used to represent the internal
  state variables of the controller. To avoid redundant degrees of freedom, the stan-
  dard symmetric stiffness matrix is generated automatically which is zero-filled but
  with 1.0 on the diagonal for each internal degree of freedom zi . So, as long as nom-
  inal values u0 and v0 are prescribed or coupled to other degrees of freedom, the
  non-standard degrees of freedom do not introduce any redundant degree of free-
  dom.
