neral Description:
  If the fields FUNCTION and HYSTFUN are given, the following applies: Nonlin-
  ear force acting in the direction of the three element axis. The element forces are
  defined by
                      Fx′ = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
                        Fy′ = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
                        Fz ′ = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
  The evolution of the three hysteresis parameters z1 , z2 and z3 is given by

                        R1 = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )

                        R2 = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
                        R3 = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
  Both element forces and displacements are given in the local coordinate system. A
  positive element force Fx′ acts at the first element node P1 in positive x′ -direction,
  and at the second element node P2 in negative x′ -direction. The third element node
  is used to define the local y ′ and z ′ directions. Alternatively the local coordinate
  system may be defined with a reference system.
  If the field ELAPLAST is given, a one-dimensional elasto-plastic material behaviour
  is modeled with the Bouc-Wen hysteresis model. The force in x′ direction is given
  by
                                Fx′ = k2 u′ + (k1 − k2 )z1
  and the forces Fy′ and Fz ′ direction are zero. The residual force is given by

neral Description:
  Discrete equilibrium model with three translational stiffnesses in direction of element
  axes. No stiffness with respect to rotations.
  The element is intended to overcome static rigid body modes that will be supported
  by later contact forces. I.e. the CA2ZERF3 stiffnesses help to avoid singularities
  during the decomposition of the stiffness matrix, but is not a support by itself – if the
  corresponding motion is not supported by adequate contact forces the unsupported
  rigid body mode will still result in an infinite movement ! For more details on the
  theory we refer to section 4.1.10 of [um550].



esses:
  No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

ess Resultants:
ethod:                    Direct evaluation of element forces (force resulting from constant
                          stiffnesses kii plus correction force RCA resulting from contact
                          analysis) at nodes, referring to local element system.
ored in book RSFR.DISP: (Nx′ , Ny′ , Nz ′ ) at both element nodes
inted stress resultants: (Nx′ , Ny′ , Nz ′ ) at both element nodes


ment Loads:
  No distributed loads available.

The plot elements are pure dummy elements which do not contribute in any way to the system
matrices. They are intended to be used as display or plot device e.g. for

   • Display of overall displacements of a fine mesh using a connected simplified mesh of plot
     elements

   • Visualization of ’invisible’ mesh properties like orientation of local systems etc.

There are no geometrical data for 2d-plot elements. Furthermore, plot elements do not refer to
any material property, therefore no material has to be assigned.

CONAL2          2 Noded Straight Edge Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-554

Line convection elements are used to include convective heat transfer at the edges of mem-
branes and shells (edge convection) or along rods and beams (line convection) in thermal
analysis. In addition, the heat capacity of the convective film may be taken into account.
Line convection elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored in any other kind
of analysis.


If the heat capacity of the convective film should be taken into account, a homogeneous
isotropic material has to be defined with TYPE = ISO (default) and material property type GEN-
ERAL. All applicable material input options for line convection elements are summarized in the
following table:




                                                                                                   Convection
               Available Material Input Options for Line Convection Elements

                                           Degree of Anisotropy
    Property
    Type            ISO        TRANS        ORTHO     MONOCLINIC     TRICLINIC     ANISO


    Scalar properties: HEATCAP

    GENERAL          x           (x)          (x)          (x)          (x)          (x)

         Input options, which are possible but obviously useless, are marked with (x).

General Description:
        First order edge convection element with convective heat flow only normal to ele-
        ment surface, intended to be placed on the edges of first order membrane and shell
        elements.
        The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient are possible:
                         Dependencies                 Formula
                         - no dependency -            α = α0
                         Temperature                  α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
                         Temperature, time            α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
                         Temperature, time, space     α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )
        where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
        the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
        Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The surrounding
        temperature must be defined as element load.
        Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
        If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
        be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
        COMPTEMP.

General Description:
        First order line convection element with convective heat flow only normal to element
        axis, intended to be placed on first order rods and beams. Optional rigid lever arms.
        The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient are possible:

                         Dependencies                 Formula
                         - no dependency -            α = α0
                         Temperature                  α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
                         Temperature, time            α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
                         Temperature, time, space     α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )

        where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
        the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
        Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The surrounding
        temperature must be defined as element load.
        Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
        If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
        be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
        COMPTEMP.

CONS9          9 Noded Quadrilateral Shell Surface Convection and Radiation Element . 4-622

Surface convection and radiation elements are used to include radiation and convective heat
transfer at the surfaces of membranes, shells and solids in thermal analysis. Especially for shell
elements, shell surface convection and radiation elements are available which take into account




                                                                                                     Convection
the temperature difference between upper and lower surface of the element. In addition, the




                                                                                                      Elements
heat capacity of the convective film may be taken into account.
Surface convection and radiation elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored
in any other kind of analysis.

  First order surface convection and radiation element with linear temperature field,
  convective heat flow normal to element surface and radiation, intended to be placed
  on triangular surfaces of first order membrane and solid elements.
  The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient are possible:

                 Dependencies                  Formula
                 - no dependency -             α = α0
                 Temperature                   α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
                 Temperature, time             α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
                 Temperature, time, space      α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )

  where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
  the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
  Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The surrounding
  temperature must be defined as element load.
  Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
  If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
  be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
  COMPTEMP.
  The surrounding temperature for radiation may be defined as element load.

2. Repetition = 3 means that data are expected for all element nodes. Input may be done
   using one data list with corresponding field name for each element node where the first
   data list is assigned to the first element node etc., or adding the data lists for all further
   nodes at the end of the data list for the first node, forming one extended data list.


3. Upper and lower surface are determined by the element normal of the underlying shell
   element, not by the orientation of the shell surface convection element.

   zero, and surrounding temperatures may not be input for corresponding elements.

   or omitted.

General Description:
     First order surface convection and radiation element with linear temperature field,
     convective heat flows normal to element surface and radiation, separated for upper
     and lower surface. Intended to be placed on triangular surfaces of first order shell
     elements, taking into account the temperature difference between upper and lower
     surface of shell. Optional rigid lever arms.
     The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient for upper and lower
     surface are possible:

                    Dependencies                  Formula
                    - no dependency -             α = α0
                    Temperature                   α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
                    Temperature, time             α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
                    Temperature, time, space      α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )

     where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
     the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
     Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The temperature
     at the upper surface is given by




                                                                                                      Convection
                                                                                                       Elements
                                      Tupper,i = Ti + 0.5∆T i

     and at the lower surface by

                                      Tlower,i = Ti − 0.5∆T i

     The surrounding temperatures must be defined as element loads.
     Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
     If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
     be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
     COMPTEMP.
     The surrounding temperatures for radiation may be defined as element loads.

V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           4-619
neral Description:
  Second order isoparametric surface convection and radiation element with incom-
  plete biquadratic temperature field, convective heat flow normal to element surface
  and radiation , separated for upper and lower surface. Intended to be placed on
  quadrilateral surfaces of second order shell elements, taking into account the tem-
  perature difference between upper and lower surface of shell. Optional rigid lever
  arms.
  The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient for upper and lower
  surface are possible:

                 Dependencies                  Formula
                 - no dependency -             α = α0
                 Temperature                   α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
                 Temperature, time             α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
                 Temperature, time, space      α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )

  where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
  the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
  Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The temperature
  at the upper surface is given by

                                   Tupper,i = Ti + 0.5∆T i

  and at the lower surface by

                                   Tlower,i = Ti − 0.5∆T i

  The surrounding temperatures must be defined as element loads.
  Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
  If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
  be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
  COMPTEMP.
  The surrounding temperatures for radiation may be defined as element loads.

The fluid elements can be classified with respect to their geometry or the order of their shape
functions. In terms of geometry there are four types of elements:

   • The Brick elements FLHEX8, FLHEX20 and FLHEX27

   • The Wedge elements FLPENT6, FLPENT15 and FLPENT18.




                                                                                                     Elements
   • The Tetrahedron elements FLTET4, and FLTET10.




                                                                                                       Fluid
   • The Pyramid element FLPYR5

Although tetrahedron elements are sufficient to mesh any geometry, better results are obtained
when brick elements are used whenever possible, restricting the use of wedges, tetrahedrons
and pyramids to those parts of the mesh where they cannot be avoided.

In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified:

   • Elements with linear shape functions: FLHEX8, FLPENT6, FLTET4 and FLPYR5.

   • Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: FLHEX20 and FLPENT15.

   • Elements with quadratic shape functions: FLHEX27, FLPENT18 and FLTET10.




V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          4-627

FSINTA3        3 Noded Triangular Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-661

FSINTA4        4 Noded Quadrilateral Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-664

FSINTA6        6 Noded Triangular Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-667

FSINTA8        8 Noded Quadrilateral Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-670

FSINTA9        9 Noded Quadrilateral Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-673




The fluid structure interface elements are used to couple solid and fluid domains for coupled
analysis. In addition, they may be used to include boundary absorption in the fluid domain.

Each node carries three displacement degrees of freedom and one pressure degree of free-
dom. For a pure fluid analysis without structure the displacement degrees of freedom are
ignored, for a pure structural analysis the interface elements are ignored at all.

If two fluid regions are separated by a thin wall idealized by shell elements (doubly wetted
surface), the problem arises that for one shell node with one set of displacement degrees of
freedom there are two different pressure values, one for each fluid region. Therefore for each
fluid region one interface element is necessary, the first one with the same nodal points as the
corresponding shell element, and the second one with different nodes at the same position in
space and the displacement degrees of freedom joined by multipoint constraints.

The orientation of interface elements must be such that the element normal points from the
fluid to the solid.
The local element system for triangular elements is defined as follows:




                                                                                                   Elements
  1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.




                                                                                                     Fluid
  2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.

  3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.

For quadrilateral elements the local element system is defined in the following way:

  1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
     plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.

  2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
     pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
     rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
     corner node).



V 19.00.287                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       4-659
4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x -and y -axis, i.e. it is normal to
   the reference surface.

FLWAVEA3       3 Noded Triangular Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-679

FLWAVEA4       4 Noded Quadrilateral Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-682

FLWAVEA6       6 Noded Triangular Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-685

FLWAVEA8       8 Noded Quadrilateral Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-688

FLWAVEA9       9 Noded Quadrilateral Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-691




The surface wave elements are used to idealize free surfaces of the fluid where the pressure
at the surface is balanced by the weight of surface waves.

Surface wave elements carry one pressure degree of freedom.

Surface wave elements are always placed on the boundary of the fluid perpendicular to the
direction of gravity acceleration. The orientation of the element normal is meaningless. The
gravity acceleration value itself must be inputted by parameter GFLWAVE within the system
variant, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.

The local element system for triangular elements is defined as follows:

  1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.

  2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.

  3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.




                                                                                                     Elements
For quadrilateral elements the local element system is defined in the following way:




                                                                                                       Fluid
  1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
     plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.

  2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
     pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
     rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
     corner node).

  3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
     the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
     rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.

  4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
     the reference surface.

INFFLA2        2 Noded Straight Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-701

INFFLA3        3 Noded Curved Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-704

INF2QAM4       4 Noded Straight Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-707

INF2QAM8       8 Noded Curved Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-710

INF2QAM9       9 Noded Curved Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-713



The Infinite Elements are special elements to model the unbounded domain. Yet they are only
available for electromagnetic and acoustic/fluid problems. Pay attention to the following features
(see also theoretical manual) :

   • The first part of the name ’INF’ indicates the element as an INFINITE element, the second
     part ’FLA2’ names the element, which is used as the modeling element (here a FLA2
     element).
   • The geometry of the Infinite Elements tends to infinity and is described with singular
     functions.
   • The geometry of the Infinite Elements will be changed through the program and depends
     on the position of the pole.
   • The nodes at infinity are not modeled since they are thought to be suppressed (”automatic
     Dirichlet boundary condition”), but they have influence on the interpolation–functions.
   • The degrees of freedom (e. g. potential) are interpolated with the standard functions, e.
     g. INFFLA2 with the QUAM4 interpolation–functions without the ones, which belong to
     the nodes lying at infinity.
   • The material is always isotropic and homogeneous. No local element system is neces-
     sary.
   • The geometrical datas are always valid for all nodes.
   • Rotated basis is not allowed.
   • The user has to choose an expansion pole which is always opposite to the infinity side of
     the element.
   • All Infinite Elements can carry only nodal point loads ($CONLOAD).
   • Because the infinite elements are modeled with iso–parametric elements, higher order
     infinite elements must have their greatest geometrical extension after the modeling in
                                                                                                     2D-Infinite


     infinite direction, otherwise they can not be recognized as an infinite element in the right
                                                                                                     Elements


     manner.

The Infinite Elements are special elements to model the unbounded domain. Yet they are only
available for electromagnetic and fluid structure problems. Pay attention to the special features
(see also theoretical manual) explained on page 4-699.

Infinite elements have isotropic homogeneous fluid material to emphasize their property of
modelling the unbounded domain, and the appropriate material input type is GENERAL. All
applicable material input options for infinite elements are summarized in the following table:

The RBC (radiation boundary condition) elements are special elements to construct an artificial
boundary and to impose conditions on this surface to simulate an infinite domain. The Bayliss–
Turkel RBC elements are based on the mode annihilating approximation technique. The idea
is to absorb the modes of the far field expansion of outgoing propagating solution to the (wave)
equation (the Sommerfeld condition annihilates the first mode of plane waves). For further
details of the theory see (†† ) (‡‡ ). The RBC elements of first order annihilate the first mode
of the far field expansion, the elements of second order the first two modes. In general the
elements of second order are more accurate than those of first order.

The theory of Bayliss–Turkel in three dimensions is based on a far field solution in a spherical
coordinate system. Thus the RBC elements must be placed onto the surface of a Finite Element
mesh which is of spherical shape only. With the RBC elements the influence of the unbounded
domain is taken into account and the problem is well posed too. So no additional boundary
conditions for the unbounded domain are necessary.



††
   A. Bayliss, E. Turkel : Radiation boundary conditions for wave–like equations, Commun. Pure Appl. Math., Vol.
   23, S. 707–725, 1980
‡‡
   A. Bayliss, M. Gunzberger, E. Turkel : Boundary conditions for the numerical solution of elliptic equations in
   exterior regions, SIAM J. Appl. Math., Vol. 42, S. 430–451, 1982




V 19.00.287                       PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                   4-765
uce reflections from the artificial boundary sufficient. Of course this is dependent on the
cified problem and should not be seen as a constant.

The RBC (radiation boundary condition) elements are special elements to construct an ar-
tificial boundary and to impose conditions on this surface to simulate an infinite domain. The
Engquist–Majda RBC elements are based on the one way wave equation approximation tech-
nique. The idea is to permit on an outer boundary only wave motions which are travelling
outward from the range of interest. For further details of the theory see (* ) († ). The RBC ele-
ments of first order approximate the pseudo–differential equation with a Taylor approximation
of first order, the elements of second order use a Taylor approximation of second order. In gen-
eral the elements of second order are more accurate than those of first order. On a rectangular
boundary, the elements of first order lead to the Sommerfeld condition for plane waves.
The theory of Engquist–Majda used here is based on plane waves. Thus the RBC elements
must be placed onto the surface of a Finite Element mesh which is of rectangular shape only.
With the RBC elements the influence of the unbounded domain is taken into account and the
problem is well posed too. So no additional boundary conditions for the unbounded domain are
necessary.



* B. Engquist, A. Majda :   Absorbing boundary conditions for the numerical simulation of waves, Math. Comput.,
  Vol. 31, S. 629–651, 1977
†
  B. Engquist, A. Majda : Radiation boundary conditions for acoustic and elastic wave calculations, Commun. Pure
  Appl. Math., Vol. 32, S. 312–358, 1979

ections from the artificial boundary sufficient. Of course this is dependent on the specified
blem and should not be seen as a constant.

RINGX         Single-node axisymmetric Flange Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-851




                                                                                                 axisymmetri
                                                                                                  Flanges
The axisymmetric flange elements are displacement models that are fully compatible with the
axisymmetric membrane elements QUAX and TRIAX. Their main application is thus the mod-
elling of enforcements (flanges, stringers, prestressing cables) in axisymmetric problems.

Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the axisym-
metric flange elements may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
explicitly.

All matrices and forces are with respect to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).

Axisymmetric flange elements may have, according to their nature, only homogeneous isotropic
material, therefore a homogeneous material has to be defined with TYPE = ISO (default). The
appropriate material property type is GENERAL. All applicable material input options for ax-
isymmetric flange elements are summarized in the following table:




V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                        4-849
Scalar properties: DAMPING, DENSITY, HEATCAP

GENERAL         x           (x)          (x)          (x)          (x)          (x)



Elastic properties: ELASTIC

GENERAL         x



Nonlinear elastic properties: NLELASTIC

GENERAL         x



Inelastic properties: PLASTIC, YIELD, CREEP, VPLASTIC

GENERAL         x



Hardening type: HARDENING

GENERAL         x



Electromagnetic properties: DIELECTRIC, ELCONDUCT, PERMEABILITY

GENERAL         x



Remaining properties: THERMEXP

GENERAL         x

     Input options, which are possible but obviously useless, are marked with (x).

FLAX3          3 Noded Axisymmetric Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-865



The axisymmetric membrane elements are displacement models that are fully compatible with
the axisymmetric solid elements QUAX and TRIAX. They can carry only axisymmetric loads.

The local element system for axisymmetric membrane elements is defined as follows:

  1. The r ′ -axis direction is determined through the tangential direction of the cross-section
     geometry.
                                                                       ′
  2. The z ′ -axis is the cross product from the r ′ -axis with the φ axis.
           ′
  3. The φ axis is identical with the global φ axis.




                              φ
                                                    E2

                          z                        φ’        r’
                                             E1
                                                                  z’
                                                     P1 = C 1

                                       r



   Definition of local element systems, element corner nodes Ci and element edges Ei for
                              axisymmetric membrane elements

For curved elements, the local element system thus varies from point to point, dependent on
the element geometry.

All matrices and forces are with respect to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).

The appropriate material property type is GENERAL. Yet, only isotropic material property is
available. All applicable material input options for axisymmetric membrane elements are sum-

QUABX2K        Axisymmetric Harmonic Thin Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-911




                                                                                                           axisymmetri
                                                                                                            Shells
The geometry of axisymmetric elements is fully described by its intersection with the global
r, z-plane where the z-axis is the axis of symmetry (rotational axis for the body of revolution).
All matrices and forces refer to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).

The local coordinate system (m′ t′ n′ ) within axisymmetric shell elements is defined as follows:


  1. The m′ -axis is tangential to the local meridian and points from the edge where the first
     element point is located to the second one.

  2. The t′ -axis is tangential to the circumferential direction and parallel to the global φ-direction.

  3. The n′ -axis is normal to the shell surface. (m′ t′ n′ ) form a right-hand system.

  4. The n′ -axis defines upper and lower surfaces of the shell, since it points from the lower to
     the upper one.

All matrices and forces are with respect to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).

If necessary, local element systems for spring elements are defined using two points R1 and
R2 located in the r, z-plane as follows:

  1. The rR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .

  2. The zR -axis together with the rR -axis form a plane system in the r, z-plane.

  3. The local element system (r ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (rR , zR ) with its origin
     at the first element node.

CONALAX        Single Node Axisymmetric Edge Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-934




                                                                                                    Convection
                                                                                                   axisymmetri
CONLAX         Single Node Axisymmetric Line Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-939

Axisymmetric line convection elements are used to include convective heat transfer at the
edges of axisymmetric membrane (edge convection) or along axisymmetric flange (line con-
vection) in thermal analysis. In addition, the heat capacity of the convective film may be taken
into account.
Axisymmetric line convection elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored in
any other kind of analysis.


All matrices and forces are with respect to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).

If the heat capacity of the convective film should be taken into account, a homogeneous
isotropic material has to be defined with TYPE = ISO (default) and material property type GEN-
ERAL. All applicable material input options for axisymmetric line convection elements are sum-
marized in the following table:



     Available Material Input Options for Axisymmetric Line Convection Elements

         Input options, which are possible but obviously useless, are marked with (x).

                         Dependencies                 Formula
                         - no dependency -            α = α0
                         Temperature                  α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )

FSINTSX3       3 Noded Curved Axisymmetric Harmonic Fluid Structure Interface Element4-963




                                                                                                           axisymmetri
                                                                                                             Fluids
The axisymmetric fluid structure interface elements are used to couple axisymmetric solid and
fluid domains for coupled analysis. In addition, they may be used to include boundary absorp-
tion in the fluid domain.

Fluid structure interface elements carry displacement degrees of freedom as well as pressure
degree of freedom. For a pure fluid analysis without structure the displacement degrees of
freedom are ignored, for a pure structural analysis the interface elements are ignored at all.

The geometry of axisymmetric elements is fully described by its intersection with the global
r, z-plane where the z-axis is the axis of symmetry (rotational axis for the body of revolution).
All matrices and forces refer to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).

The orientation of axisymmetric interface elements must be such that the element normal points
from the fluid to the solid. The local element system for axisymmetric interface elements is
defined as follows:

  1. The m′ -axis is tangential to the local meridian and points from the edge where the first
     element point is located to the second one.

  2. The t′ -axis is tangential to the circumferential direction and parallel to the global φ-direction.

  3. The n′ -axis is normal to the element surface. (m′ t′ n′ ) form a right-hand system.

FLWAVEX3       3 Noded Curved Axisymmetric Harmonic Surface Wave Element . . . . . 4-968




                                                                                                    axisymmetri
                                                                                                      Fluids
The axisymmetric surface wave elements are used to idealize free surfaces of the axisymmetric
fluid where the pressure at the surface is balanced by the weight of surface waves.

Axisymmetric surface wave elements carry one pressure degree of freedom.

Axisymmetric surface wave elements are always placed on the boundary of the fluid perpen-
dicular to the direction of gravity acceleration. The orientation of the element normal is mean-
ingless. The gravity acceleration value itself must be inputted by parameter GFLWAVE within
the system variant, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.

The geometry of axisymmetric elements is fully described by its intersection with the global
r, z-plane where the z-axis is the axis of symmetry (rotational axis for the body of revolution).
All matrices and forces refer to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).
Axisymmetric surface wave elements have isotropic fluid material, and only fluid density is used.
All applicable material input options for axisymmetric surface wave elements are summarized
in the following table:

5.1    General

For design optimization purpose, all parts of the structure which may be modified are assigned
to so-called Design Elements. They are used to define possible modifications for elements
and nodes belonging to the design element, and are intended for simple and clear description
of interpolation within the design element (interpolation is not yet provided in current version).
Design elements are used according to following rules:




                                                                                                     Elements
                                                                                                      Design
   • Each design element contains one or more finite elements by unique assignment. To-
     gether with the elements, all nodal points connected to those elements are associated to
     the design element.

   • Each design element may have any number of design variables, at least one. All possible
     modifications within the design element are defined dependent on those design variables.

   • Each design element has a fixed number of design nodes, a defined geometry and cor-
     responding interpolation functions. Design nodes are needed for interpolation within the
     design element and shape optimization only, and may be omitted elsewhere.

   • Each design element has a fixed type of Geometrical Data Record. For optimal sizing
     problems only elements with matching Geometrical Data Record may be assigned.

   • For optimal sizing problems property dependencies may be defined for the whole design
     element. They are valid for all corresponding finite elements, independent on its location
     within the design element. Design nodes are not used and may be omitted.

   • For interpolation of properties within the design element, property dependencies are de-
     fined at the design nodes of the design element; then the property is interpolated accord-
     ing to the interpolation function of the design element and the location of the element
     within the design element. For that case, the design nodes of the design element must
     be inputted.
     Interpolation of properties is not yet available in current version.

   • For shape optimization the coordinates of the design nodes are made dependent on the
     design variables, and the coordinates of all nodal points associated to the corresponding
     design element are modified according to the design element interpolation functions.

 mechanical analysis:

DISPlacement: Nodal point displacements

VELOcity: Nodal point velocities

REACtion DOFTYPE=DISP: Nodal point reaction forces

REACD DOFTYPE=DISP: Nodal point reaction forces on dependent DOFs

RESIdual DOFTYPE=DISP: Nodal point residual forces

RIGID MODES DOFTYPE=DISP: Nodal point rigid body modes

 thermal analysis:

TEMPerature: Nodal point temperatures

REACtion DOFTYPE=TEMP: Nodal point reacting heat flux

REACD DOFTYPE=TEMP: Nodal point reacting heat flux on dependent DOFs

RESIdual DOFTYPE=TEMP: Nodal point residual heat flux

RIGID MODES DOFTYPE=TEMP: Nodal point zero temperature modes

 fluid analysis:

PRESsure: Nodal point pressures

REACtion DOFTYPE=PRES: Nodal point reac

REACD DOFTYPE=PRES: Nodal point reac on dependent DOFs

RESIdual DOFTYPE=PRES: Nodal point residual

RIGID MODES DOFTYPE=PRES: Nodal point constant pressure modes

 electromagnetical analysis:

MPOTEntial: Nodal point magnetic potentials

EPOTEntial: Nodal point electric potentials

REACtion DOFTYPE=POTE: Nodal point reac

REACD DOFTYPE=POTE: Nodal point reac on dependent DOFs

     trapolation due to OUTTOL may lead to differences between true and calculated position.

anning results (verification of model):

me load-independent* contact results are available for model verification:

TIAL CONTACT DEFinition
   Initial contact definitions with 3-6 scalar values per node: the definition counter, the defi-
   nition type, the family type of the involved guiding CA-DOFs and, for surface contact, an
   isolation-indicator, the patch kink angles before smoothing and an indicator for doubled
   contact pairs
TIAL CONTACT GEOmetry
   It is the nadir vector (geometrical gap vector from node to surface nadir) as a result of the
   neighborhood search
TIAL CONTACT SYStem
   It contains 3 normalized vectors building the axes of the contact system, i.e. the contact
   normal (Nx ) and frictional y/z (Fy /Fz ) direction respectively

   It is a single scalar value for each contact node in each load pattern indicating the geo-
   metrical situation prior to simulation, i.e. basically the sign of the input gap width given by
   $CONTACT LOAD (see page 3-567 ff.)

Standard results:

After the contact analysis the contact reaction forces RC the contact pressure pC the final
gap width δ, the relative displacements ∆r, the relative velocities ∆v, and the contact residuals
ε are directly available. Each of the six results is split into a normal and tangential vector (or
scalar) according to the local contact system. The vector values are given with respect to the
global coordinate system. In case of slipping also the scalar frictional energy density Φslip is
available as a result.

CONTACT STATUS
    Contact status (decimal coded)
CONTACT FORCE
    Normal RCnorm (x,y,z) and frictional RCf ric (x,y,z) force
CONTACT PRESsure
    Scalar contact pressure and shear vector
CONTACT PRESsure VECtor




                                                                                                     Results
    Contact pressure vector and shear vector
GAP [WIDTH]
    Final gap δnorm (signed scalar value): open gap if > 0, penetration if < 0
GAP VECtor
    Final gap vector in normal δ norm (x,y,z) and tangential δ tang (x,y,z) direction
GAP DISPlacement
    Relative gap displacement in normal ∆r norm (x,y,z) and tangential ∆r tang (x,y,z) direction
GAP VELOcity
    Relative gap velocity in normal ∆v norm (x,y,z) and tangential ∆v tang (x,y,z) direction
CONTACT INTERference
    Contact interference (linear dependent CA-DOFs)
CONTACT RESIdual
    Residuum in gap displacements in normal εnorm (x,y,z) and tangential εtang (x,y,z) direc-
    tion
CONTACT FORCE RESIdual
    Residuum in contact forces for contact zero-force (CA0) and gaskets (GSK) DOFs
FRICTION ENergy
    Dissipative frictional energy
FRICTION ENergy DENsity
    Dissipative frictional energy density
FRICTION RATIO
    Frictional coefficients, saturation and slip-force declination angles
CONTACT DEFinition
    Is linked to INITIAL CONTACT DEFinition for calculations without geometrical update

The contact geometry update contains the final displacements before the last contact geometry
update for the corresponding load pattern or time step. This displacement before the last update
step is used as the reference geometry for the last contact iteration. Thus the contact geometry
update can be used to check the influence of the last contact geometry update step.
It is only available for the setting CAGEOUP=ON. If the contact geometry update steps did not
reach the tolerance criterion CAGEOUPTOL, the result is exported in any case, otherwise only
if it is addressed by the user.

ntact interference is a nodal point vector with a vector length > 0 for linear dependent CA-
Fs, i.e. singularities in the active flexibility matrix (if any). The vector direction corresponds
he CA-DOF in question. The length of the vector shows the ’degree’ of linear dependency:

.0: No singularities (or no active contact).
.0: Node is part in some duplicated CA-Definition or over-constrained by MPCs and/or
    boundary conditions.

.0: Number of iteration steps where the interference is active.
.x: Partial/interpolated dependency.

e result is not generated if all active CA-DOFs are linearly independent.

mal pressure (scalar or vector) and frictional shear vector are area-related nodal point re-

a) ITEM CONTACT PRESsure
   Maximum normal pressure (as scalar) and shear vector with maximum norm at each node
   (e.g. appears as ’Contact Pressure’ and ’Contact Shear’ respectively in Medina post-
   processor).
   This is a default export item, i.e. exported with a simple GO command already.
   Compared to the next item this result type has the following advantages/disadvantages:
     ⊕ Shows critical maximum for nodes with several contacts (e.g. edges or sandwich
       contacts).
     ⊕ Sign of normal pressure indicates pressure/tension (e.g. for fixed contacts).
     ⊕ Enables simultaneous view of contact pressure and shear as color and vector in a
       single plot.
                                                                          p

                                                                                     c2
     ⊖ No vector information for normal direction (user must know about normal direction

b) ITEM CONTACT PRESsure VECtor
   Normal pressure vector (sum) and average shear vector (sum) at each node (e.g. ’Contact
   PressVec’ and ’Contact ShearVec’ in Medina). This item is only exported if explicitly re-
   quested.
   Compared to the previous item this result type has the following advantages/disadvantages:
     ⊕ Normal direction as vector information.
     ⊕ Vector sum at edges and for multi-contact nodes.

          shells).

Theory:
In contrast to the calculation of stresses the calculation of contact pressure is not a derivative of
the element displacements, but is done by a direct mapping of the discrete contact forces taking
into account the areas and shape-functions of the neighboring element faces. This approach
has several advantages:
    • Contact pressure is available for all element faces, i.e. even for elements which do not
      have any elasticity in normal direction (e.g. shell, membrane or plot elements).




V 19.00.287                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                6-33
 • Pressure values are calculated at the contact nodes directly (no gauss point extrapola-
   tion).

marks

1. The area-related contact pressure and shear result use as reference surface all element
   faces moistened by the corresponding contact definition. I.e. the reference surface is
   derived from the adjacent finite-element mesh and not taken from a surface definition
   used in the contact definition !
   This makes the reference surface independent of the contact definition type, so that this
   area-related results are available for simple nodal point contacts as well as for both sides
   of a surface-to-node or surface-to-surface contact !
   For line-like contacts the length of the moistened element edges are multiplied by the
   value of the UCI switch CALINEWIDTH (default 1.0) to get a reference area. For singular
   node-to-node contacts the value of UCI switch CAPOINTAREA is taken as a reference
   area (default 0.0).

2. For incompatible meshes an additional balancing between both sides of contact is ap-
   plied, taking into account the local mesh size. For equally sized meshes this means just
   an average determination, but for ample different meshes local details of the finer side
   are not smeared by a coarse partner mesh.

3. Contact forces as well as contact pressure often show very high gradients at the border
   of the contact region – especially at geometrical sharp edges (edge pressure). This is not
   a simulation or discretization error, but meets the correct progression also known from
   analytical press-fit solutions. Depending on the geometrical characterstics a very fine
   meshing of a sharp edge might even lead to singular effects with almost infinite stress
   values.†

4. The direct mapping algorithm used for the calculation of area-related contact results is
   suited for elements with linear, quadratic or incomplete quadratic shape functions. How-
   ever, mixed-case elements with a linear shape function in normal and a quadratic shape
   function in tangential direction (i.e. thick shell elements TRIMS6 and QUAMS8/9 or
   quadratic gasket elements GKPNT15/18 and GKHEX20/27) may show a slightly discon-
   tinuous pressure distribution from mid to corner nodes – similar to the non-smooth contact
   forces at quadratic shaped elements.

5. At the symmetry border of cyclic symmetric models only one half of the effective reference
   area can be derived from the contact adjacent element faces (the second half acts via the



  praxis edges of real parts mostly show small roundings or peak stress values at sharp edges are lowered by
icroscopic small areas of plastification wihtout affecting the part’s function. Hence, for the outer most series
  nodal points it is often acceptable to tolerate a STATIC contact pressure above the material’s limit of elasticity
 thout this demanding a more expensive NLMATERIAL calculation.




4                       PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                                        V 19.00.287
     the border of this symmetry also see only half the effective reference area, but as the
     very same nodes also get only half the contact forces this effect is compensated and the
     contact pressure at the border of symmetry is correct, too.

The contact residuals indicate the numerical error for all relative contact displacements, i.e. the




                                                                                                          Results
numerical error in the final gap width (δ norm , δ f ric ) as well as in the relative gap displacements
(∆r norm , ∆r f ric ).
Of course, this is an error estimation for the contact iteration only. The overall accuracy may be
worse, see the Pro-File Accuracy Limit, Load Check and overall residual forces RESI.
Equally, for a nonlinear load history $NLLOAD the contact residuals of each LPAT include the
sum of all previous load patterns (summarized residuals).

As surface contact allows the contact between incompatible meshes each node on a surface
may be influenced by several (partially inherited) status values:
      • The primary contact status value reflects the contact situation directly at the node’s loca-
        tion, e.g. contact of node with a patch of the opposing surface (i.e. the standard contact
        status at that node).†
      • A surface node may inherit an additional secondary contact status from the nearest nadir
        point of an ’opponent’ contact node.*      Optionally this secondary contact status may
        be shifted with -0.5 by setting the UCI switch CASURFST=SHIFT, see page 2-33. This
        setting helps to clearly distinguish between primary and secondary status values.
      • If a contact node is part of a surface-to-surface contact definition this node will show the
        maximum value of the primary and secondary status.
      • Moreover all orphan contact nodes, i.e. contact nodes for which no contact partner was
        found (see also isolation type) get a status value of 0.0. Nodes not belonging to any




                                                                                                                      Results
        contact definition will get no status value.

e data sets "Effective frictional coefficient" and "Saturation of sticking forces" allow to eval-
e how far a sticking contact area from the slipping state is. The data sets "Slip saturation
 cit" and "Slip force declination angle" lead the information about a quality of a frictional
 tact solution.

1. Effective frictional coefficient
                                                       |Rf ric |
                                            µef f =                                           (E6-1)
                                                      |Rnorm |
     Obviously, it must hold for sticking contact area µef f ≤ µ0 , for slipping contact area µef f =
     µ (see the picture F6-6).




 0                    PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                             V 19.00.287
              µ0               Sticking
                                                                   Slipping

              µ




 Figure F6-6: Changing of the effective frictional coefficient value along the contact surface




                                                                                                      Results
  2. Saturation of sticking forces
                                                     |Rf ric |
                                          Sat. =               100%                         (E6-2)
                                                   µ0 |Rnorm |
     Obviously, saturation of sticking forces must be no bigger than 100%.
  3. Slip saturation deficit
     The Coulomb friction law says |Rslip | = µ |Rnorm |. The quality of its fulfilment is shown by
     slip saturation deficit value.
                                                     |Rf ric |
                                      Sat. = 1 −                   100%                     (E6-3)
                                                    µ |Rnorm |
     Ideally, the value of the deficit must be zero.
  4. Slip force declination angle
     The Coulomb friction law prescribes the direction of the frictional force relative to slip
     displacement vector. The value of the slip force declination angle shows the declination
     of the frictional force from its direction calculated based on the slip displacement vector.
     For isotropic friction law the declination angle can be found as

                                             ∠(−Rslip , r slip )                            (E6-4)

     I.e. the frictional force must point in an opposite direction to the slip displacement vector.
     It does not hold for the orthotropic friction !
     Ideally, the value of the declination must be zero. Note that for the small force or displace-
     ment values (with values close to an accuracy limit), the directions can be only badly
     defined. In such cases for the very accurate solution, the declination values can be quite
     large.

Please note, that for a non-linear load history $NLLOAD (see page 3-838 ff.), respectively a
non-linear analysis, the initial gap width δ 0 always refers to the undeformed state. It does not
correspond to the value listed as ’Starting Gapwidth’ in the contact results table of a time step
in the result file. In cases where the initial gap width between time tn−1 and tn is constant the
’Starting Gapwidth’ for time step tn is simply identical to the final gap width of tn−1 . If the initial
gap width is changed in time, then the ’Starting Gapwidth’ for time step tn is obtained by:

                                δstart (tn ) = δ(tn−1 ) − δ0 (tn−1 ) + δ0 (tn )

Equally, for a nonlinear load history $NLLOAD the gap displacement ∆r gives the relative
movement with reference to the undeformed mesh – not with reference to the previous time
step !

     If a node is part of several contact definitions the final definition type is build by a dec-
     imal coding of all corresponding definition types. The definition types are collected in
     descending order with the decimal point after the first status value. E.g. if an edge node

    = 1 : Contact node whose contact definitions are based on local DOFs only (standard
          L).

          (L+D).

          CA-DOFs (L+D+E/P/S).

      = 1 : Surface partner, i.e. a surface node from a surface-to-node contact.

      = 7 : Isolated surface node (orphan patch), i.e. within the given tolerances, the neigh-
            borhood search found no contact partner for the node’s adjacent surface patches.*
      = 8 : Purely isolated node (orphan contact), i.e. within the given tolerances, the neigh-
            borhood search found no contact partner for the node on the opposing surface.

ote that this contact doublet indicator is not available if all contact pairs are unique, i.e. is only generated if there

he exact criterion is as follows: If a point NA from surface A establishes a contact with surface B and the distance
om the nadir of this contact to a patch point NB is less than 10∗TOLNOD then any contact pair arising from node
B with surface A will be ignored if the nadir of that contact would also lie in 10∗TOLNOD distance to node NA .

he exact criterion is as follows: If the corresponding contact point NA of a contact pair has only dependent
egrees of freedom and if there exists another contact point NB in the same contact definition nearly at the same
osition (tolerance CATOLDUPDEP) without any dependent degrees of freedoms (which is assumed to be the
uiding node) the contact pair at point NA will be ignored.

                                                                                                      Results
This load-independent* result is available for model verification directly after the model’s input
and consolidation (e.g. after task scanning with TASK STORE). The pressfit definition contains
2–3 scalar values for each pressfit node:

  1. The pressfit definition type may be used to verify that the proper kind of coupling definition
     was used:
     = 1 : Pure surface partner, i.e. an adjacent patch at the node participates in a pressfit
           surface, but the node itself is not a pressfit node (surface node from a $PRESSFIT
           surface-to-node coupling).
     = 2 : Standard pressfit node, i.e. the node itself is the base of a local coupling pair from
           a $PRESSFIT node-to-node or surface-to-node coupling.
     = 3 : Master guiding node (gid)

  2. With the pressfit dependency type one can verify which nodes where introduced as de-
     pendent or guiding nodes in MPCs internally generated by the $PRESSFIT def.:
     = 1 : Guiding nodes (usually 1st partner)
     = 2 : Dependent nodes (usually 2nd partner)

  3. The pressfit isolation type is provided in order to verify the neighborhood of pressfit
     couplings. Values > 1 indicate an orphan coupling situation (also see UCI switches
     PFDISTOL and PFOUTTOL on page 2-43 of this manual):



* In the post-processor the load-independent results may show up under load pattern zero.

crete meaning of scalar values:
alar 1 : Surface Definition Count
              0.0   : Node is not part of any surface definition.

alar 2 : Surface border type (decimal coded for n>1):

                      face definition.

 rder to have consistent patches, the model has to be partitioned due to certain rules. This is
formed internally within the SPR computation so that no manual action is needed. However,
me settings are available to influence the automatic SPR model partitioning.

 • No SPR patch nodes at MPC interfaces, i.e. MPC interfaces are treated like exterior
   boundaries regarding the SPR procedure. Hence, e.g. at an MPC ISURFACE between
   a HEXE8 and TET10 volume mesh, SPR stresses will be generated for both volume
   meshes separately. I.e. there will be no SPR patch with HEXE8 and TET10 elements.
 • Split model due to element families.
 • Material borders are also separators (except e.g. short fibre materials).

6.3.2 Absolute Error Indicator (AEI)

The Absolute Error Indicator (AEI) σAEI is a scalar measure of the discretization error in terms
of stress within one element. It is defined as

                                  σAEI = max kσ FE − σSPR k ,
                                          V

where V denotes the element volume, σFE is the standard element stress
                                                                     √ and σ SPR the SPR
stress. The stress difference is measured in the Frobenius norm kAk = A : A. Because the
AEI is based on the SPR stress the same restrictions apply regarding mesh partitioning and
boundaries.




V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                         6-199
 be reduced by a mesh refinement.

ample example LS19 on page 2-243 ff. of [um550] shows an application of SPR stresses
d the AEI.

The export process has a default result selection rule in order to avoid explicit selections for
many cases. The rule is as following:

  1. Primary results are always selected.

  2. Each secondary result which is generated explicitly is selected as far as the postprocessor
     is able to support the item. (Exceptions are documented in the corresponding output door
     sections.)

  3. Verification item if "DEFAULT SET MODEL = verification" is selected. Verification item
     should only be used for testing purpose in conjunction with TASK STORE.



Explicit result item selections

Using the EXPORT ITEM (see page 2-373 ff.) command, further selections may be done in
addition to the default selection. If only explicit selections are desired, the default selection
must be cleared previously.


7.1.1 Naming rule for Export Files




                                                                                                    Export
The naming convention for the postprocessing files is designed to be as common for the dif-
ferent postprocessors as possible. The specific naming rules are documented for each post-
processor separately. Of course, the names are machine dependent. Some restrictions are
documented for each postprocessor, too.

There are several parameters influencing the result file names:

  1. Project name

  2. Component (in case of substructuring)

  3. Situation (if several variants are used)

  4. Export mode (direct/combined)

  5. Exported result item (for several postprocessors)

  6. Task loop

                      Part of the name in case of several variants. If the standard name is
                      used, the name is build as S_<icount> instead of the complete name.

PERMAS. The generated output is written in PERMAS ( ref. chapter 3 ) input format. Therefore
this output may be used as model/result input for a subsequent PERMAS run or for other
postprocessing purposes.

For easy processing the output file is written in a fixed format.

The structure of file is as following:

 !#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 !#        Result file written by PERMAS Version xversxxx

 !# Conf.: xxxxxxxxxxxx Comp.: xxxxxxxxxxxx Sit.: xxxxxxxxxxxx

 & xxxlabelxxxx        =         1
 !#------------------------< Data item description >---------------------------

 !# LINES = 999999999

 !#----------------------------------------------------------------------------
          1 0.000000E+00 0.000000E+00 0.000000E+00

                 .               .             .

   • The HDF format has two primary objects

     Group     : is like a directory of a file system
     Dataset : is like a file of a file system

   • and Attributes to annotate data.

Each result item is stored in a HDF Group named according to the item name, e.g. ’ELEMENT
STRESS’ and may contain several HDF Datasets corresponding to e.g. LPATs or xy-curves.
All result items belong to a HDF Group named like the situation they belong to. This group is
the Situation Group. The situation belongs to a HDF Group according to the component name,
and if the model has a multilevel configuration, this component belongs to a HDF Group with
the configuration (top component) name.

 /.File Header
 /[configuration/]component/
 /[configuration/]component/situation/
 /[configuration/]component/situation/.Analysis
 /[configuration/]component/situation/.Model
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item/.ColDes




                                                                                                  Export to
                                                                                                  PERMAS
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item/.RowDes
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item/Column1
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item/Column2
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item/.Abscissae
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item/.Label
 /[configuration/]component/situation/item/Curve1


There is a ’.File Header’ HDF Dataset in the HDF Root Group of the binary file. This dataset is
written as a ’string’ datatype with a fixed length of 80 characters and several lines.

The Situation Group contains one additional HDF Dataset named ’.Analysis’. This dataset is a
’string’ datatype with a fixed length of 40 characters, containing the analysis command of the
situation, e.g. ’STATIC’. It can also contain the Postprocessing Model as a HDF Dataset named
’.Model’.

Each right-hand side of a result item is stored in a HDF Dataset named ’Columni’ with the
column index i of the item. The value (e.g. LPAT, TIME or FREQUENCY) of the Column is
stored in the HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’ at the position i. The label of the result position (node,
element, ...) is stored in the HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’.



V 19.00.287                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                       7-21
e description of the dimensions and the dimensionality is done in FORTRAN notation. The
 ces start with 1, and the first index is running fastest.

ch result HDF Dataset is a two dimensional array for real data and a three dimensional array
he case of complex data. The result data components (e.g. DOFs) are stored in the first
 ension and the datapoints (nodes, elements, ...) in the second dimension of the real data
ay. Complex values are stored as real and imaginary part of the complex data in the first
 ension of the three dimensional array. The result data components are stored in the second
 ension and the datapoints are stored in the third dimension of the three dimensional data
ay.

nodal point results and element results with result data at elements or result data at center
elements have a HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’ which is a vector with the nodal point IDs or the
ment IDs. The values are 64 bit values.

e column description HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’ is a vector with load pattern IDs, column IDs,
e values, frequencies or a text description. The values are 64 bit values, the strings have a
 d length.

Result Item

The Result HDF Group can have some attributes:

Text          : The description of the item
Data Object   : The permas data object label
Data Object2 : Second label for complex results

                                                                                                     PERMAS
Column Descriptor ’.ColDes’

The HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’ is a vector containing the right-hand side description. The IDs are
64 bit values or strings with a length of 40 characters. The type depends on the analysis:

integer   : The value is an integer for all results with LPAT or COLUMN as descriptor
float     : The value is a float for all other results e.g TIME, FREQUENCY . . .
string    : A string used for a better readability of some verification results e.g. ’Surface Nor-
            mal’ of the ’Surface System’.

The vector length matches the number of HDF Dataset ’Columns’. The position in the vector
belongs to the ’Column’ with the ID of the position (we start the counting at ONE).
 Position 7 belongs to Column7

The column descriptor may have an attribute named Label which contains the column type
label as a string with a length of 12 characters. Its content can be ’LPAT’, ’Time’, ’Frequency’,
. . ..




V 19.00.287                   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          7-23
Original Column ID: This attribute contains the Column ID of the result column. This is
          important for e.g. an eigenvalue analysis, or if not all columns are written on the
          HDF file.

Column type label: The Column type label attribute is introduced to have an additional easy
         access to the same data as in the column descriptor. Its name is taken from the
         contents of the column descriptor attribute ’Label’ (e.g. LPAT . . .). The value is the
         value from the HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’.

sult Items for Nodal Point Data

e HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’ is a vector with the nodal point IDs. The IDs are 64 bit integer
ues.

columns have the same dimension. The values are 32 or 64 bit values according the default
ing

cified at the beginning of the UCI-file by DEFAULT (see page 2-66 ff.). They are, according
he analysis result:

l      : It is a two dimensional HDF Dataset. The result data columns are the first dimen-

         with the dimension of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.
mplex : It is a three dimensional HDF Dataset. The first dimension is two and contains
        the real and imaginary part of the complex value. The result data columns are
        the second dimension and the nodes are the third dimension. The third dimension
        matches with the dimension of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.

cified at the beginning of the UCI-file by DEFAULT (see page 2-66 ff.). They are, according

 4                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           V 19.00.287
Result Items for Distributed Element Data

The HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’ is two dimensional with the element IDs, which are 64 bit integer
values. The first dimension is THREE. The first value is the element ID, the second the row
pack value and the third the start pointer to the column data.

All columns have the same dimension. The values are 32 or 64 bit values according the default
setting

                           DEFAULT SET HDF_DATASIZE = 32 or 64

specified at the beginning of the UCI-file by DEFAULT (see page 2-66 ff.). They are, according
to the analysis result:

real     : It is a one dimensional HDF Dataset. The result data columns are stored in the
           second value of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.
complex : It is a two dimensional HDF Dataset. The first dimension is two and contains the
          real and imaginary part of the complex value. The result data columns are stored
          in the second value of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.


Row pack rule attributes




                                                                                                    Export to
                                                                                                    PERMAS
Code C2 : This attribute contains the row pack rule for ’.RowDes’ column 2 (e.g. 2.3.2.5). It
          is a decimal coded value with following meaning described from right to left. Each
          field shows the width of its decimal portion. The ’Most Right’ value ’Pos 1’ must be
          used to get the correct data length. The other values can be used for displaying the
          data.
           P os1 : This portion is (in this example) 5 digits wide and holds the number of values
                   for this element.
           P os2 : This portion is (in this example) 2 digits wide and holds the dimension of
                   ONE data point, e.g. 6 for Tensor, 3 for vector, 1 for scalar.
           P os3 : This portion is (in this example) 3 digits wide and holds the number of layer
                   or ZERO if not layered.
           P os4 : This portion is (in this example) 2 digits wide and holds the data point code
                   for data display.
                   0      : No explicit position
                   1      : Data at center of element
                   2      : Data at element nodes
                   3      : Data at layer center
                   4      : Data at all layer for all nodes
                   5      : Data at all nodes for all layer

Example program to read one data block

The following program shows an example how to read one data item from file.

       CHARACTER LINE*80,FORM*80,NAMOBJ*13,TEXT*40
       DIMENSION DATA(6)
       LOGICAL   END
C
         ..............
         Next data item
         ..............

C--< Read one complete data block>-------------------------------------
C
      CALL RDBLOC(IUNIT, N A M O B J , T E X T , L I N E S , F O R M )
C
 1000 CONTINUE




                                                                                                    Export to
                                                                                                    PERMAS
C
C Read one data line
      CALL RDLINE(IUNIT,FORM,LINES,NCOL, N O P , D A T A , L I N E ,
     *            E N D )
      IF( .NOT. END )THEN
C
C Save line in own data structure
          CALL XXSAV(NOP,DATA,NCOL)
          GOTO 1000
      ENDIF
C-------< Data block processed >--------------------------------------
C
        .............
        .............
        .............
C
      STOP
      END




V 19.00.287                 PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                          7-333
Read one data line from result file

--> IUNIT : FORTRAN unit number
--> FORM    : Format specification
--> NLINES : Number of lines to process
--> NCOL    : Number of columns in data line
<-- NOPOEL : Nodal point or element number
<-- DATA    : Numerical values
<-- LINE    : Last line if end of block was found (character*80)
<-- END     : .TRUE. if end of data line was found
----------------------------------------------------------------------
(C) Copyright INTES GmbH, Stuttgart, Germany
-----------------------------------------------
    CHARACTER*(*) FORM,LINE
    LOGICAL        END
    DIMENSION      DATA(*)
    CHARACTER*80 LINES(100)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

                            ... Read in line and test for end of block
     READ(IUNIT,’(A80)’)LINES(1)
     IF( LINES(1)(1:1) .EQ. ’$’)THEN
         END = .TRUE.
         LINE = LINES(1)
         GOTO 999
     ENDIF

Next line found get rest of data
    IF( NLINES .GT. 1 )THEN
        DO 10 I=2,NLINES
           READ(IUNIT,’(A80)’)LINES(I)
 10     CONTINUE
    ENDIF

Convert data
    READ(LINES,FORM)NOPOEL,(DATA(I),I=1,NCOL)
    END = .FALSE.
---
999 CONTINUE
    RETURN
    END




34                PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)               V 19.00.287
C
C Get information from data comment block
C
C --> IUNIT : FORTRAN unit with connected input file
C <-- NAMOBJ: Name of data object
C <-- TEXT : Description text from data object
C <-- LINES : Number of lines for one data item
C <-- FORM : Fortran format to convert data
C-----------------------------------------------------------------------
C (C) Copyright INTES GmbH, Stuttgart, Germany
C!-----------------------------------------------
      CHARACTER*(*) NAMOBJ,TEXT,FORM
      CHARACTER      INAM*13,ITEXT*40,FFORM*65
C-----------------------------------------------------------------------
C
      NAMOBJ = ’ ’
      TEXT   = ’ ’
      FORM   = ’ ’
C
C Get book name and text
      READ(IUNIT,’(16X,A13,7X,A40)’)INAM,ITEXT
      NAMOBJ = INAM
      TEXT   = ITEXT
C
C Get number of lines




                                                                                   Export to
                                                                                   PERMAS
      READ(IUNIT,’(11X,I9)’)LINES
C
C Get format for data line
      READ(IUNIT,’(10X,A65)’)FFORM
      FORM = FFORM
C
C Skip next line
      READ(IUNIT,’(A65)’)FFORM
C----
      RETURN
      END

marks:

1. The file extension may be written in upper or lowercase letters, depending on the actual
   machine.

2. ASCII output is not supported for the results and the postprocessing model.
   The XY-data and SUM items are done as ASCII output.

3. The default names for a PERMAS situation and component are assigned if a foreign input
   door contains no explicit specification of the names.

4. The number of digits of the task loop identifier is evaluated from the number of loops in
   the TASK LOOP. (e.g. 100 leads to a 3 digit task identifier).

7.4.1 File Management

The output of the selected items (see page 2-373 ff. of the PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)
) to the HyperView interface is done on one file. The default parameter POSTCAT (DEFAULT
(see page 2-66 ff.)) has no influence on the export process.


Naming rule for export files:


            (< project >)(< sit >)(< comp >)(< combine >)(< task >).H3D




Parameter       Type   Explanation

< project >    name    Project description.
                       Part of the filename if only one situation is defined or the standard situ-
                       ation names (DFLT_SIT) are used
< sit >        name    Name of the result variant.
                       Part of the name in case of several Variants. If the standard name is
                       used, the name is build as S_<icount> instead of the complete name.
< comp >       name    Component name.
                       Part of the filename in case of substructure analysis. If the standard
                       name (DFLT_COMP) is used, the name is build as C_<icount> in-
                       stead of the complete name.




                                                                                                     HyperView
                                                                                                     Export to
< combine >            Identifier for a combined (artificial) model.
                       Only in case of substructuring as appendix to the component name
                       (_C).
< task >               Task loop identifier. Part of the filename in case of export inside a task
                       loop. (-itask). (see remark 4)
H3D                    Is the file extension of the Version 11 HyperView file.


Remarks:

  1. The file extension may be written in upper or lowercase letters, depending on the actual
     machine.



V 19.00.287                 PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                           7-351
4. The number of digits of the task loop identifier is evaluated from the number of loops in
   the TASK LOOP. (e.g. 100 leads to a 3 digit task identifier).

5. The sign of the phase angle of complex results is changed during the export process.
   The formula is in PERMAS u = r ∗ cos(ωt + ϕ)
   and in HyperView u = r ∗ cos(ωt − ϕ).

GRID File Format


     Field-1      Field-2   Field-3    Field-4   Field-5   Field-6   Field-7   Field-8   Field-9

        GRID        ID        CP         X1        X2        X3        CD       PS       SEID

 ID            1 000 000>I>0       Unique nodal point ID
 CP            Integer≥0           Coordinate system ID (always blank)
 X1 thru X3    Real                Nodal point location
 CD            Integer≥0           Displacement coordinate system ID (always blank)
 PS            I≥0 or blank        Permanent single–point constraint (always blank)
 SEID          I≥0 or blank        Superelement ID (always blank)
