36   PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)   V 19.00.287
The degree of anisotropy is a fundamental property of all types of material. In many practical
applications the material behavior can be considered as isotropic and only few constants are
needed to describe it, but some types of material, e.g. fiber-reinforced plastics, wood or rein-
forced concrete show a distinct anisotropic behavior which has to be taken into account. The
description of general anisotropic behavior is an expensive task, so e.g. for the constitutive ma-
trix C which relates stresses and strains in linear elasticity twenty-one independent constants
are needed. Fortunately most anisotropic materials have any planes of symmetry for their be-
havior, reducing the number of independent constants and so the amount of work to describe
it. For user convenience different types of anisotropic behavior are implemented in PERMAS,
identified by their so-called degree of anisotropy.


The simplest case is isotropic material behavior. No dependency on orientation of material in
space exists, there is an infinite number of planes of material property symmetry.


In contrast, if there is not any plane of material property symmetry, the material is called (gen-
eral) anisotropic or triclinic.


If there is only one plane of material property symmetry the material is called monoclinic.


If there are two orthogonal planes of material property symmetry, symmetry will exist also rel-
ative to a third mutually orthogonal plane. The intersections of the three planes define the
principal directions of the material. Using the principal directions to establish the stress-strain
relation leads to a so-called orthotropic material.


If there is one plane in which all material properties are equal in all directions the material is
called transversely isotropic.

8.7.5 Triclinic or General Anisotropic Material

The linear elastic behavior of triclinic or general anisotropic material is described by twenty-
one independent constants. In PERMAS there are two different options available, degree of
anisotropy = TRICLINIC for input of engineering constants as well as degree of anisotropy =
ANISO for direct definition of the stiffness matrix elements. If engineering constants are input
the following constants are needed: Three Young’s moduli E1 , E2 , E3 , three Poisson’s ratios
ν12 , ν23 , ν13 , three shear moduli G12 , G23 , G31 , nine coefficients of mutual influence (η12,i ,
η23,i , η31,i ), i = 1, 2, 3, and three Chentsov coefficients µ23,12 , µ31,23 , µ31,12 . The corresponding

                                        FD ∼ − sgn(ε̇)ε

If and only if the motion is harmonic, elemental structural damping forces in a linear system
may be formulated according to


                                      F D,E = − igE kE ρE

where kE is the elemental stiffness matrix, gE the structural damping factor of the element and
ρE are the elemental displacements. This leads to a complex elemental stiffness matrix


                                       k̄E = (1 + igE )kE

The structural damping factor gE may depend on frequency. Complex stiffness matrices con-
taining structural damping forces can be processed in frequency response analysis. To include
structural damping forces in transient response analysis, equivalent viscous damping forces
are calculated with the elemental viscous damping matrix

                                                  gE
                                        dg,E =        kE
                                                 2πfE

where fE is the element reference frequency. For a harmonic motion with frequency f = fE the
equivalent viscous damping forces are equal to the structural damping forces, for f > fE the
equivalent viscous damping forces are higher, for f < fE lower than the corresponding struc-
tural damping forces. If the structural damping factor is a function of frequency, for calculation
of the equivalent viscous damping forces the function is evaluated for f = fE .


The structural damping factor gE is assumed to be a scalar quantity, therefore the input does
not depend on the degree of anisotropy of the material. For each kind of homogeneous ma-
terial one damping value or one damping function may be input, using the data block header
$DAMPING.

Since the thermal expansion coefficient may depend on temperature, the thermal strain may
be written as
                                              ZT1

where T0 is the temperature at which the thermal strain is zero. If the thermal expansion
coefficient is constant, the expression reduces to

                                       εϑ (T1 ) = αd (T1 − T0 )

In analogy to that formula for temperature-dependent coefficients a mean value, the total ex-
pansion coefficient α is defined by

                                    εϑ (T1 ) = α(T1 , T0 )(T1 − T0 )

with
                                                          ZT1

                                 α(T1 , T0 ) =                  αd (T )dT
                                               T1 − T0
                                                          T0

The total expansion coefficient describes the thermal expansion between initial temperature T0
and actual temperature T1 , consequently a temperature-dependent coefficient is a function of
both temperatures. Data, however, are available for the thermal expansion between a refer-
ence temperature Tref (e.g. 0◦ C) and actual temperature T1 . Therefore the thermal strain for
temperature-dependent coefficients is calculated according to

                    εϑ (T1 ) = α(T1 , Tref )(T1 − Tref ) − α(T0 , Tref )(T0 − Tref )

If, however, the thermal expansion coefficient does not depend on temperature or temperature-
dependency may be neglected, differential and total coefficient are identical, i.e.                 Material
                                   α = αd     f or    αd = constant

and
                                        εϑ (T1 ) = α (T1 − T0 )

Remarks:

  1. The name rule for complex arithmetics is as follows:
      < label >   basic label with amplitude data.
      < label >F to store the phase data.
      < label >R for the real part.
      < label >I  for the imaginary part.
                                                                                         Appendix




V 19.00.287                  PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)                  F-5
   labels of the corresponding item, leading to following labels:


                                Item                     Name
                                ACCEleration             USASST
                                DISPlacement             USRSST
                                VELOcity                 USVSST
                                ELement STRESS           SIGSST
                                STRESS RESultants        RSFRSST
                                Nodal Point STRESS       NPSTSST
                                     etc.

   Note, that these label names are only defaults and may be changed using RESULT =
   parameter. Therefore, they have to be selected explicitly for export.

3. Random response results may be spectral densities or root mean square values as fol-
   lows:

    < label >SD      to store the spectral density.
    < label >RS      for the RMS-values.

   leading to

                Item                                  Spectral density   RMS value
                Displacement                          USRSD              USRRS
                Velocity                              USVSD              USVRS
                Acceleration                          USASD              USARS
                Element stress                        SIGSD              SIGRS
                Element stress resultants             RSFRSD             RSFRRS
                von Mises element stress              —                  EMISRS
                von Mises element stress at node      —                  EMISENRS


4. XY data is stored in two data objects with the following convention:
    < prename >X descriptor table with curve names.
    < prename >Y data sequence with curves.
   The prename has at most 5 characters.
